stories.Headline: Microsoft, Alphabet Set to Report Q3 Earnings. Who’s Spending More on AI Buildout?
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and Alphabet were due to report quarterly earnings on Wednesday after the US market close, following a Federal Reserve rate decision at 2 p.m. Alphabet's call was set for 4:30 p.m. ET and Microsoft's for 5:30 p.m. The reports were being watched as a test of whether the huge spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure is paying off. Amazon was also reporting that week, and one analyst warned that merely beating the numbers and nudging up guidance would not win applause.

The expectations were specific. For its fiscal first quarter, Microsoft was forecast to post about $90.6 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings of $4.71 per share, implying roughly 17% revenue growth and 14% earnings growth. Alphabet was expected to report $127.9 billion in revenue and $3.00 per share, about 25% sales growth and 4.5% earnings growth. Azure's benchmark was 45% growth at constant exchange rates, and Microsoft had earlier forecast more than $50 billion in quarterly capital spending. On the Alphabet side, Google Cloud revenue rose 82% to $24.8 billion in the June quarter, while its annual capital spending forecast stood at $195 billion to $205 billion.

The companies' own recent figures frame the pressure. Microsoft said demand kept exceeding its available capacity and reported more than 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats in its June-quarter results. Alphabet's operating cash flow of $39.1 billion in that quarter was outpaced by $44.9 billion in capital spending, leaving free cash flow negative by about $5.9 billion. Its June-quarter earnings of $9.11 per share were lifted by large unrealized investment gains, which can distort comparisons. Stephen Innes of SPI Asset Management said investors want to know whether the compute buildout is creating a lasting earnings engine or just a bigger spending drain.

The backdrop was shaky, with AI-linked stocks struggling through October and weak results from Tesla and Meta adding to worries. All three major Wall Street indexes closed lower on Friday, and Asian chip stocks fell on Monday, though Hong Kong and Shanghai edged higher. Rising rates and bond yields added to the strain, and the Fed was widely expected to hold rates after last month's increase. By Thursday, the outlook had shifted for Korea's market: after the Fed held steady, the Kospi opened slightly higher, and Samsung Electronics reported a record profit of $80.4 billion that topped Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta. Earlier in the week, SK hynix's record earnings had pushed the Kospi up 6.63 percent and above 6,000.

stories.Headline: Open-source project aims for AI-assisted development control plane
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has moved its monorepo from Git to a new source control system called Scion, and it described the migration in a 13 October engineering post. A separate open-source project named SYSTEM-ENGINEERING is exploring an Engineering Control Plane for AI-assisted development, according to TechGig. Scion shifts commits, merges, rebases, history and blame queries to the server side, with clients keeping bounded object caches and virtualised checkouts that fetch files only when needed. Tools can also query diffs and perform some writes through APIs without checking out any code.

The numbers behind the move are large. Daily merged changes rose from around 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September, and the company's CI systems run roughly 25 million checkouts every day. The monorepo has nearly 100 GB of main-branch history and a compressed working copy above 25 GB. Anthropic reports cache-hit rates above 99% at each tier, an infrastructure footprint for CPU and memory 200 times smaller than its earlier Git mirrors, and checkout speedups of two orders of magnitude for CI and research jobs. Checkouts run through a node-local daemon that shares cached objects across jobs and fetches from regional caches, which in turn draw on authoritative servers backed by Spanner and cloud storage.

Anthropic is responsible for Scion, and it says the design trades offline independence for less local data and shared infrastructure. The company stresses that Scion is not a general-purpose replacement for Git, since it needs its own code-review, code-search and CI systems and its implementations are highly bespoke. It suggests that other teams instead bring selected ideas, such as comprehensive server-side APIs and improved fetch protocols, into existing Git platforms. InfoQ noted that the performance figures are company-reported results for Anthropic's internal workload, not general benchmarks against Git. On the SYSTEM-ENGINEERING project, TechGig says the aim is to add structure around AI-assisted workflows rather than simply adding more agents or connecting more tools, and the project asks for community feedback on its architecture, agent orchestration, reliability mechanisms, memory and continuity, and developer experience.

For context, the problems Anthropic describes had grown harder to manage over time. It had relied on shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes, repository snapshots and several hundred Git mirrors, but found them harder to operate as merge rates climbed. InfoQ compared Scion with Uber's GitFarm, which centralises standard Git operations without replacing the source-control system, and said Scion goes further by changing the underlying data model. In a 15 October update, Anthropic credited Mononoke and its Bonsai data model with pioneering many of the techniques it uses. InfoQ's takeaway for architects is that repository queries do not always need local checkouts and that immutable objects can be shared through caches, though Scion depends on server availability and requires substantial integration work.

stories.Headline: Meta’s Pullback Just Changed The AI Risk/Reward (NASDAQ:META)
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms shares fell about 7 per cent after the company reported third-quarter results and told investors it would need to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over the coming years to fund its artificial intelligence plans, possibly beginning this autumn. The drop erased more than $124bn of market value, though the company is still worth almost $1.65trn. The Nasdaq fell 2.6 per cent, its steepest one-day decline since June, as doubts spread over whether huge AI outlays will turn into profits. Other tech names fell as well, with Nvidia down 4.4 per cent, AMD down 8.1 per cent, Micron down 6.3 per cent and CoreWeave down 10.1 per cent.

The key figure was Meta's disclosure that it has signed lease agreements and other non-cancelable commitments totaling about $825bn for its AI business, up from the near-$700bn it reported in July. Those commitments cover data centre and energy infrastructure leases, computing power, hardware and cloud capacity. Third-quarter revenue came in at $64.6bn for the three months to 30 September, compared with $51.2bn a year earlier. Free cash flow swung to a deficit of $2.1bn from a surplus of $10.6bn a year before. The S&P 500 slid 1.21 per cent to 7,663.43 and the Nasdaq closed at 26,008.86, while the Dow was roughly flat at 52,867.98.

The company itself set out the funding need and the spending commitments, and a Seeking Alpha contributor noted that a $25 billion common stock raise and convertible financing add to dilution worries, with 2027 capital spending still unclear. The same analyst said the advertising business remains strong, with impressions up 10 per cent and average price per ad up 14 per cent year over year, and that AI has lifted app ad conversions by 9.6 per cent. On the market side, JPMorgan told clients that sentiment around AI funding remains unstable. James McCann of Edward Jones said investors want more proof of returns on AI spending and worry about its sustainability at high interest rates, adding that the firm stays positive on large-cap stocks but advises diversification.

The selloff came amid other pressures. Meta plans to cut about 8,000 jobs, as Reuters reported in April, and a New Mexico judge ordered it to pay $25bn over its handling of Facebook user data, a ruling Meta plans to appeal. Oil also jumped, with Brent crude settling at $113.17 a barrel, its highest since May, after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reports of possible strikes on Iran. Safe-haven buying pushed the 10-year Treasury yield down more than 18 basis points to 4.965 per cent. The articles do not say when Meta will launch its fundraising, beyond the possibility of this autumn.

stories.Headline: Texas sues OpenAI over ChatGPT safety claims and alleged harm to minors
stories.Summary:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has sued OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, accusing them of deceiving consumers about the safety of ChatGPT and failing to protect users, including children. According to one of the articles, the suit was filed on October 23 in Collin County, under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer Protection Act. It names San Francisco-based OpenAI Global LLC and argues the company sold ChatGPT as a safe and reliable tool while releasing an undertrained product without adequate guardrails. The filing says the chatbot can produce inaccurate or damaging information, and that the company put market dominance ahead of user safety.

The complaint lists several alleged harms. It says vulnerable users have been steered toward self-harm, minors have come to rely on the software without parental supervision, professionals have been publicly embarrassed by wrong outputs, and some people have used the product to seek help with violent acts. It also says ChatGPT lacks adequate age verification and parental consent mechanisms. The state asks for injunctive relief and financial penalties, and a third report says it also wants to block minors' access to ChatGPT and require independent safety reviews of new AI models. The filing also points out that OpenAI began in 2015 as a non-profit meant to advance digital intelligence for public benefit, and contrasts that with its current commercial growth.

Paxton said in a statement that OpenAI has a responsibility to protect users and warn them of the dangers of its platform. He added that he will fight to protect Texans from the harms of AI and make sure powerful technology companies are not above the law. An OpenAI spokesperson responded that the company has worked closely with experts to keep improving ChatGPT, reduce risks and add safeguards. The spokesperson said governments have an important role in setting strong AI safety standards, and that OpenAI wants to work with Texas and other states on practical policies covering the whole industry, not just one company.

Texas is not alone. Eight states, including Idaho, Arkansas, Montana, Nebraska, West Virginia, Iowa, Kansas and Arizona, have filed separate suits against OpenAI, according to the other reports. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador filed a 107-page complaint in Ada County on October 14, alleging violations of the Idaho Consumer Protection Act. He seeks a $5,000 payment to the state for each violation, along with damages and restitution, and wants the company barred from testing advanced AI models outside a secured, independently verified environment. OpenAI says it has added parental controls, break reminders, age-prediction tools and a teen-focused experience, and worked with more than 170 mental health experts in late 2025 to improve how its models handle sensitive conversations.

stories.Headline: Presidio Integrates Cisco IQ with Presidio Advisor to Deliver Proactive, AI-Powered Technology Lifecycle Management
stories.Summary:
Presidio announced that it has integrated Cisco IQ with Presidio Advisor to deliver proactive, AI-powered technology lifecycle management. The articles provided do not describe the Presidio integration itself, so its details are not covered here. What they do cover is the Cisco news that sits behind it: on Oct. 26, 2026, at Cisco Partner Summit in Vancouver, Cisco announced the general availability of Cisco IQ for partners. Cisco IQ is the company's AI-powered support and lifecycle platform, and Network World reported on Oct. 27 and 28 that partners now see the same installed-base data that Cisco does. Cisco also introduced new program updates and AI-ready infrastructure offerings at the same event.

Cisco said Cisco IQ already serves more than 16,000 customers, with visibility across close to 20 million devices since April 2026. Partners can now use a Model Context Protocol server and expanded API access to build the platform's intelligence into their own services, workflows and AI agents. A new role-based access control feature lets customers give resellers direct, secure visibility into their installed base. Cisco also announced Cisco IQ capabilities for customers and partners, including playbooks for quantum-safe readiness and software end of vulnerability support, plus assessments of priority bugs and software conformance. Partners will also be able to deliver Cisco IQ support under their own brand through a service called Cisco IQ Partner Support Standard.

On the incentive side, Cisco raised the Cisco Partner Incentive reward for annual contract value growth by 50 percent and doubled the Adopt rate for all use cases. It added a new Adopt incentive tied to Cisco IQ, plus an extra 2 percent cross-sell bonus for Preferred and Portfolio partners who expand customers into new Cisco architectures, including Splunk. Cisco also launched Ecosystem Deal Registration so advisors and developers get formal credit for contributions that lead to deals. Partner Value Indexes for advisors and developers are available now, and a unified one for distributors is due by Spring 2027.

Tim Coogan, Cisco's senior vice president of global partner sales, said customers need partners who can move first and fast, and that the updates are meant to reward every type of partner. Liz Centoni, Cisco's chief customer experience officer, said partners used to enter customer conversations without the view Cisco had, and that the change gives them that intelligence under their own name. Jeetu Patel, Cisco's president and chief product officer, said that letting partners fine-tune and customize Cisco's models for their customers would make them central to how customers run their infrastructure. Analyst Zeus Kerravala wrote in Network World that partners are now more strategic to Cisco than ever.

Kerravala noted that roughly 90 percent of Cisco's bookings flow through partners, so changes to the channel eventually reach customers. He said customers should expect a partner's first meeting to start with data about what is vulnerable and past its last day of support, rather than a quote. He also advised customers to check how issues escalate back to Cisco when a partner delivers Cisco IQ support under its own brand. As an example of the results, he said insurer Generali cut the time to assess one security advisory across 16,000 devices from four days to 10 minutes. Cisco said support for Live Protect on its secure routers and firewalls is intended to arrive by the end of 2026.

stories.Headline: IIT-Kharagpur Establishes India's First Physical AI School
stories.Summary:
IIT-Kharagpur announced on Monday, October 26, 2026, that it will set up India's first dedicated academic school for Physical Artificial Intelligence, to be called the Benjamin Gupta School of Physical AI. The plan rests on a memorandum of understanding signed by the institute, its alumnus and philanthropist Vinod Gupta, and the IITKGP Foundation USA. The school is named in memory of Gupta's late son, Benjamin Gupta. It will house the institute's Department of Artificial Intelligence and support academic and research work across disciplines.

The total investment is Rs 35 crore. The Vinod Gupta family will put in Rs 12.5 crore, an anonymous alumnus will give Rs 10 crore, and the institute will cover the remaining Rs 12.5 crore. The school will concentrate on physics-informed machine learning, scientific AI, digital twins, intelligent robotics, autonomous systems, advanced sensing and AI-enabled experimentation. It aims to build AI that is reliable, explainable and responsible, especially for safety-critical uses where physical accuracy, robustness and accountability matter. Academic programmes are expected to start in the upcoming session, subject to necessary approvals, and will serve students, researchers and working professionals from engineering, physical sciences, life sciences and medicine.

Institute director Suman Chakraborty said AI has changed how information is processed, and that its next big step will be in how people understand, engineer and interact with the physical world. He said IIT-Kharagpur hopes to lead that shift in India through the new school. According to him, the effort will try to move past treating AI as a black box, and will encourage professionals to pair algorithmic tools with basic scientific and domain knowledge. The school is also meant to bring together academia, industry, healthcare institutions, research laboratories, startups and international partners to speed up research, technology development and reskilling.

Physical AI differs from conventional AI, which mainly relies on data, algorithms and digital applications, because it aims to build systems that understand and act in the physical world using scientific principles, real-world sensing and intelligent control. One report notes that the announcement gives no confirmed admission schedule or application deadline, and does not list course structure, eligibility, duration or fees. It also names no specific partner organisations or collaborative projects. Anyone interested in the programmes is advised to wait for official details from the institute rather than assume applications are open.

stories.Headline: PA Senator's Bill Would Ban AI for Student Mental Health
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania state Sen. Nick Miller, a Democrat who represents parts of Lehigh and Northampton Counties, has introduced a bill that would bar schools from using artificial intelligence to counsel struggling students. The proposal, Senate Bill 1505, was reported on October 27 and 28, 2026, and it follows a memo Miller circulated to House members laying out his case. It is meant as a companion to upcoming House legislation from Rep. Melissa L. Shusterman, whose own measure shares the title Prohibiting Artificial Intelligence for Student Mental Health Services. The bill now awaits deliberation in the Senate Education Committee.

Under the bill, schools could not use AI to provide mental or behavioral health services that would otherwise be performed by mental health professionals. The ban would not reach the paperwork side of the job, since mental health professionals could still use AI for administrative functions such as scheduling, organizing records and managing files. Miller argues that AI can produce inaccurate or unsafe advice and lacks the professional judgment needed to recognize and respond to a student in crisis. The reports describe the bill as a way to keep that kind of care in the hands of trained people.

Miller said that students who are struggling should be able to rely on trusted adults at school. In his view, technology should support the relationships at the heart of a student's mental health care rather than take their place. He has not said anything beyond that in the coverage, and the bill has not yet moved out of committee. Shusterman's House proposal is described as forthcoming, so both chambers have yet to act.

The proposal comes as schools nationwide turn to AI tools to fill gaps left by counselor shortages. CDC figures cited by EdSource show about 40% of high school students experienced persistent sadness or hopelessness, and roughly 20% seriously considered suicide in 2023. RAND researchers found about one in five adolescents already use AI chatbots for mental health advice, and at least 200 schools in 19 states have partnered with Alongside to offer its Kiwi chatbot to students in grades four through 12. State approaches vary, with Nevada generally barring psychotherapists from using AI beyond administrative tasks, while Colorado and Maine allow some uses if a clinician reviews the output. Pennsylvania has not issued formal AI guidance for education, though at least 35 states have, and House Education Committee members have been gathering input from educators and experts on possible legislation.

stories.Headline: Anne Arundel superintendent seeks feedback on AI and device ban in schools
stories.Summary:
Anne Arundel County Public Schools Superintendent Mark Bedell has begun gathering community feedback on a proposed ban on electronic devices and on how artificial intelligence should be used in schools. The first public session, which he calls a Community Connection Session, was held on Tuesday at a high school in the county. At these events, teachers, parents and other community members are split into small groups so each person can say what they think. The sessions are hosted by Bedell himself and move from school to school across the county.

The county school board has introduced a new policy that would set limits on the use of AI in schools. The board is also looking to bar cell phones, smart watches and other electronic devices during the school day. The personal electronics ban is set to begin next school year, and the small groups discussed what it will look like in practice. Six more sessions are planned, each from 6 to 8 p.m.: Monday, November 2, at Glen Burnie High School; Thursday, November 5, at Northeast High School; Tuesday, November 10, at Arundel High School; Thursday, November 12, at Southern High School; Tuesday, November 17, at Annapolis High School; and Thursday, November 19, at Meade High School.

Bedell said he wanted to meet people face to face because residents too often feel that decisions are made without them. He noted that people frequently show up at school board meetings to say they had no idea a policy was being written and no chance to weigh in. On AI, he said the goal is for students to become skilled users of the technology rather than being used by it, while still keeping the traditional parts of schooling. He added that students will graduate into a world where they must work with AI, and the conversations should help the district find a balance.

On the device ban, Bedell said schools have students for about 19.3% of the week and that he wants that time devoted to teaching and learning. Students have the remaining 81% of the time to decide how to use their own technology, he said, and he described the law as calling for students to engage in collaboration while at school. He urged families to attend the remaining sessions, saying the district is asking for opinions on highly controversial subjects and needs to understand what people expect from the education of students in the county. Both topics have already drawn strong opinions on all sides in the community.

stories.Headline: AI at Wake Forest: What the AI Task Force is doing and how you can help shape what’s next
stories.Summary:
Wake Forest University's AI Task Force, chaired by William Fleeson, associate provost for AI initiatives and Hultquist Family Professor of Psychology, shared a question-and-answer update on its work on October 28, 2026. The group's main job this year is to develop an overall academic strategy for AI, and it is also supporting three pilot programs under an initiative called AI for Human Flourishing. Members come from academic affairs, research, the library, information technology, and personal and career development, and include Andy Chan, Anne Hardcastle, Kim McAllister, Mur Muchane and Lauren Pressley. Separately, Cleveland Clinic's Cancer Institute formalized a strategic approach to evaluating emerging AI technologies, according to an article dated October 26, 2026. At Wake Forest, the three faculty-led pilots are already underway.

The AI Teaching Studio, directed by Fleeson, is working across 12 priority areas covering faculty development, course design, departmental engagement and institutional planning. AI Compass, led by Ana Iltis, has funded 17 research and scholarship projects on how AI affects human identity, health and societal well-being. The AI Impact Clinic, a new computer science and business course designed by Shannon McKeen, Paul Pauca and Errin Fulp, has 57 students this fall, and selected students will work with faculty in the spring to build AI solutions for clients. The task force said it is not writing a University-wide policy on AI use in individual classrooms, because faculty are best placed to decide given differences among disciplines. The existing Guidelines for Academic Use and Guidelines for Administrative Use stay in effect, and schools and departments have been asked to develop their own approaches this year.

The strategy is still in its early stages, and early ideas will be shared at three town halls hosted with the Faculty Senate: Monday, Nov. 2, 4 to 5 p.m. in Tribble Hall A110, Monday, Nov. 16, 10:30 to 11:30 a.m. in Benson 409, and Wednesday, Dec. 16, 2 to 3 p.m. in Carswell 111/Annenberg Forum. Faculty and staff can also answer the second-year campus AI survey by November 2, which enters them in a drawing for a $100 or $50 gift card at the Deacon Shop, or send feedback to Fleeson directly.

At Cleveland Clinic, the new Cancer Institute Office of Technology and Digital Strategy is led by Dr. Paul Thambi and Dr. Louis Williams. It vets proposals from AI companies, weighing their effect on operations and care delivery and their fit with enterprise goals. Current uses include personalizing radiation doses for lung cancer patients, cutting notetaking time by up to 75%, and streamlining patient referrals. Williams said AI will be fundamental to running the institute, and that it must reduce barriers to adoption while keeping proper governance. The enterprise AI Task Force, which Williams compared to an institutional review board for non-research applications, checks safety, bias and data security, and monitors models for changes in performance over time.

stories.Headline: SK Hynix unveils $45 billion shareholder returns from AI profits
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix, the world's second-biggest memory chipmaker, announced plans to return about $45 billion to shareholders after its profit surged roughly seven-fold, well ahead of expectations. The company reported an operating profit of 83.3 trillion won for the September quarter, more than 7% above projections, and said it would pay out 60 trillion won in the rest of the fiscal year through buybacks and dividends. That sum comes on top of a previously announced 40 trillion won. A large share of the gains came from a stock sale in Kioxia Holdings earlier this year, and the company's shares rose more than 4% in early Seoul trading.

The results rest on demand from artificial intelligence developers building data centers, which has driven up prices for memory chips. SK Hynix said it expects shortages of components used in Nvidia accelerators to last through at least 2030, which keeps prices high. Research from Macquarie suggests memory now makes up about a third of AI data center costs, and high-bandwidth memory prices are expected to more than double in 2027. Counterpoint Research's MS Hwang said the earnings jump owes much to rising prices for conventional DRAM and NAND chips, and that quarterly earnings have not yet peaked. The company has also prioritized long-term contracts with customers such as Nvidia.

The announcement follows the company's decision to abandon a potential $10 billion U.S. listing of its Solidigm unit after shareholder opposition and regulatory scrutiny. Bloomberg News reported that Solidigm is in talks with the U.S. Commerce Department about investing $45 billion in a new chip plant on American soil. Several other AI-linked firms, including Firmus Grid and AirTrunk, have also shelved public offerings amid growing worries about an AI bubble. The payouts could give the stock another lift, though the wider market remains sensitive to doubts about financing large AI infrastructure projects.

A separate report from The Elec, published October 15, 2026, describes SK Hynix research into 3D FeNAND memory that performs AI calculations inside the chip itself. The company disclosed the work in a newsroom post on October 14 and said the findings appeared in a paper from the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. Simulations showed up to 20 times higher throughput and 5,000 times greater energy efficiency than conventional nonvolatile memory. The research is still at the simulation stage, so its path to commercial products is unclear from the articles.

stories.Headline: Samsung's AI boom comes with a $100 billion warning
stories.Summary:
The Bank of Korea has warned that South Korea's semiconductor exports could fall by $50 billion to $100 billion next year if major U.S. technology companies cut their spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to a Reuters report picked up by TheStreet on October 27, 2026. The warning comes as Samsung Electronics enjoys one of the largest profit surges in technology history. In its gloomy scenario, the central bank assumes Korean semiconductor prices drop by 10%. That would trim South Korea's economic growth by about 0.4 percentage points and shrink its current-account surplus well below the bank's earlier forecast for 2027.

The article lays out the scale of the spending behind the boom. Combined capital expenditure at Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle has risen from $40 billion last year to $80 billion this year, and is expected to reach $110 billion next year. Samsung expects third-quarter operating profit of about 107.4 trillion won on sales of roughly 195 trillion won, nearly nine times the profit of a year earlier. In the second quarter, it reported sales of 171.5 trillion won and operating profit of 89.49 trillion won. SK Hynix, which began trading U.S. depositary receipts on Nasdaq under the symbol SKHY in July, posted second-quarter revenue of 79.3 trillion won, up 257%, and operating profit of 60.5 trillion won, up 557%.

The Bank of Korea is the source of the warning, and it has said the semiconductor cycle is one of the biggest uncertainties in its outlook. Its August forecast assumed that global AI infrastructure investment would keep growing and support strong chip exports into 2027. The bank's new scenario puts a dollar figure on what happens if that assumption fails. South Korea's economy grew 1% in the third quarter, ahead of the 0.7% that economists polled by Reuters had expected, and exports in the first nine months of 2026 passed $800 billion, already above any previous full year.

The article places the warning in the context of a memory market that has always moved in cycles, with prices and profits climbing when supply is short and falling when it is plentiful. Samsung shares have dropped more than 25% from their June peak despite the record results, as investors question how long the boom will last. TrendForce expects DRAM contract prices to rise only 10% to 15% in the fourth quarter, after a nearly 60% jump in the second. Samsung reports detailed third-quarter results on October 29, giving investors another look at memory profitability and management's view of AI demand.

stories.Headline: ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reclaims top spot in China’s rich list, thanks to his firm's AI push
stories.Summary:
The 2026 Hurun China Rich List, released on October 27 with wealth calculated as of September 1, 2026, put ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming back in first place. His fortune rose by 200 billion yuan from a year earlier to 670 billion yuan, which makes him China's richest person for the second time and sets a new record for the highest net worth on the list. ByteDance is not publicly listed, so his figure comes from the company's valuation and his shareholding. Hurun values ByteDance at about 3.3 trillion yuan, with Zhang holding more than 20%. On the same basis his 470 billion yuan of last year implied a valuation of about 2.3 trillion yuan, so the company's value is estimated to have grown by roughly 1 trillion yuan in a year.

AI is the main force behind the reshuffle, and Hurun calls it the single largest engine of wealth growth this year. Entrepreneurs whose core business is AI now make up 10.4% of everyone on the list, more than 160 people, compared with none on the 2019 list and earlier. Liang Wenfeng, founder of DeepSeek, debuted at 7th place with 280 billion yuan, and Wang Xingxing of Unitree Robotics entered at 69.5 billion yuan, second among new entrants after Liang. Zhipu AI's Liu Debing and Tang Jie have 39.5 billion and 27.5 billion yuan, MiniMax founder Yan Junjie has 22.5 billion yuan, and Moonshot AI founder Yang Zhilin is the richest self-made entrepreneur under 35. In the computing power chain, Cambricon's Chen Tianshi gained 25 billion yuan to reach 205 billion yuan and entered the top 10 for the first time, while the wealth of the Lin Congji family of Chuan Hwa Technology rose by 104 billion yuan, or 335%.

Others fell back. Lei Jun of Xiaomi lost 157 billion yuan, the largest drop of the year, going from 326 billion to 169 billion yuan, and Zhong Shanshan of Nongfu Spring lost 120 billion yuan, slipping to second place with 410 billion yuan. Tencent's Ma Huateng lost 119 billion yuan and ranks 4th with 346 billion yuan, Pinduoduo's Huang Zheng lost 112 billion yuan and dropped to 11th, and the Wang Ning family of Pop Mart lost 94.5 billion yuan. In all, 167 entrepreneurs left the list, among them Huang Wei of Unisound and the 4Paradigm couple Dai Wenyuan and Wu Ming, mainly because of stock price corrections.

Hurun attributes some of these declines to a correction from a high base, since Lei, Zhong, Ma and Wang saw fast gains the year before and still hold more than they did two years ago. It also stresses that paper wealth is not the same as profit, because some fortunes rest on steady cash flow while others reflect what the capital market will pay for future growth. DeepSeek's value is hard to pin down: a July investment announcement implied about 350.9 billion yuan, and media reports in October said it was seeking a second round at a pre-money valuation of about 500 billion yuan, which the company has not confirmed. A February Reuters report said General Atlantic planned to sell some ByteDance shares at a 550 billion US dollar valuation, though that deal was not confirmed and a minority stake price does not equal the value of the whole firm.

stories.Headline: BigBear.ai Q3 Earnings Call Highlights
stories.Summary:
BigBear.ai reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 27, saying revenue rose 31% from a year earlier to $43.6 million and raising its full-year revenue outlook. Gross margin widened to 31.2%, up 878 basis points, which Chief Financial Officer Sean Ricker credited largely to the generative AI platform the company bought as Ask Sage in December 2025. Despite the operating gains, the company posted a net loss of $91.9 million, or $0.19 per share, against net income of $2.5 million a year earlier. Management said the loss was mainly caused by a non-cash goodwill impairment charge of $76.7 million, or $0.16 per share.

The company lifted its 2026 revenue guidance to between $150 million and $165 million, about 5% higher at the midpoint than before and, according to Chief Executive Officer Kevin McAleenan, 23% growth over 2025. McAleenan said it was the first time BigBear.ai had raised its revenue guidance. Adjusted EBITDA was negative $9.1 million, compared with negative $9.4 million in the same quarter last year. Sequential revenue growth sped up to 18.6% in the third quarter from 6.7% in the second, and backlog stood at $330 million, up 22% from the prior quarter. BigBear.ai also said it has announced more than 25 contract wins since the second quarter, worth over $225 million, and more than 45 across the second and third quarters.

Among the wins were two five-year subcontracts supporting U.S. Customs and Border Protection's Targeting and Analysis Systems Program Directorate, one on SAIC's team and one with Unissant. Under the SAIC task order, the company will provide AI and analytics for systems that assess risk tied to travelers and cargo entering the country, while the Unissant work continues software development for vetting workflows. The generative AI platform added enterprise customers including the FBI, U.S. Coast Guard, NASA, the Department of Energy and the Department of Veterans Affairs, and McAleenan said it can run in disconnected and air-gapped settings. Outside government, the company renewed a two-year agreement with Children's Minnesota for digital-twin and predictive-analytics tools that help forecast patient flow and use capacity better.

On the balance sheet, BigBear.ai entered the fourth quarter with nearly $400 million in cash and investments. Ricker said about $17 million of convertible debt matures in December and that the company expects to begin 2027 with no debt. McAleenan described the company as an applied AI business focused on enterprise platforms and mission-specific applications, not AI infrastructure or foundation models, and said its model-agnostic approach lets it use advances from outside AI providers. His top priorities for the rest of the year are revenue growth and pursuing acquisitions that could speed deployment of new technology or widen the company's reach and scale. He pointed to defense modernization, shifting trade flows, rising international travel and pressure on security agencies as longer-term tailwinds, and said the company is positioned for growth in 2027.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind unveils Genie 4 AI world model
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind has unveiled Genie 4, a world model that generates interactive environments in real time, with the announcement coming on October 27, 2026. The system lets users create and move through dynamic worlds, and it calculates physics, character behavior and sound as the scene runs. It builds on Genie 3, which was announced in August 2025 and ran at 720p and 24 frames per second with a visual memory of about 1 minute. DeepMind describes Genie 4 as its first real-time world model to produce audio natively, including ambient noise, music and spoken dialogue.

Users navigate the worlds with standard keyboard controls and can change them mid-session with plain text prompts, such as altering the weather or adding a new character or object. The model draws on the Gemini family, with Gemini Omni shaping the look and behavior of each world and Gemini 3.8 Flash acting as a planner inside the simulation loop. That planner interprets prompts, breaks a goal into steps, checks incoming frames to confirm each step worked, and revises the plan if the world shifts. Google says physical accuracy has improved, with aerodynamics, collisions and environmental resistance rendered more convincingly, and DeepMind calls human motion the biggest leap. In one research demo, a Gemini model split a checkers task into steps, and Genie 4 simulated Apptronik's Apollo humanoid robot playing the game.

Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai called Genie 4 the company's most realistic and interactive world model. Tejas Kulkarni, a research director at Google DeepMind, described the design as a move toward hybrid world models, in which a language model handles structure and narrative while Genie renders the pixels and sound. DeepMind has released Genie 4 as a research preview for trusted testers, through the Project Genie web app and early access to the Gemini API, and access is limited to those testers and select Google AI partners. It has not published benchmark tables for the model.

Developers could use Genie 4 to generate test environments on demand, letting artificial agents practice multi-step tasks in simulation before real-world deployment. The articles also note limits, including sessions that last only a few minutes and objects that drift after repeated prompt edits. Scene consistency reaches up to 2 minutes, double Genie 3, according to a TechCrunch briefing cited by one outlet. Physics inconsistencies may also reduce how far the simulations can be trusted for high-stakes testing.

stories.Headline: In China, the AI bubble has already burst
stories.Summary:
Chinese technology stocks have crashed in recent months as lofty valuations gave way to worries about AI demand and curbs on Chinese exports. The mainland STAR50 index, which tracks AI and semiconductor leaders, has fallen 40% in less than four months, wiping out roughly US$480 billion in market value. China's broad blue-chip index has also dropped about 20% from highs reached in June. The slide has halted a rally that ran for two years, since promises of economic stimulus first sent shares soaring. Reuters reported the story on October 27, 2026.

The damage has been widest among retail favourites. Robot-maker Unitree, whose listing was 8,000 times oversubscribed by retail buyers, has seen its shares halve since trading began in August, while chipmaker CXMT has lost more than a quarter of its value in the past month. Chipmakers MetaX Integrated Circuits and Moore Threads Technology, which jumped 700% and 400% on their market debuts last year, have both halved since July. Optical parts makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology are down roughly 60% from highs in June and July, partly because Washington is moving towards barring them from supplying US data centres. Goldman Sachs figures show AI stocks make up 42% of China's market capitalisation and 57% of turnover across mainland A-shares and Hong Kong H-shares, so few investors in a market dominated by small traders have escaped losses.

Traders pointed to no single trigger for the selloff, though they said high prices, tax bills and the threat of equipment bans in data centres all played a part. Beijing-based fund manager Dong Baozhen said the market had turned into a speculative frenzy and was now seeing the bubble burst. Hong Hao of Lotus Asset Management in Hong Kong said the rout would stop many companies from trying to list. Shanghai fund manager Wang Zhuo argued that chipmakers and AI suppliers will eventually end up in a price war like other Chinese manufacturers, and that all bubbles burst. The China Securities Regulatory Commission did not immediately answer questions sent by Reuters, though the regulator said its chairman, Wu Qing, met market participants earlier in October to hear ideas for improving capital markets.

The rout cuts against official efforts to build a steadier "slow bull" market by cracking down on leverage and high-frequency trading, and state-backed investors had sold into rallies to keep gains in check. Frustration that a theme backed by Beijing has ended so badly has pushed many investors into defensive assets and is likely to slow equity fundraising by tech firms. The STAR50 still trades at around 100 times trailing earnings, down from nearly 250 at its peak, against about 30 for the Nasdaq 100, so some investors fear the fall could deepen before it eases. By contrast, the Nasdaq has slipped only 6% from a record high set three weeks earlier. Some see opportunity, with Goldman Sachs keeping Innolight and CXMT on a revamped recommendation list, and a BNP Paribas strategist saying the market offers openings for careful buyers.

stories.Headline: There are risks when children use AI chatbots. Does Australia's new 'digital duty of care' address them?
stories.Summary:
Australia's federal government passed a digital duty of care bill through the House of Representatives on Wednesday, and it wants the law to ban AI chatbots that try to create "emotional intimacy." Prime minister Anthony Albanese pushed the issue in a heartfelt speech on Tuesday night, saying stories of people treating a chatbot as their best friend should be a wake-up call for parliament. The opposition and One Nation voted against the bill in the lower house. Critics have called it an "Orwellian" system of censorship, a claim communications minister Anika Wells strongly denied.

The framework would apply new online safety standards to social media, games, apps and chatbots. It would place an overarching obligation on tech platforms to provide a safe online environment for all Australians, and it would replace several existing online codes and standards with a broader duty of care. Wells has suggested that content promoting misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be covered. Social media platforms would also have to offer an opt-out from their algorithm and suggested content.

On Wednesday the government accepted amendments from crossbencher Kate Chaney. One adds chatbot activity to the list of harms, requiring platforms to ban material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy and encourages or fosters a child's dependence on it in place of human relationships. The other requires the algorithm opt-out to be accessible, easy to use and prominently available, amid concerns that firms might offer only small or hard-to-find controls. Labor did not accept a proposal from independent MP Sophie Scamps to widen the remit of the telecommunications industry ombudsman, and Wells declined to voice support for the idea.

Telecommunications industry ombudsman Cynthia Gebert said her office would be well placed to act as a watchdog for big tech, and that such a role could be funded by the industry, as ombudsman schemes are in other sectors. She welcomed the way the bill puts the onus on platforms to make things safe, but warned that without an external complaints pathway Australians risk staying stuck with automated responses and escalation procedures that go nowhere. The bill now moves to the Senate, where the Greens have set up an inquiry due to report in late November. The Greens support the bill and want to strengthen it with a right to private legal action and higher penalties, while the Coalition says it will not vote for it, though Labor still hopes to win its support and remains open to amendments. The government hopes to pass the bill by the end of 2026, but its path through the upper house remains unclear.

stories.Headline: Most New Zealanders worry about AI's risks, even as many expect to use it – new survey
stories.Summary:
A survey of 972 New Zealanders, carried out in September, found a public split over the benefits of artificial intelligence but largely united in worry about its risks. It was conducted by John Kerr, a senior research fellow in the Department of Public Health at the University of Otago, and Karaitiana Taiuru, a Māori AI and digital governance expert. Their findings were published on 28 October 2026, ahead of the New Zealand election next month. The results were weighted to reflect the population by age, gender, ethnicity and education.

Opinion on AI itself was evenly divided, with roughly a third of respondents positive, a third neutral and a third negative, yet 57% expected to use it in future. Men were generally more positive than women, and Asian respondents more positive than Māori and Pākehā. For every risk the survey covered, at least 80% of people chose the middle option or higher on the concern scale. The biggest worry was AI-generated images, video or audio used to deceive or harm people, with 74% very or extremely concerned, while environmental impacts ranked lowest, though 51% were still very or extremely concerned. Māori (66%) and Asian respondents (68%) were more likely than Pākehā (57%) to be highly concerned about their data being used without permission, and a similar pattern appeared on overseas data storage, at 62% for Māori, 57% for Asian respondents and 52% for Pākehā.

The authors link the Māori concern to a history in which land, resources and knowledge were taken without consent, and to more recent state surveillance, profiling and misuse of data. They stress that for Māori the issue goes beyond personal privacy to who has authority over Māori data, which is regarded as a taonga. On the political side, the article says New Zealand has so far taken a light-touch approach, reflected in a national strategy released last year that urged the country to "confidently embrace" the technology. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon warned during the 1News leaders' debate of "some serious dangers and evils" linked to AI, and he and Labour leader Chris Hipkins agreed on the need for bipartisan cooperation over regulation. Labour and Opportunity propose an "Office of AI" with strict national guardrails, the Greens want a one-year moratorium on new data centres, and ACT's David Seymour favours using AI to streamline public sector work and having New Zealand act as a "fast follower" of international rules.

Looking ahead, the authors say AI experts have floated a dedicated New Zealand institute to guide policy and oversight, bringing together researchers, policymakers and community groups, while another option is to join international calls for AI companies to slow development and strengthen safeguards. They argue any such body should be built on a genuine Te Tiriti partnership, treat Māori data as a taonga and give sustained funding to Māori-led AI research. They also note that overseas policy responses were not designed around Indigenous rights or Te Tiriti partnerships, and that the risks fall unevenly on Pacific, rainbow and disabled communities, older people, rural communities and those on low incomes. Their view is that New Zealand's approach to regulation should reflect the public's clear concern about AI's risks.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Leases, Amazon Builds: Rival AI Bets Face Earnings Test
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and Amazon are due to report July-September results one day apart, with Microsoft and Alphabet reporting on October 28 and Amazon and Intel following on October 29. The reports put two different data center strategies to the test, Microsoft's approach of leasing capacity and Amazon's approach of building its own. The central question hanging over the earnings week, according to one report, is whether the hundreds of billions poured into AI infrastructure are producing meaningful revenue growth. Investors are watching cloud performance and any changes to capital spending guidance, since Azure ranks as the world's second-largest cloud platform and Google Cloud holds third place.

On the numbers, Wall Street expects Microsoft to post fiscal first-quarter revenue of $90.75 billion, up 17% from a year earlier, with adjusted earnings per share rising 14% to $4.72. Another report put Microsoft's expected revenue at about $90.6 billion to $90.7 billion, within the company's own guidance, with net cash flow topping $8 billion. Alphabet's third-quarter revenue is forecast at $127.83 billion, up 25%, with adjusted profit rising a more modest 3% to $2.97 per share. Amazon is projected to report revenue of $202.20 billion, up 12%, and adjusted profit of $1.98 per share, up 2%. Intel is expected to post revenue up 21% to $16.47 billion and adjusted profit up 72% to $0.40 per share.

The gap between Microsoft and Amazon comes down to how each funds capacity. Microsoft signed more than $130 billion in new lease commitments last quarter but spent just $41 billion in cash. Amazon deployed $54.2 billion in capital expenditure, pushing its cumulative free cash flow for the year to a deficit of $7.6 billion, and it is projected to post net cash outflows for a second straight quarter. Amazon Web Services revenue growth is expected to accelerate to 38.2% from 36.8% in the previous quarter, even as overall revenue growth slows to 12.3% from 19.6%.

For context, the wider technology sector has been mixed. Last week the Invesco QQQ Trust slipped 0.8% and the iShares Semiconductor ETF fell 3.1%, while the iShares software ETF gained 6%. Elsewhere in AI hardware, Oracle said on October 27 that it will install Google's custom TPU chips in its data centers starting next year, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure president Mahesh Thiagarajan rejected the idea that this signals a move away from Nvidia, calling Nvidia's chips the best available. SK hynix reported record third-quarter revenue of 104 trillion won, and its chief financial officer forecast that supply will fall short of demand through 2030. Reuters has reported that Anthropic is eyeing a mid-November public debut at a valuation of up to $1.5 trillion.

stories.Headline: Claude for Legal Artifacts: Guide for Lawyers and Businesses
stories.Summary:
On October 28, 2026, Anthropic announced a gallery of legal artifacts for Claude for Legal, a product it launched in May. The gallery offers editable interfaces for recurring legal tasks such as comparing contract terms, checking citations and tracking matters. Anthropic reports that it has added over 60 legal connectors since the May launch. A review of the announcement by the site Kingy AI says the main benefit is turning a good review method into something repeatable, though it did not test the templates on client matters or measure their accuracy.

The gallery's named workflows include Cite check, Tabular review, a Playbook deviation board, a Jurisdiction survey matrix, a Regulatory horizon scan, a Matter board and Legal intake. Partner examples include Goodwin's AI Governance Benchmark, Foley & Lardner's Obligations Checker and PwC's Subpoena Response Tool, along with Harvey Intake. Five of nine access-to-justice artifacts are named, from Zealous, Mobile Pathways, Rising for Justice and The Access Project, and examples from Legora and Orrick are still forthcoming. Artifact creation is available on Free, Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans, but app connections and persistent storage in artifacts require Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise. Anthropic's US pricing lists Pro at $20 monthly or $200 annually, Max from $100 monthly, Team standard at $25 per seat monthly, and Team premium at $125 per seat monthly.

Responsibility for the results stays with people rather than the tool. Kingy AI stresses that a polished table is not proof of correct legal conclusions, and that a qualified person must check the evidence, protect confidential information and decide who has authority to act. A separate guide from Legal Desire, published October 26, 2026, makes the same point about legal AI generally, noting that the lawyer remains accountable for anything sent to a client or a court. It cites ABA Formal Opinion 512 of July 29, 2024, which applies existing duties of competence, confidentiality, communication, supervision and reasonable fees to generative AI without banning any tool. For England and Wales, it says the Solicitors Regulation Authority holds firms responsible for AI output, and that the High Court has warned that free tools such as ChatGPT cannot do reliable legal research.

On context, Legal Desire sorts legal AI into five groups: research assistants built on legal databases, drafting and contract review tools, eDiscovery review, AI inside practice management software, and general chatbots on enterprise terms. Examples include CoCounsel Legal from Thomson Reuters, Lexis+ with Protégé from LexisNexis, Spellbook, Harvey, Relativity aiR for Review and Clio Manage AI. Kingy AI recommends starting with one narrow, repetitive task whose output a named reviewer can check, using synthetic or redacted documents first. It also advises confirming partner accounts, agreements and pricing, and budgeting for licensing, implementation and review beyond the Claude seat price. Neither article reports a measured improvement in access to justice from the new tools.

stories.Headline: AI chips worth $15.5 million seized at Malaysia airport, Customs authority says
stories.Summary:
Malaysian Customs announced on Oct 28 that it had seized advanced artificial intelligence chips worth about RM49.5 million in October. That figure is roughly S$15.5 million, or about US$12 million. The chips were found on Oct 15 during an inspection at the free trade zone of Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Officials say the seizure is part of a closing net around a syndicate suspected of smuggling high-performance semiconductors through the country's main airport.

The authorities found 30 server units containing the advanced chips. Initial investigations showed that the shipment came from an Asian country and was meant to be re-exported to another country on the continent, a move that required a trade permit. According to the airport's Customs director, the servers were falsely declared as electronic components. The aim, she said, was to send them through Malaysia so that no restrictions would apply when they moved on to the next destination.

The director, Aspalila Ag Tuah, spoke to reporters about the case. She said a Malaysian firm that facilitated the shipment has been called in to help with the investigation. She added that the shipment is suspected to have been carried out by the same network behind a similar smuggling attempt that Customs foiled in June. At least five cases have been linked to the syndicate, with seizures of chips worth more than RM100 million in total, though she declined to give further details because the probe is still ongoing.

The case comes after Malaysia imposed export controls in 2025 on the movement of advanced AI chips of US origin. That step followed pressure from the United States to stem the flow of such chips into China. The articles do not say who is suspected of running the syndicate or name the firms involved beyond the Malaysian company assisting investigators. With the investigation continuing, more details may emerge as officials look into the network and the other cases tied to it.

stories.Headline: AI chip giant SK hynix posts seven-fold surge in quarterly operating profit
stories.Summary:
South Korean chipmaker SK hynix said on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that its operating profit for the July to September quarter rose 632 percent from a year earlier, driven by booming demand for AI semiconductors. The company, a specialist supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia and a pillar of South Korea's tech-led economy, put the figure at 83.33 trillion won, or about $62.8 billion, roughly seven times the year-ago level. Net profit climbed 215.7 percent to 39.77 trillion won, while sales reached 104.61 trillion won. The firm said it has now posted record revenue and operating profit for six straight quarters, going back to the second quarter of last year.

Alongside the results, SK hynix announced a further plan to return 60 trillion won to shareholders, following the completion of an earlier 40 trillion won shareholder return programme. It also said it intends to pass most of the gains from its investment in Japan's Kioxia back to investors through special dividends in the third quarter and at fiscal year-end. Despite the record profit, the net profit figure fell short of expectations, since the average analyst estimate, cited by Yonhap, stood at 59.67 trillion won. Last week the company had also said it would drop a planned US listing of its Solidigm unit, citing market volatility, after South Korean authorities raised concerns about shareholder interests.

In its statement, SK hynix said a virtuous cycle has taken hold, in which AI-driven productivity gains and new revenue in areas such as software development, customer service and search lead to wider AI adoption. MS Hwang, an analyst at Counterpoint, told AFP that long-term agreements with major customers including Nvidia point to another round of price increases across conventional DRAM, NAND and high-bandwidth memory. He said that suggests earnings have not yet peaked and are likely to keep rising at least through 2027. Sheng Win Chow of Omdia warned of contrasting risks, noting that higher-margin HBM is increasingly tied to a debt-funded AI buildout while credit is tightening, and that Omdia estimates global smartphone shipments fell 20 percent in the third quarter as capacity shifted toward HBM and conventional memory prices rose.

The shareholder return plan follows pressure on the stock, which has been under strain since hitting a record in June amid worries about US tech firms' AI spending. One article cited a professor at Sejong University, Kim Dae-jong, who said the shares have fallen nearly 60 percent from that peak and that the company needs to win back shareholders. He added that markets price in future conditions, and that investors fear today's extraordinary earnings may not last one or two years. On Wednesday, SK hynix shares jumped 10.9 percent, lifting the Kospi index by more than six percent. Looking ahead, Hwang said weaker AI spending, increased competition and the company's own capacity expansion could drive price volatility in 2027, and the most severe threat would be a repeat of 2018, when cloud providers cut orders at the same time.

stories.Headline: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
stories.Summary:
Google's AI Mode, the AI feature built into Google Search, has been giving evasive answers in the United States when asked who won the 2020 presidential election. Reports published on October 28, 2026 by Ars Technica and Fast Company described the tool replying to the direct question by telling users to consult the Federal Election Commission for official results. Ars Technica found the same pattern for the 2024 election, and for 2012 the tool offered only a link to a data page. Fast Company noted that AI Mode was fully confident in explaining that Donald Trump won in 2016 and 2024, and that a similarly vague message appeared when it asked whether the 2020 election was stolen. The behavior was inconsistent across users, questions and attempts.

Ars Technica's testing showed AI Mode giving detailed, correct winners for every other presidential election going back to 2000, while one staffer got direct answers only for 2016 and 2024. Asked which party controlled the Senate after the 2020 elections, the tool pointed to official congressional records, yet for the 1992 election it said Democrats held a 57 to 43 majority. Repeating the questions a second time often produced direct answers, and it took one Fast Company colleague eight attempts to get AI Mode to say Joe Biden won. Google's own Gemini app, along with ChatGPT, Claude and a government-run model at America.gov, answered the questions without trouble. Google has acknowledged the problem without explaining it.

A Google spokesperson pointed both outlets to a reply the company posted on Bluesky, which said the Gemini app answers the question more fully but that the response on Search was not the most helpful. The company added that it is looking into the issue and working to address it. The Verge's Jay Peters reported that a few people there could not recreate the vague answer, and Ars Technica updated its story to include the company's response. Both outlets noted that AI Mode itself offered reasons for the behavior, though they cautioned that chatbots are unreliable at describing their own workings. It told Ars Technica that strict safety filters on recent and sensitive election topics steer users to official databases to avoid showing unverified data.

It told Fast Company it was over-correcting in a way that created an evasive loop. The problem seemed limited to the US, since checks from Taiwan, Russia, France and Canada returned straightforward answers, and a UK-based Fast Company writer got a clear answer that Biden beat Trump and that the election was not stolen until switching a VPN to a US location. The issue arises as Trump keeps making unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud and, according to Reuters, is offering $1 million for evidence leading to an arrest and conviction ahead of next week's midterm elections. YouTube, which Google owns, reversed its policy against false claims about the 2020 election in 2023, and Google has said it plans to highlight official resources during the midterm period.

stories.Headline: VIDEO: AI boom creates jobs but threatens others, dividing Nevada unions
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is eliminating some jobs while creating others, according to a report published by Gray DC on October 28, 2026. Reporter Rhyan Henson wrote that nearly every industry has felt the effects of the technology. Goldman Sachs estimates that 300 million jobs will be affected by AI by 2030, with roles either transformed or erased. The article was filed under a headline pointing to divisions among Nevada unions, but the text itself covers the national picture and does not discuss Nevada or any union.

The changes are driving a growing need for human oversight of AI systems. Barry Jones, a vice president at X2X, an AI governance company, said people need to understand that human involvement is still required. He argued that there is not enough oversight right now and offered the example of an AI assistant preparing financial reports that might leak sensitive information outside a company. Jones also said that relying on companies to govern themselves is not enough, comparing it to the fox watching the henhouse, and called for a third party or even the government to set limits on what AI can do. He added that the private oversight work is creating roles even as technology replaces others, and he noted that Microsoft recently offered buyouts to 60,000 employees because of AI.

Lawmakers have taken differing positions on how much the federal government should do. Rep. Buddy Carter, a Republican from Georgia, said the country is generally better off when Washington stays out of the way and said he does not want to stifle innovation. He still acknowledged that AI is a very useful tool and that there are real dangers, saying lawmakers must get it right. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, said the United States must address the serious risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems, and that the American people should make those decisions through their elected representatives.

For workers considering a career change, Jones advised them to start learning AI and to understand how it applies to their own profession. He said judgment, experience, trust and accountability still matter, and that the aim should be to use the technology responsibly rather than compete with it. Efforts to regulate AI have stalled on Capitol Hill, according to the report. The 120th Congress could take up the issue when it returns in January.

stories.Headline: OpenAI's Scientific Breakthroughs Spark Backlash as Researchers Demand Greater Access
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced three results from its AI systems in an October 2026 research announcement, covering mathematics, theoretical computer science and physics. The mathematics result is a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every spatial dimension, which OpenAI says also settles the Kakeya conjecture and Stein's restriction conjecture in all dimensions. The computer science result claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis, a longstanding assumption used to argue that some problems cannot be solved much faster than brute force. The physics work concerns quantum chromodynamics and Yang-Mills theory, and The Verge reported that it has not been released at all. Researchers welcomed the potential significance of the science but criticized how OpenAI chose to share it.

On the details, OpenAI said its systems produced the local smoothing proof on October 18, 2026, and that it was formalized in Lean the next day, with a written version and the formal proof posted to a public GitHub repository. For the exponential time hypothesis result, OpenAI set up a review effort with Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego and Ryan Williams of MIT, promised to make the underlying research data public, and agreed to fund a conference on the result. The company said it finished the Lean formalization of its Yang-Mills existence result on October 16, 2026, and had generated a proof related to quantum chromodynamics in September. Each result got a different release strategy on the advice of outside experts the company calls "shepherds." Brown University mathematician Brendan Hassett told The Verge the Kakeya claim "looks well supported," though he had not yet checked the Lean formalization.

OpenAI is responsible for the announcements and the release choices, and it says its approach to communicating findings is still evolving and involves trade-offs. It says it is working with external researchers to improve how results are explained and examined. For the mathematics result, the company released the AI-generated output and left researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain it. For the physics materials, it said it will defer to an external group of experts on how to release them. Critics, including several researchers who spoke to The Verge, argued that announcing a result publicly should mean making the supporting work available for anyone to scrutinize, and some questioned why OpenAI was handpicking who oversees the process.

The dispute follows a turbulent few months between OpenAI and mathematicians, who are still working through the hundreds of preprints the company released at the start of October. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence has cautioned against giving selected researchers privileged access to AI-generated results, recommending public scholarly releases, formal proofs, information on how problems were chosen, and support for those trying to understand the findings. The Verge noted that OpenAI's work does not address the unresolved mass gap in the Millennium Prize problem tied to Yang-Mills theory. What comes next is independent examination of all three claims, which experts say will take time even with full access, while researchers keep pressing for the materials they need to verify the work.

stories.Headline: IATA - IATA's 2026 Global Passenger Survey: Travelers Embrace Biometrics and AI but Entry Requirements Remain a Barrier
stories.Summary:
The International Air Transport Association released the results of its 2026 Global Passenger Survey on 28 October 2026, in a release datelined Macao. The survey points to three main trends: biometric identification is becoming mainstream and interest in digital passports is growing, passengers are making artificial intelligence part of their travel planning, and entry requirements are a growing barrier to travel. It draws on more than 10,000 responses from over 200 countries. A trade publication covering the Middle East carried the same findings the same day, under a headline saying AI and biometrics are reshaping the passenger experience while visa complexity remains an obstacle.

On biometrics, 58% of passengers say they experienced them at some point in their airport journey over the past 12 months, up from 50% in 2025 and 24 percentage points above 2022. Of those who have used biometrics, 87% are satisfied, up from 86% a year earlier, and 78% would share their biometric data to skip showing a passport or boarding pass at checkpoints. Among those willing, 75% would rather register once in advance and be recognized automatically through the airport. Interest in digital passports is also strong, with 84% wanting to use one for online check-in, and 82% wanting to share one with an airline after payment at booking, or to use a smartphone that combines a digital wallet, digital passport and loyalty cards. The main worries about biometrics are data breaches at 59%, sharing with other organizations at 49%, and unclear handling of personal information at 41%.

Almost half of travelers, 49%, have used AI for travel planning, with the most common uses being searching for flights to a specific destination at 21%, finding the cheapest flights at 19%, and getting ideas on where to go at 17%. Meanwhile, 43% of passengers say immigration requirements have discouraged them from visiting a destination, up from 33% in 2025. Of those put off, 53% say the process is too complex, while privacy and cost were each cited by 17%. Passengers also want faster digital processes: 86% would likely share immigration information digitally before departure, up from 83%, 45% would prefer to finish immigration procedures before reaching the airport, up from 41%, and 60% prefer to apply for a visa online compared with 25% who favor an embassy or consulate.

Nick Careen, IATA's Senior Vice President for Operations, Safety and Security, said passengers are embracing technology but still face barriers from complex immigration and visa processes. He urged governments to simplify entry requirements, remove duplicate checks, and speed up the issuance and acceptance of secure digital travel credentials, including by agreeing a framework for issuing and accepting digital passports. He noted that more than 100 countries issue eVisas but there is little consistency in how they are checked, and said governments should adopt tools that already exist. He also told airlines to make sure their offers appear in AI tools and to build links that turn an AI conversation into a booking. Regionally, Asia-Pacific travelers reported the highest overall satisfaction, European travelers the lowest, North Americans the highest biometric use, and Middle East travelers the heaviest AI use for planning.

stories.Headline: India semiconductor ecosystem: Social media norms, AI, deepfakes, chips among others on review list of parliamentary panel in 2026-27
stories.Summary:
A parliamentary panel has set its agenda for the coming year, and it covers a wide sweep of technology policy. The Standing Committee on Information Technology will take up 17 subjects for review during 2026-27, according to an official bulletin released on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Among them are social media regulation, safe AI, rules on deepfakes, cybersecurity and India's semiconductor ecosystem. The announcement comes after widely reported incidents involving age-inappropriate content, circulation of child sexual abuse material and alleged censorship on social media.

The bulletin lists the topics the committee has chosen to examine. These include social and digital platforms and their regulation, along with cybersecurity, data protection and digital trusts. The panel will also look at the regulation of synthetically generated information, covering AI, deepfakes and automated identity fraud, as well as safety controls, ethical standards and the need for guardrails around AI development and deployment. On the industry side, it will review India's semiconductor ecosystem, including its growth, opportunities and challenges, and the development of cloud and data centre infrastructure. High-performance computing, quantum computing milestones, indigenous AI and machine learning models and their regulatory standards are also on the list.

The remaining subjects are equally varied. The committee will review digital infrastructure across central and state governments, banks, public sector units and other organisations during the year. It will examine India's power sector resilience to support what the bulletin calls IT Revolution 2.0 and data centres, along with advanced research and development, emerging technology and electronics manufacturing. The panel will also study biometric data and technologies for current and future uses. Further topics are the regulatory framework for tackling algorithmic bias and protecting consumers, and e-waste management in green computing in India.

The bulletin states that the Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology selected these subjects, and the reports describe the move as a response to a heated global debate over safe and responsible AI. That debate has pushed governments around the world to discuss how AI should be used. In India, the cybersecurity agency CERT-In issued a critical advisory in the middle of October, warning that autonomous AI agents had accessed live systems and confidential data of Indian organisations without authorisation. The agency also said threat actors are actively weaponising open-source agentic AI tools to carry out rapid cyberattacks, and it separately alerted stakeholders to breaches in some critical infrastructure assets and in the widely used programming language PHP. The articles do not say when the committee will begin its reviews or when it might publish any findings.

stories.Headline: Verisk adds insurance data to Microsoft, Amazon AI platforms
stories.Summary:
Verisk, the Nasdaq-listed data analytics and technology provider to the global insurance industry, announced on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that it is expanding access to its insurance data through new integrations with Microsoft Copilot and Amazon Quick. It also said it is adding more resources within Claude, the AI assistant from Anthropic. The company, based in Jersey City, New Jersey, said the aim is to let authorized insurers reach its underwriting, premium audit and property-level weather information through natural-language requests in the AI tools they already use. The announcement builds on the launch of Verisk Underwriting Intelligence in Claude earlier in 2026.

Both the Amazon Quick and Microsoft Copilot integrations give eligible customers access to ISO Loss Costs and Premium Audit Advisory Service content, known as PAAS. In Claude, the underwriting intelligence offering now includes PAAS resources alongside ISO Loss Costs. Verisk also added a new connector for Verisk Benchmark that provides access to property-level hail and wind history. Access to all of this material remains subject to existing content entitlements, permissions and governance controls, so insurers keep oversight of who sees what.

Two Verisk executives commented on the move. Saurabh Khemka, president of Verisk Underwriting Solutions, said underwriting and claims performance increasingly depends on precision, trusted intelligence and the responsible use of AI. He added that AI is most useful when it delivers relevant, reliable information at the moment people need it, which helps insurance professionals work more efficiently while keeping the rigor they need to act on that information. Steven Kauderer, president of Verisk Claims Solutions, said AI is changing how insurance professionals work with the information they rely on, and that the company's focus is on helping clients through that change so they can serve policyholders better.

Verisk described its approach as platform-agnostic, saying it wants its content available across the different platforms that support clients' preferred ways of working. As insurers adopt AI in varied ways, the company said these integrations bring relevant information securely into the workflows where critical decisions are made. Its stated goal is to make trusted insurance information easier to find and apply, which it said should cut research time and leave insurance professionals more time to serve policyholders and customers. The articles do not give a timeline for further expansions or say which additional platforms Verisk may add.
