Artifex-2026, a two-day event on animation and filmmaking, opened on Wednesday at the Manipal Institute of Communication under Manipal Academy of Higher Education. The event was organised by the institute's Animation Department. At an interactive session, B. S. Srinivas, director and chairman of Arena Animation and Vedatma College of Design, Technology and Management in Bengaluru, looked at how AI is changing the filmmaking pipeline. He covered stages from pre-production and scene creation through visual effects, dubbing, colour grading and post-production.

The session stressed that AI-assisted tools can help smaller teams do work that once needed more time, money and staff. Srinivas also discussed AI in animation, virtual production and digital character creation. He raised concerns about copyright, consent, authenticity, employment and quality control. According to a release, the session concluded that AI can speed up workflows and widen creative options, but human imagination, empathy and storytelling remain central to filmmaking. On September 15, 2026, the Commission on Higher Education issued CHED Memorandum Order No. 21, series of 2026, which covers AI use in teaching, learning, research and institutional operations. The order sets safeguards for academic integrity, data privacy, human judgment and student welfare.

At the media briefing on October 22, representatives from HP, Fortinet and Nutanix addressed educator training, cybersecurity and student-facing technology. HP Philippines said it runs customised AI Academy programmes for teachers, including one with Ateneo de Naga University, and a similar programme for schools in Pasig City. Fortinet Philippines, through Bambi Escalante, described a cybersecurity skills gap of roughly one professional for every 2,000 to 3,000 employees, against an ideal of about one to 200. Nutanix's Daryush Ashjari said its platform lets students try different technology layers while IT teams manage them. stories.Headline: Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics face Illinois lawsuits alleging delivery robots collected biometric data
stories.Summary:
Two class-action lawsuits filed in Cook County, Illinois, allege that delivery robots from Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics secretly scanned people's faces and hands and shared that data with artificial intelligence companies. The suits say the people involved never gave permission for this collection. One plaintiff, Mitchell Breidinger, says he ordered groceries through DoorDash in September 2025 and a Coco robot arrived even though he had not asked for a robot delivery. Another plaintiff, Barry Schain, says he received three Uber Eats deliveries by Serve robot without requesting one, and his suit was filed five days after an October 4 delivery in Lincoln Park. Both lawsuits were reported on October 27, 2026.

The lawsuits argue the companies violated Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act, which requires written notice before biometric data is collected, an explanation of how it will be used, and explicit permission first. Violations can carry fines of $1,000 to $5,000 each. Breidinger alleges the robot's cameras recorded his face, head and hands while LiDAR sensors captured the shape of his body parts. He further claims a remote operator watched the delivery live and that the data went to OpenAI and other companies.

Schain's suit alleges Serve collected video and sensor data and licensed it to third parties. Both companies deny the allegations. A Coco Robotics spokesperson called the lawsuit "frivolous" and said the company has not collected biometric data in Chicago. Serve Robotics told The Associated Press that it does not use its data to identify individuals and that its systems are not designed to identify people or create biometric profiles, and it has said its cameras and sensors are used only for navigation.

The cases come amid wider scrutiny of surveillance technology, including Flock Safety's automated license plate readers, which have sparked debate this year. Chicago residents have also complained about delivery robots blocking sidewalks and crashing into bus shelters. The city's robot delivery pilot program is set to end in May 2027 unless officials extend it. If the allegations prove true, the cases may prompt further investigation into how businesses inform people about data practices involving their devices.

stories.Headline: AI's data problem is governance in disguise
stories.Summary:
A Workiva survey of Australian finance, risk and sustainability leaders, published as the 2026 Midyear Executive Benchmark Survey, found that 95 per cent of respondents want AI to deliver measurable return on investment within the next year. The article's author, writing for IT Brief Australia on 29 October 2026, says that timeline is ambitious for reporting work, where accuracy and accountability are essential. The survey also found that only 14 per cent of executives said their organisation's data quality was sufficient for AI use in reporting, while 21 per cent said data quality problems had significantly limited their use of AI and blocked deployment in key workflows. A further 44 per cent said they had worked around these issues, though the author notes this slowed progress.

The author argues that these results point to a governance problem rather than a purely data problem. Where the same figure lives in several spreadsheets, a slide deck and an email thread, AI does not fix the inconsistency but spreads it faster and at greater scale, with a confidence that makes errors harder to detect. The survey also found that 79 per cent of respondents were at least somewhat confident in AI outputs without human review, which the author sees as a risk. The article says the gap calls for connected and controlled data infrastructure, built on three elements: a single source of truth, clear control over ownership, permissions and version history, and lineage built in so any figure can be traced to its source. It also says that 39 per cent of Australian executives reported that their most recent AI audit found data lineage gaps or traceability issues.

The article stresses that traceability matters because financial statements, board papers and sustainability disclosures, including the mandatory climate reporting now phasing in across Australia, must withstand auditors, regulators and investors. The author suggests that an AI process that cannot be audited turns a productivity gain into a liability. The 21 per cent of respondents who said they were blocked are described as being in a safer position than those who have normalised manual workarounds, which the author says erode traceability over time. The author proposes a simple test: take one AI-assisted figure from the last board report and try to trace it to its source, and if that takes days or depends on one person's memory, the organisation is not yet AI-ready.

stories.Headline: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
stories.Summary:
Amazon, on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, posted an internal memo on its website that sets out how software engineers and managers should use artificial intelligence tools. The memo, first circulated to staff in September, tells employees not to treat "tokenmaxxing," the practice of running AI as heavily as possible with little regard for results, as a sign of success. Amazon had earlier shut down an internal leaderboard in May after discovering that employees were inflating their token usage to climb the rankings. The company says it has not put caps on how many tokens employees may use.

The memo says that token usage, the rate of AI tool adoption, and counts of code changes or reviews are "deeply flawed" ways to measure AI use, since they can drive up costs and add complexity. It does not tell staff to ignore those figures entirely, however, and says they should be weighed "with care and judgment" alongside other data. Instead, Amazon says it prefers to measure teams by long-term outcomes. Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, said the company has also looked at "feature velocity," meaning how many launches and successful production changes teams deliver.

The memo is credited to Terk Terkowitz, a vice president and distinguished engineer in Worldwide Amazon Stores, and it says that teams which have embraced AI have gained productivity while those that have not have fallen behind. It also says an engineer who finds that AI does not help their work should document why and share it, which the memo describes as showing sound judgment rather than failure. Terkowitz wrote that leaders must understand their teams' work and stay close to their products and businesses. Brooker added that the company accepts some wasted effort as the cost of experimentation, though it wants to avoid spending tokens on problems that do not matter.

The memo comes amid a wider industry reckoning over AI costs. Companies have been struggling with rising AI bills and with how to tell whether the tools produce real returns, and some have set limits on token use, switched to cheaper open-source models for certain tasks, or rethought their AI spending after what one report called "token shock." Amazon has moved quickly to fold AI into its operations under CEO Andy Jassy, who has predicted AI will change the scope and speed of work and could shrink corporate staffing over the next few years. The articles do not say what further steps Amazon plans beyond the guidelines in the memo.

stories.Headline: Daeryuk Aju, Lin sign AI compliance MOU with Deloitte Anjin
stories.Summary:
Three firms, Daeryuk Aju, Lin and Deloitte Anjin, signed a memorandum of understanding on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at a conference room on the 20th floor of Donghun Tower on Teheran-ro in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. The agreement commits them to jointly support corporate AI compliance certification and the development of management frameworks for AI use. It was reported by Herald Business and Chosunbiz, both of which note that the signing took place in Seoul. The move responds to tightening rules at home and abroad, including the enforcement of Korea's Basic AI Act and the European Union's AI Act.

The cooperation covers a broad set of tasks. These include assessing AI compliance and governance frameworks, building certification criteria based on objective evaluation standards, and advising on domestic and international AI laws. It also covers AI risk diagnosis, stronger internal controls, and the creation of responsible AI policies and operating frameworks. The firms will additionally address privacy, security and intellectual property risks that come with AI use. They plan joint research on AI regulation and industry trends, along with joint seminars, and four seminars are set for November 11 to December 1 at Donghun Tower.

Lee Gyu-cheol, managing partner of Daeryuk Aju, said corporate responses to AI rules are moving beyond simple legal review toward organization-wide management systems. He expects the firm's legal expertise, combined with Deloitte Anjin's AI and risk management capabilities, to produce more practical compliance services. Lim Jin-seok, managing partner of Lin, said certification could become a new standard for earning trust from customers and the market, not just a tool for responding to regulators. Gil Gi-wan, CEO of Deloitte Anjin, said the collaboration aims to help companies use AI more safely and responsibly.

The three firms recently launched the AI Compliance Certification program, known as AICC, which examines corporate AI compliance and accredits companies that meet objective standards. Chosunbiz reports that the program will set evaluation criteria reflecting industry characteristics and levels of AI use. A Daeryuk Aju official said AICC is expected to help companies keep their AI systems stable, much as the firm's Serious Accidents Punishment Act certification has aided in preventing serious workplace accidents. The first seminars are scheduled to present the criteria to firms in finance, heavy industry, broadcasting, telecommunications, platforms and physical AI.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence transforms the workforce, regulations
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs estimates that 300 million jobs will be affected by artificial intelligence by 2030, and the technology is already reshaping industries day by day, transforming some jobs and erasing others. Nearly every sector has felt its effects, which has increased the call for oversight of how AI is used. Reporting from Gray DC on October 28, 2026, described the trend as one that is bringing a greater need for governance. The coverage focused on how quickly the changes are arriving.

Barry Jones, a vice president at X2X, an AI governance company, argued that human involvement must remain part of AI work and that current oversight is not sufficient. He gave the example of an AI assistant preparing financial reports, which could be useful but could also expose critical financial information if it operated outside a company's internal controls. Jones said self-governance by companies is not enough and that a third party, including government, should set out what AI systems may and may not do. He also pointed to private-sector job cuts, noting that Microsoft recently offered 60,000 employees buyouts because of AI.

Members of Congress gave differing views on the government's role. Representative Buddy Carter, a Georgia Republican, said he preferred less federal involvement but acknowledged that AI can be very useful while also carrying real concerns and dangers that must be addressed correctly. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, said the United States must deal with the serious risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems and that the American people, through their representatives, should make those decisions. Efforts to regulate AI have stalled on Capitol Hill, although the 120th Congress could take up the issue when it convenes in January.

For workers seeking a career change because of AI, Jones advised learning the technology and understanding how it applies to their profession. He stressed that judgment, experience, trust and accountability still matter, and that the goal should be to learn to use AI responsibly rather than to compete with the machine. The articles do not describe any specific regulation adopted so far. What happens next depends on whether Congress acts in January on the stalled proposals.

stories.Headline: Pate McMichael discusses AI’s impact on election advertisements on WFAE’s Charlotte Talks
stories.Summary:
The most recent article here reports that Pate McMichael, director of the North Carolina Open Government Coalition and an instructor of journalism at Elon University, joined WFAE's Charlotte Talks for an Oct. 27 episode titled "Artificial Intelligence in Elections." The program looked at concerns about AI-generated campaign advertisements, deepfakes and misleading content that could sway voters before the 2026 midterm elections. Host Mike Collins led the discussion, which focused on how artificial intelligence is growing in influence across political campaigns. The article was published Oct. 28, 2026, and it is the only source provided for this account.

McMichael argued that political ads are supposed to inform voters, and that the Supreme Court's rulings on campaign spending were premised on the idea that voters need more information. He said many of these ads leave viewers doubting whether claims are accurate, and that people increasingly want more transparency around them. The discussion also covered regulation: the article says 31 states have enacted some form of rules governing AI in political campaigns, while North Carolina has not adopted similar legislation despite several attempts by state lawmakers. One common requirement, according to the article, is disclosure when an ad uses AI. McMichael pointed to Alabama, Florida, Tennessee and Texas as states that require such disclosures, though he noted they are written differently from one another.

McMichael also said voters need to know who is paying for ads, since the article describes weak transparency around funding for online and social media advertising. He asked why lawmakers would not require disclosure if transparency is the goal, and he suggested that voters deserve more insight into how an ad was made and who funded it. The article does not attribute any specific legislative proposal to him beyond those comments. Other participants in the conversation were Michael Bitzer, professor of politics and history at Catawba College, and Scott Brennan, director of New York University's Center on Technology Policy, who joined to discuss emerging technology, political communication and election integrity. The article notes that the full conversation is available online.

stories.Headline: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Ended the Illegal and Discriminatory Practices of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion
stories.Summary:
The White House published a fact sheet on October 28, 2026, saying that President Donald J. Trump has removed what it calls wasteful and unmeritocratic diversity, equity, and inclusion programs from government, education, and the private sector. The document claims that on his first day back in office, Trump rescinded orders from the previous administration and signed an executive order ending DEI programs and preferences in the federal government. It describes a long series of follow-on actions across 2025 and 2026, including orders targeting federal contracting, the armed forces, the Foreign Service, the Department of Education, the Smithsonian, higher education accreditation, school discipline, and disparate-impact liability. The fact sheet lists these as the administration's work, and the articles provided do not independently confirm the claimed results.

The fact sheet describes several specific measures and settlements. It cites a $221 million settlement with Columbia University in July 2025, a $50 million settlement with Brown University that same month, and a $60 million settlement with Cornell University and a $75 million settlement with Northwestern University in November 2025. It also says the administration paused $210 million in federal funding to Princeton and launched a review of $9 billion in federal funding for Harvard University. The document further reports that the Department of Health and Human Services froze over $100 million in funding to Duke University's medical school, and that the Small Business Administration ended race-based criteria in its 8(a) Business Development Program. Each of these is presented as an action taken by the administration, with the stated reasons attached.

The fact sheet is attributed to the White House, and its content is written from the administration's point of view. It states that the actions were taken to restore merit, fairness, and equal treatment under the law, and it characterizes DEI programs as illegal, discriminatory, or ideologically driven. Several universities, companies, and agencies are described as having changed their policies in response, including the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, which closed its DEI office, and about 90 percent of the top 400 S&P 500 companies, which cut at least some references to DEI through March 2025. The provided articles do not describe responses from the institutions named, nor do they include independent assessments of the claims or outcomes.

stories.Headline: House Democratic Committee Leaders Request Frontier AI Companies Report Misalignment & Safety Incidents to Congress Within 48 Hours
stories.Summary:
House Democratic leaders on three committees sent letters on October 28, 2026, to five leading frontier AI companies asking them to report misalignment and safety incidents to Congress. The lawmakers said the request follows a rise in reports of AI models taking unintended and potentially unsafe actions during testing. The letters went to Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceX, which the article lists as SpaceXSI. The letters were signed by Ranking Members Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey, Zoe Lofgren of California, and Jamie Raskin of Maryland. The lawmakers asked each company for a full accounting of identified incidents by November 11, 2026.

They also requested that companies notify the committees within 48 hours of discovering any new or previously unknown incident. For incidents that appear to involve critical infrastructure, the request is for notification within 24 hours. The Democrats framed these steps as a way to gather the best available information before Congress takes up AI governance. The Democratic leaders wrote that there are currently no mandatory reporting requirements or common guidelines about which incidents should be reported, to whom, in what detail, and at what intervals. They said companies have therefore set their own standards on a voluntary basis, and that the Trump Administration has relied on voluntary disclosures and self-regulation by the AI industry.

In their view, that approach depends too heavily on companies choosing to disclose incidents that could expose them to liability and reputational damage. They also said Congress must act to address gaps in AI governance. The three committees share jurisdiction over the development and deployment of AI as well as potential penalties for its misuse, according to the article. The article does not say whether the companies have responded to the letters or what steps Congress will take next.

Articles.Title: House Democratic Committee Leaders Request Frontier AI Companies Report Misalignment & Safety Incidents to Congress Within 48 Hours

stories.Headline: Medical AI Competition in China Highlights Potential for ASEAN Health Care Cooperation
stories.Summary:
A national medical imaging AI competition took place on October 22 and 23 in Nanning, in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, bringing together researchers, clinicians and technology companies to test tools that help doctors detect disease. The event also explored health care cooperation between China and Southeast Asian countries. The 2026 National Healthcare Security Medical Imaging AI Recognition Competition attracted 1,332 registered teams, including participants from ASEAN member states, and 66 team entries reached the finals. Co-hosted by China's National Healthcare Security Administration and the Guangxi regional government, and organized by the Healthcare Security Administration of Guangxi, it covered eight categories such as lung cancer detection on CT scans, brain tumor analysis on MRI and breast cancer screening on mammography. Imaging scans have grown so detailed that a chest CT once producing about 100 images can now yield thousands, which makes spotting small abnormalities in time harder.

One finalist, SenseLung from Shanghai, has built AI tools that flag suspicious lung nodules, analyze them and generate structured reports for radiologists, with work also reaching disease screening and patient follow-up. Detection alone does not settle whether a tool is useful. Hospitals use different equipment and scanning protocols, so a model that performs well at a major medical center may fall short at a smaller hospital, and the competition therefore judged how well algorithms handled images from varied sources. The same concern applies across ASEAN, whose countries differ widely in health care systems, digital development and access to medical resources. For hospitals weighing AI-assisted diagnosis, fit with existing equipment and clinical workflows can matter as much as results in controlled tests.

The competition also showed the value of clinicians working with developers. In the mammography category, a team from Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region People's Hospital and a local technology company built a model to identify breast masses and tiny calcium deposits, with radiologists guiding engineers on clinical needs and refinements. Guangxi, which borders Vietnam, has long been a gateway for China's exchanges with ASEAN, and the China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center and the Fangchenggang International Medical Opening-up Pilot Zone add platforms for cooperation. Guangxi authorities have said the region plans to work with ASEAN partners on cross-border clinical validation and demonstration projects to test how medical imaging AI can be adapted to different health care settings. Such work involves more than transferring software, since differences in equipment, procedures, patient data, privacy rules and regulation can determine whether AI can be safely used in practice.

China is also developing medical imaging cloud infrastructure to help institutions share and retrieve imaging records, which, with appropriate safeguards, could support AI development and evaluation. Zhang Huimao, director of radiology at the First Hospital of Jilin University and president-elect of the Chinese Society of Radiology, said such data infrastructure could serve clinical care as well as the development, testing and evaluation of AI models. Strong competition results, however, do not automatically make a tool ready for hospitals, because models need validation across institutions, equipment and patient groups, along with regulatory approval where required. Guangxi has introduced a three-year action plan to move competition technologies toward commercial use, covering product validation, industry development, clinical testing and cooperation with ASEAN partners.

For China and ASEAN, the benefits could reach beyond the exchange of technology, particularly in areas with few specialist radiologists, where reliable AI tools might help doctors spot suspicious findings sooner and work more efficiently. The articles stress that AI is meant to support physicians rather than replace them, since doctors must weigh symptoms, medical histories and other test results when making decisions. The competition offered a glimpse of what AI could contribute to medical imaging. Turning promising algorithms into dependable tools for hospitals across borders will require further testing, adaptation and cooperation, with the aim of improving patient care.

stories.Headline: Malaysia seizes servers with advanced AI chips suspected of violating export controls
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's customs department announced that it had seized 30 servers fitted with advanced artificial intelligence chips in a suspected export-control violation. The servers were intercepted at the free trade zone at the country's main airport during an inspection on October 15, and officials believe a syndicate was using Malaysia as a transit point to send the chips on to another Asian country. The shipment is worth about 50 million ringgit, or $12.2 million. The servers had arrived from an Asian country and were falsely declared as electrical components to avoid detection.

Malaysia introduced permit requirements last year for the export, transit and transshipment of high-performance AI chips of U.S. origin. The rules followed pressure from Washington, which wants to keep sensitive technology from reaching China through third countries and has tried to limit China's access to advanced semiconductors. Officials say the servers were re-exported without the permit that the rules require. Customs also linked the shipment to a syndicate behind five attempted smuggling operations, including one in June when authorities seized 72 servers containing advanced AI chips at the same airport zone.

The customs department, through airport customs director Aspalila Ag Tuah, described the scheme in its statement and at a briefing for reporters. A Malaysian company that helped arrange the shipment has been asked to assist the investigation. Aspalila declined to say where the chips came from or where they were ultimately headed, saying the case remains under investigation. The Associated Press and Macau Daily Times carried the report.

stories.Headline: With Musk and Huang at odds on AI neoclouds, can China weather the storm?
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk and Nvidia chief Jensen Huang have publicly disagreed about whether the specialist cloud providers that rent out graphics processing unit capacity, known as neoclouds, can survive their mounting debts. Musk has warned of impending collapses and consolidation among the more than 200 such ventures, while Huang remains bullish and argues that strong market demand will unlock the capital the sector needs. The South China Morning Post reported the dispute on October 28, 2026, as investor anxiety over an artificial intelligence bubble grew. The article presents the split as a sign of liquidity pressure across AI infrastructure providers worldwide, including in China.

The piece places the debate within a broader pattern of heavy spending. Tech giants and specialised data-centre developers in China are committing tens of billions of dollars to build computing capacity before clear ways of earning money from it have emerged. Analysis published the same day on eu.36kr.com examines the position of Anthropic, an AI company whose prospectus describes commitments of roughly 6.37 trillion US dollars in computing power. Anthropic's annual recurring revenue stood at about 65 billion US dollars by July, which the report says is an order of magnitude below those commitments. The report also notes that Broadcom, SpaceX, Google and Amazon each have commitments reaching hundreds of billions of US dollars.

The analysis argues that Anthropic has in effect promised much of its future revenue to these large suppliers. It describes a "take-or-pay" arrangement in which a minimum payment is owed regardless of actual use, and says Anthropic's cash and equivalents stood at 112.4 billion US dollars at the end of the first half of the year. Against that, the report says the company needs financing to cover its procurement orders. It also reports that some investors have lowered their expected IPO valuation from 2 trillion to about 1.5 trillion US dollars, because sequential revenue growth slowed to roughly 43 percent in the third quarter.

The eu.36kr.com report also points to competition from China, saying the gap between top Chinese and American AI models had narrowed to about 3 percent in October. It notes that Chinese models such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro are priced far below Anthropic's offerings, and that Anthropic has cut prices, including about 90 percent on its smallest model. The report expects Anthropic's growth rate to slow as its base grows larger. What happens next for the neocloud sector is not settled in the articles, which leave open whether demand will close the financing gap that Musk and Huang disagree about.

stories.Headline: Ahead of US midterms, ChatGPT draws images "depicting election interference or that may discourage voting" in a cartoon style, ignoring photorealism requests (Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET)
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has set up an election "war room" ahead of the US midterms, which it said it would run starting the week of the vote and continuing until all ballots are counted. The company calls it the Election Operations Center, and it is meant to spot the spread of misinformation and other attempts to disrupt the elections. The center will monitor real-time events and take in reports of unexpected model behavior or suspected violations of OpenAI's terms. Its focus is largely on abuse of the company's own tools, such as ChatGPT. The announcement came via an exclusive to Politico's Decoded newsletter.

Josh Lawson, OpenAI's head of civic and strategic risk, is leading the center. He told Politico the company has put considerable effort into helping users get reliable voting information and combating misuse of its tools. He described the center as building on years of similar work, bringing teams together to respond quickly to emerging issues as people head to the polls. Politico reported that the company is bringing hundreds of employees together for the effort. OpenAI, in other words, is presenting itself as a defender of the democratic process.

The move comes amid broader worries that AI could distort the midterms through misleading images, audio and video, along with misinformation generally. Politico noted that bad actors may try to use OpenAI's tools and those of other companies to disrupt free and fair elections. A separate report by CNET, whose headline appeared alongside these articles, said ChatGPT draws images depicting election interference or that may discourage voting, typically in a cartoon style, even when users ask for photorealism. The articles do not say how often such images are produced. They also do not describe what enforcement steps the center will take in specific cases.

Taken together, the reporting shows a company preparing for a period of heightened scrutiny rather than announcing a new rule for users. The articles do not say how the center will coordinate with election officials or outside groups. The timing of the announcement, shortly before the vote, suggests the company expects the most activity in the days around election day. Further details about the center's operations, and any findings it produces after the midterms, would be needed to judge how it performs.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's S-1 shows an 85% gross margin in H1 from running its models, a reality check for skeptics who said pay-as-you-go model sales wouldn't be profitable (Stephanie Palazzolo/The Information)
stories.Summary:
The headline reports that Anthropic's S-1 filing shows an 85% gross margin in the first half, drawn from running its models, a figure reported by Stephanie Palazzolo of The Information. That result runs against the view of skeptics who argued that pay-as-you-go model sales would not be profitable. The same week, markets were already reconsidering the AI boom, with shares of the large technology companies falling and the selling spreading to chipmakers and cloud providers. The articles place the figure in that context of doubt about whether AI revenue can support heavy spending.

The source articles describe a broader market pullback rather than any new requirement or rule. The Straits Times reports that the S&P 500, weighted toward Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Nvidia, was barely above its August peak. It also says the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 14% in the month to October 23, and that CoreWeave, the largest listed specialist AI cloud provider, lost more than 38%. The same piece notes that Treasury bonds rallied despite rising inflation, which usually pushes them lower.

It adds that the spending is increasingly funded by debt and circular deals. Markets are asking whether AI revenue can justify a build-out that the article describes as costing about a trillion dollars. The article recalls that Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella warned in 2025 that the company might end up with chips sitting in inventory that it could not plug in. That warning frames the concern about spending outpacing returns.

The articles do not assign responsibility for any wrongdoing, and the filing's margin figure is presented as evidence against the skeptics. The Straits Times piece says the initial euphoria over AI has hit a speed bump after three years in which investors treated AI spending as a down payment on the future. The articles do not say what will happen next or how the market will settle. They describe the Anthropic margin as a reality check that could shift the debate, but they leave open whether that view will hold.

stories.Headline: Using artificial intelligence to step up the fight against doping
stories.Summary:
Officials from the World Anti-Doping Agency and representatives from 26 countries gathered in Santorini, Greece, for the 3rd Anti-Doping Summit of Central and Eastern European Countries, where the use of artificial intelligence in the fight against doping was a central topic. The event examined new technologies that could support data analysis, improve test planning and assist investigations. Some of these tools can process large volumes of information, which could benefit many competent organisations. However, participants also recognised that the same tools could be exploited by people trying to cheat. The discussions aimed to set out how these technologies might be used responsibly and effectively.

Sébastien Gillot, director of WADA's European Office, said that artificial intelligence gives anti-doping bodies a powerful means of spotting trends and patterns that offenders may be using. He noted that the technology could help improve testing in particular. He also warned that tools helpful to investigators could equally be used by those who cheat, so the sector needs to understand how to deploy them to its advantage. Dora Hegyi, a former Hungarian gymnastics champion and vice-chair of WADA's Athletes' Council, said the talks covered how athletes could become better informed and how national bodies could work more efficiently. She added that participants also discussed the legal questions and what athletes themselves think about the use of AI.

Penny Konitsioti, a lawyer and vice-chair of the Disciplinary Committee of Greece's National Anti-Doping Organisation, said that athletes must be told at the outset when a platform's search could later be used in legal proceedings. She argued that this warning should be clearly stated in the terms of use rather than buried in small print. She also stressed that artificial intelligence should support competent authorities, such as by helping gather evidence or assisting a sports judge, but should never replace established procedures or human judgement. Participants agreed that safeguards must accompany any technological progress, including human oversight of disciplinary cases.

Transparency and the protection of personal data were strongly emphasised, since modern digital systems create new opportunities but also demand careful handling of sensitive information. Hegyi argued that trust is needed, meaning AI systems should be developed with athletes rather than only for them, if future programmes are to succeed. Transparency, data security and human oversight were identified as essential to maintaining confidence in the testing system. Participants also discussed changes to therapeutic use exemptions and results management procedures. The summit reaffirmed that the global anti-doping community aims to apply reliable, consistent procedures while fully respecting international rules and athletes' rights.

stories.Headline: North Carolina Must Adapt to AI
stories.Summary:
The 2026 North Carolina midterms have put artificial intelligence on the ballot, and a recent political ad in the 11th Congressional District shows why. The ad, which targets Democratic nominee Jamie Ager, was almost entirely artificially generated and depicts a barn dance with drag queens that never happened. Reporting from The Daily Tar Heel, published October 27, 2026, raised questions about who will set the rules for AI and what it will mean for the political landscape. A Wesleyan Media Project estimate cited in the reporting puts spending on AI-generated ads in this midterm cycle at at least $137 million, with 88 percent coming from Republican-affiliated sponsors.

AI shapes campaigns in less obvious ways too, including targeted advertising, AI-generated search summaries, and unreliable candidate information. At present, no state or federal rule in North Carolina requires political ads to disclose that AI was used to create them, so the burden falls on voters to tell real content from artificial content. Scott Brennen of New York University's Center on Technology Policy told the paper that political ads rarely change voters' choices, though they can be effective at mobilization. Sourojit Ghosh, founder of UNC's UNSEEN Lab, warned that algorithms choose which messages users see based on what they seem to believe, which can subtly shape opinion.

AI is also a policy question on the ballot, since the outcome will help decide rules for data center development, surveillance, and AI use in elections, education, and government. Republican U.S. Senate nominee Michael Whatley has accepted funds from groups tied to CyrusOne, which runs a data center campus in Durham, and he supports tax breaks for data centers. Democratic nominee Roy Cooper has said local residents should have the final say on data centers, even if that means backing moratoriums, and he has called for federal guardrails and oversight. President Donald Trump has argued the United States must win the AI race against China, and Brennen said Trump appears to be opposing any regulation despite growing bipartisan interest in some.

Because federal action is limited, Michael Bitzer of Catawba College said data center questions are increasingly being settled at the local level, and the Orange County Commission plans to approve a new data center policy later this year. The entire North Carolina General Assembly is also up for reelection, and it is currently controlled by Republicans, who largely back AI development and limited regulation. Pending bills include S963, which would require a Department of Justice license before distributing a health-information chatbot, and House Bill 301, which would expand social media safety rules for minors and require school districts to adopt AI policies. Bitzer said the election will be an early test of how AI is used in campaigns, and he expects it to be used heavily in future elections.

stories.Headline: MP Spurious Liquor Case: Accused Used AI to Learn Brewing Methods
stories.Summary:
Police in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas district say an arrested man used artificial intelligence to learn how to brew liquor at home by mixing chemicals and water. The fake liquor was blended with real alcohol and poured into empty licensed bottles bought from scrap dealers, then sold mostly in rural areas. Police arrested 10 people on Monday, October 27, and seized six cartons of country liquor, according to Dewas Kotwali Police Station in-charge Shashikant Chaurasia. Police said the arrested man, Ajay Rathore, had been using AI since September to look up home-brewing methods. Reports also say he ordered chemicals through a private firm in Indore, though the officials did not name the chemicals.

Investigators say Rathore collected empty licensed bottles from scrap dealers between October 2 and 7 and prepared the fake liquor with help from other accused. Among those arrested are two managers and two salesmen from three licensed liquor shops in Dewas and Indore districts, who allegedly supplied alcohol illegally. Police say the adulterated liquor was sold to local residents between October 6 and 12. The Indore warehouse of the private firm that supplied the chemicals has been sealed, and relevant provisions of the Excise Act have been added to the FIR. Viscera samples from the two deceased, along with the recovered liquor, have gone to the Forensic Science Laboratory, and the cause of death will be confirmed once the report arrives.

Police say two other employees of a licensed liquor shop are also involved, and a search for them is underway. Villagers in Chandana, Binjana and nearby areas of Dewas claim at least 10 people died after drinking poisonous liquor between September 27 and October 16. State Congress President Jitu Patwari alleges that 22 people died and at least 40 lost their eyesight over the past month. The district administration first dismissed the death claims. After the controversy grew, the state government formed a five-member high-level investigation team to probe the matter.

The reports note that the death toll claims remain under investigation and that the forensic findings are still awaited. Police have not confirmed how many of the deaths were linked to the adulterated liquor. Each account is based on statements from police officials and local claims as reported by PTI. The next step is the forensic report, which will determine the cause of the deaths, along with the work of the state investigation team.

stories.Headline: AI is changing our world. First, let's understand what it is.
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has been around for decades, but generative AI has made it feel suddenly everywhere. A Pew Research Center survey from June found nearly half of U.S. adults use AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, and one in four of them use one every day. About a third of American homes have devices with AI built in, such as doorbells, thermostats or smart speakers. Use is growing even as many people remain skeptical, with more adults expecting a negative rather than positive impact on them and on society.

Generative AI differs from older tools such as the iPhone's Siri, which worked with limited data inside preexisting code. Newer systems learn from enormous quantities of data and produce original text, images, audio, video and computer code in response to user prompts. The field changed quickly after a 2017 Google paper on the "Transformer" framework, and by late 2022 OpenAI had released GPT-3 to the public. Companies including Google, OpenAI and Anthropic have since raced to build more advanced models, and many are now described as agents that can act on their own without a human prompt. Gerol C. Petruzella, an academic technology consultant at Williams College, argues that this shift means society must figure out new rules for a world where humans are no longer the only entities able to act independently.

The article was written by Ben Niewoehner and introduces a three-part series by Petruzella in The Berkshire Eagle, which will examine AI's effects on local businesses and systems, daily life, and what separates the technology from profit-driven hype. Petruzella defines AI broadly as any technology that does things that would traditionally have required human cognition. He says AI is already part of the digital tools and apps people use, and it is becoming part of the environment in which people work and live. The series is meant to explore how the technology will affect Berkshire County in the coming months and years.

The Ministry of Defence has signed a memorandum of understanding with Sarvam AI to advance the adoption of artificial intelligence across the Indian Army, Indian Navy, and Indian Air Force. The agreement was reported on October 28, 2026, and was announced by the ministry in a social media post. Sarvam AI's entry into the defence sector is its first. The partnership is expected to support the development of AI-based solutions tailored to the requirements of the armed forces.

According to the ministry, HQ Integrated Defence Staff and Sarvam AI will work together on AI applications, research, knowledge management, training, and decision-support. The articles say the arrangement is meant to fit the central government's growing emphasis on homegrown defence technology and its plans to expand indigenous AI across critical sectors. Sarvam AI's pitch rests on competitively priced solutions that keep data within India, backed by its India-hosted infrastructure and language capabilities. Its Anvaya platform is aimed at defence and intelligence work, including on-premise deployments. The specific applications, deployment timelines, and financial terms of the partnership have not been disclosed.

The ministry itself announced the collaboration, describing the scope of the work in its social media post. The articles do not name any individual officials as responsible for the arrangement. Sarvam AI has previously outlined its ambitions at its developer conference, Sarvam Epoch, held in August, where it described plans spanning AI models, compute infrastructure, coding agents, voice technology, document intelligence, and workplace applications. Its roadmap also includes hardware such as smart glasses.

The wider context is a defence technology market that Inc42 projects will grow from $7.6 billion in 2025 to $19 billion by 2030, at a compound annual growth rate of 20 per cent. In that forecast, AI-related technologies are expected to make up 48 per cent of the market by 2030, up from 28 per cent in 2025. The same report says 89 per cent of Indian defence tech startups already integrate AI into their offerings. The articles frame the next step as turning investment and adoption into reliable systems that strengthen technological self-reliance, though they do not describe a fixed timetable for the partnership's results.

stories.Headline: Google AI Privacy: How Personal Data Fuels Ads
stories.Summary:
Google's privacy policy, which took effect on October 16, 2026, now allows personal content from Gmail, Google Photos, and Google Drive to help shape personalized ads when users connect those apps to other Google services. The change sits alongside a new feature called Personal Intelligence, which lets AI Mode in Search and Gemini draw on a user's messages, inbox, and photos to answer questions. Android Authority first noticed the exception, and other outlets followed. Google's earlier policy had said it did not show personalized ads based on content from those services, and that statement remains, but it now carries an exception for users who opt in to share the data with other services.

The policy exception matters because Google's help documentation says that summaries, excerpts, generated media, and inferences drawn from connected emails and files may be used, and that the same inferences and summaries may be used to show advertisements. Google says the raw messages stay where they are, and that Gemini Apps chats are not currently used for ads, with users to be told if that changes. Turning off personalized ads in My Ad Center may not stop connected-app data from being processed for AI personalization, and disconnecting an app does not delete data already retained. Some connected data may also be read by human reviewers and used for product improvement, including AI training. Google's advertising business produced $82.3 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025, about 72 per cent of Alphabet's revenue for that period.

Google's public statements say the company does not sell users' information, and that advertisers do not get access to Gmail or Photos. The company's advertising policy also says it does not personalize ads around health, race, religion, or sexual orientation. Google has described the Personal Intelligence feature as opt-in, and its help pages present the connected-content features as separate from other Google AI services. Critics of the arrangement argue that a single consent click covers two different uses, and that the explanation sits in a policy most people never read. In 2017, Google stopped scanning consumer Gmail to personalize ads after years of criticism.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, requires consent to be free, specific, informed, and unconditional, and limited to the purpose stated. Parts of the Act are already in force, but the main obligations are scheduled to take effect on May 13, 2027, and the consent manager provisions on November 13, 2026. The Act places on the company the burden of proving valid consent for a new use of data, and it is for the Data Protection Board to decide whether one click can cover advertising. Ads in AI Mode for users with Personal Intelligence turned on are now being tested, and Google has said it expected ads to work this way for connected users later.

stories.Headline: GitHub Copilot Fusion halves AI coding costs, matches frontier performance
stories.Summary:
GitHub, the Microsoft-owned platform, unveiled Copilot Fusion on October 28, 2026, at GitHub Universe 2026, describing it as an AI coding capability that performs close to leading models at half the cost. Unlike conventional coding assistants that depend on a single model, the system coordinates several models and decides how to deploy them for a given task. According to the articles, it uses three execution patterns, called single, cascade, and critique, to select the most suitable approach based on complexity and requirements. GitHub's internal evaluation reported that Copilot Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max on the Coding Agent Index benchmark, while finishing tasks at half the cost and in 40 percent less time. Jay Parikh, Executive Vice President of CoreAI at Microsoft, announced the capability and said it first determines what a task requires before choosing an execution pattern.

Alongside Copilot Fusion, GitHub introduced Copilot Projects, which lets developers coordinate multiple AI agents across different code repositories, and the company said this feature is now open to all users. It also launched Copilot Automations, which let developers build AI-powered workflows that run on a schedule, respond to specific events, or start manually. Enterprise customers can reach Copilot capabilities without a separate subscription, paying instead for AI credits based on usage. The Octoverse 2026 report recorded 34.3 billion code commits and 1.3 billion pull requests on the platform during the year, which the company partly linked to growing use of AI agents. To absorb that load, GitHub has added 4 million CPU cores, 160 petabytes of high-speed storage, and 50 terabits per second of network capacity so far this year.

GitHub is also moving to a multi-region deployment on Microsoft Azure, which it expects to finish in early 2027, and it unveiled a redesigned Git architecture meant to handle much higher volumes of agent-generated activity. Parikh's comments and the company's internal benchmark figures are the main claims behind the cost and performance results, and the articles present them as GitHub's own assessment. The New Stack, which covered the launch on the same day, framed Copilot Fusion as a model selection and orchestration system and said it is now generally available. Together, the announcements show GitHub pairing new tooling for multi-agent work with a substantial expansion of the infrastructure needed to run it.

stories.Headline: Azerbaijan to establish Artificial Intelligence Observatory
stories.Summary:
On 27 October 2026, the Ministry of Economy of Azerbaijan and IE University of Spain signed a framework cooperation agreement to establish and develop an Artificial Intelligence Observatory focused on competitiveness and economic transformation. Deputy Minister of Economy Samad Bashirli announced the deal at the opening ceremony of IE University's Leadership and Innovation Center, which was set up with the backing of the Ministries of Economy and Science and Education. One report describes the agreement as part of the AI Hub initiative, and names the university partner as the University of Artificial Intelligence, which differs from the IE University named in the other report. The announcement came the same day as the ceremony, and the reports were published that afternoon and evening.

The observatory is meant to bring together academics, government bodies and business representatives to produce knowledge on Azerbaijan's economic development and to inform policy decisions. Its work will centre on applied research into economic diversification, productivity, competitiveness and international comparisons. The reports say the goal is to turn research findings into practical policy recommendations, and one adds that discussions will be held to support this. The articles do not give a budget, a timetable, staffing numbers or a launch date for the observatory.

Bashirli said the centre would help build human capital, strengthen the country's economic competitiveness and raise its innovation potential. He stated that the aim is to link international knowledge with national economic priorities and to turn investment in people into higher productivity and concrete economic results. He also said that Azerbaijani startups and entrepreneurs would be connected with international innovation networks, investors and experts, and that startups, investors, and technology park residents and operators would be able to benefit from tax incentives lasting up to 20 years, along with incentives for research and development, entrepreneurship investment and hiring international specialists. One report includes a letter from Mikayil Jabbarov that stresses developing human capital and modern technology as priorities.

The reports attribute the announcement to the government, with Bashirli speaking on its behalf, and the framework agreement is between the ministry and the university. The articles offer no comment from other parties or critics. They place the observatory within the country's wider push to diversify its economy and build innovation, and they note the support mechanisms already in place for startups. Beyond the stated plan to carry out the research and hold discussions, the articles do not say what will happen next.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] Guidewire Delivers Core Platform for Agentic Insurance
stories.Summary:
Guidewire, the insurance software company listed on the NYSE as GWRE, launched a new platform approach to agentic insurance on October 28, 2026, at its Connections conference in Las Vegas. The company says the platform gives insurers an open, secure, and complete foundation for using AI across the insurance lifecycle. It brings together applications, data, workflows, and controls so that insurers can move from isolated AI experiments to governed agents that improve the speed and precision of decisions. Guidewire presents this as a practical model for doing so.

The platform places agents on the same system that runs the company's core applications, so they can work with an insurer's current data and workflows. Controls define what each agent can know and do, with consistent security and an audit trail that stays current through ongoing updates. Guidewire describes its growing portfolio across underwriting, claims, and technical infrastructure, including Advanced Product Designer, PricingCenter, Risk Accumulation App, UnderwritingCenter, ProNavigator, Concierge, and Kaleidoscope. Several features, marked as early access or roadmap items, are available only to certain customers, and the company notes that some release features may not be available in all regions.

Mike Rosenbaum, Guidewire's chief executive officer, said that insurance is a business of decisions made in context and that embedding agents in core operations gives them the context and controls they need. Diego Devalle, the company's chief product development officer, said the scalability and observability that support the core now support agents as well, which lets insurers put them to work on live claims and policies. Amy Mollin, vice president of product management, said agents built into ClaimCenter capture losses, summarize files, and flag risk so adjusters have more time for important conversations. Karlyn Carnahan of Celent said the next challenge for insurers is making these capabilities work within existing systems. Tatjana Lalkovic, chief technology officer at Definity, said Guidewire's Developer Assistants help her company's teams move from idea to implementation faster.

The announcement comes as insurers face pressure from competitors to become more agile with products and pricing, and as many have moved past early AI experiments. Guidewire says it is also using AI in its own professional services, where it reports materially shorter migration and implementation timelines. The company is demonstrating the platform at Connections, where more than 3,000 insurers and partners from 36 countries are gathered for its annual customer conference. Guidewire will continue to expand its portfolio of agents, though the announcement itself does not specify a timeline for further releases.

stories.Headline: Nvidia backs Simplismart in $14 million funding for AI efficiency
stories.Summary:
On October 27 and 28, 2026, reports described how Bengaluru-based AI infrastructure startup Simplismart raised $14 million in a Series B round led by Dallas Venture Capital, with Nvidia investing alongside Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. The four-year-old company, founded in 2022 by Amritanshu Jain and Devansh Ghatak, is now valued at about $100 million including the new money. Its software sits between AI models and computing hardware, automating how models are deployed and managed so that customers can tune response speed, request handling and computing consumption. Simplismart employs 58 people.

The funding is aimed at reducing dependence on GPUs, the specialized chips used to run AI models, by helping companies get more out of the hardware they already have. The company plans to use the money to expand its presence in the United States and North America, grow its team, and further develop its inference platform. It also intends to build partnerships with cloud providers and sovereign AI players. Simplismart has also been developing a dynamic GPU scheduling layer intended to match workloads with available capacity across regions and time zones, which would help cloud providers improve utilization. The company does not own computing infrastructure itself, instead supplying the software layer that lets providers offer AI services on their own hardware.

Jain and Ghatak said the advantage in AI now lies in how models are run rather than simply having access to them, pointing to cost per interaction, response speed and reliability as demand grows. Dayakar Puskoor, managing partner at Dallas Venture Capital, said inferencing is becoming one of the biggest factors in AI economics. Jain also said Nvidia has collaborated with Simplismart on technical integrations, including its Dynamo inference software, and has introduced the startup to potential customers and partners. The company has said its software helped video-generation platform InVideo cut GPU serving costs by 56 per cent.

The context is a shift among enterprises toward controlling what it costs to run AI applications in production, as open-weight models offer alternatives to proprietary models accessed through paid interfaces. Simplismart's annualised revenue run rate grew 14-fold over six months to an eight-figure sum, and more than half of its revenue comes from the U.S., even though it has more customers in India. Its clients include HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema, and Indian cloud provider Yotta uses its technology to power the serverless inference layer of Shakti Studio. Simplismart competes with Nvidia itself, major cloud providers and numerous other startups building tools for faster and cheaper AI operations. Jain said the company wins where clients have strict service-level agreements and total cost of ownership requirements.

Sean Hinze, a managing director at Neuberger Specialty Finance, said the firm sees significant value in the power generation assets that support Crusoe's growth. He added that behind-the-meter power is becoming increasingly important to the AI buildout.

Crusoe closed a $3.9 billion Series F round in September at a valuation reported near $31 billion, and it has built data centers for OpenAI, Microsoft and Google in Texas. It is also planning facilities in Tulsa, Oklahoma, Colorado and Norway. Goldman Sachs forecast last year that global electricity demand from AI and cloud computing could reach 84 gigawatts by 2027, and it said demand could add more than 100 gigawatts by the mid-2030s. stories.Headline: Autonomous machine learning
stories.Summary:
Two sources cover very different things, so I will treat them separately. The first is a research article titled "Autonomous machine learning," published in Science China Information Sciences on 28 October 2026 by Wenwu Zhu, Xin Wang and Zhiqiang Xu. The article itself is only partly visible here: it lists a set of references on self-supervised learning, active learning, AutoML, meta-learning and self-directed learning, and notes funding from the Beijing National Research Center for Information Science and Technology under Grant No. BNR2026TD03005. The authors are affiliated with Tsinghua University in Beijing and Xi'an Jiaotong University. The visible text does not state the paper's findings, so no claims about its results can be drawn from it.

The second source, published on 27 October 2026, describes geoscientists in China who used high-resolution 3D seismic imaging together with machine learning to map fault networks in the deep Tarim Basin. Earlier surveys relied on seismic data gathered from widely spaced grids, which could not detect smaller fracture lines. The researchers instead ran 3D reflection surveys in the Shunbei central region and applied machine learning classifiers to millions of seismic data points, which found many low-order branch connections between major fault fragments automatically. The article says this speeded up fault mapping and reduced human bias, though it reports no specific figures for the speedup. Physical sandbox experiments using sand and silicone were also used to model deep basement faulting, and they suggested that large regional faults absorb tectonic strain early on, leaving secondary faults inactive.

The article attributes the work to geoscientists focusing on China and does not name individual researchers. It presents the findings as relevant to understanding continental deformation, planning oil and geothermal extraction in desert environments, and avoiding dangerous drilling problems. stories.Headline: Korea should not sacrifice AI boom over chip dependence fears: IDB economist
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, October 27, 2026, Laura Alfaro, chief economist and economic counselor at the Inter-American Development Bank, told a press conference in Seoul that Korea should keep pursuing the artificial intelligence boom rather than slow growth out of worry about its heavy reliance on semiconductors. She made the remarks at the Global Financial Stability Conference 2026, hosted by the Ministry of Finance and Economy and the Korea Development Institute. Her position was that the country should instead cushion itself against swings through stabilization funds and greater structural flexibility. The comments were reported by the Korea Times and the JoongAng Daily, the latter with a wire contribution from Yonhap.

Alfaro compared Korea's exposure to chips with the "resource curse" that has affected Latin America, where economies dependent on minerals and oil suffer when commodity prices fluctuate sharply. To manage such cycles, she recommended a stabilization fund that would set aside part of the gains made during boom periods and draw on them during downturns. Such a fund could also limit excessive appreciation of the domestic currency and soften the effects of large, rapid capital inflows. She also called for more flexibility in labor markets and government spending, saying the core problem in boom-and-bust cycles is an inability to adjust in downturns. The JoongAng Daily reported that Korea has proposed a Future Fund, drawing on sources including windfall tax revenue from chipmakers, with a general account and four program accounts covering youth, growth engines, regional development, and education and talent development.

Alfaro said she was not familiar with the details of the government's proposed Future Response Fund but supported its underlying rationale, and the JoongAng Daily quoted her as saying the "spirit" of the Future Fund sounds like what needs to be done. Asked whether debt repayment should take priority over building assets, she said neither approach was necessarily superior, since both amount to saving. She also described herself as "AI positive" and argued that concern over volatility should not deter investment in the technology, since productivity gains from AI offer a route to growth in a region facing shrinking birth rates. Separately, she said Latin America's green energy and mineral resources, such as copper, could support mutually beneficial exchange with Korea in AI, given how energy-intensive the technology is. The reports do not indicate any formal government response to these remarks or what steps will follow.

stories.Headline: AI is part of solution for climate change, COP31 pledge says
stories.Summary:
Turkey, which hosts this year's UN COP31 climate summit, has launched a voluntary pledge saying artificial intelligence can help tackle global warming even as data centers add to fossil-fuel pollution. The Antalya AI Pledge will be unveiled at the summit, which starts later this month in the coastal city of Antalya. It recognizes that AI carries environmental risks but could also be used to fight climate change. It is not yet clear which countries will sign up, and the United States, the biggest developer of data centers, is no longer part of the COP process. The pledge asks countries, NGOs and financial institutions to identify voluntary commitments, such as requiring AI providers to disclose their energy and environmental impact data.

It also calls for data centers to run on clean power sources and floats possible targets. Nations would return to next year's summit in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to review progress. Data centers are emerging as a major new source of greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in the U.S., where big tech companies are building new gas-fired power stations to supply them. Their share of global energy use is expected to more than double by 2030, according to BloombergNEF.

Evan Tachovsky, chief data and AI officer at the World Resources Institute, a climate nonprofit, said the pledge sets the right direction but lacks accountability mechanisms to steer countries and tech companies toward better practice. The institute's statement adds that the pledge leaves out commitments to involve communities in data center decisions and safeguards for water and air quality. It urges strong guardrails, including clean power, full disclosure of energy and water use, and companies paying for their own grid upgrades. Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, said last month that AI was energy guzzling and driving up fossil-fuel pollution.

European Union Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said the bloc was examining whether to sign up. The context is a series of UN warnings that the world is on course to overshoot the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 Celsius above pre-industrial levels, which requires sharp emissions cuts this decade. The institute says the pledge's first stocktake at COP32 offers a chance to move from soft intentions to real accountability. Whether countries sign on, and whether the pledge gains enforceable targets, remains to be seen.

stories.Headline: Human in the loop is not yet an AI agent recovery plan
stories.Summary:
Keeping a human in the loop is a common way enterprises govern what AI agents do, but a new study suggests that approval alone does not prepare organizations to recover when things go wrong. Krista Case, principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research, discussed the findings with Dave Vellante, co-founder and chief analyst at theCUBE Research, during a broadcast tied to the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit on October 28, 2026. The research examined how organizations are governing agent actions and preparing for incidents. Case said companies are still leaning heavily on human approval to secure AI actions while pushing to move faster at machine scale. The study drew on 25 enterprise technology and security leaders, 19 of whom had agents in production.

None of those 19 allowed agents to carry out high-risk actions without human involvement. Yet only four of the 25 had tested an AI or agent incident scenario. Vellante compared the gap to organizations that test failover in disaster recovery but never test failback. Case explained that restoring an agent does not reverse the records, transactions and downstream workflows it already touched, so recovery may require rebuilding the sequence of actions the agent took.

Eleven of the 25 practitioners said they lacked full ability to reconstruct agent actions across systems. Speed makes the problem harder, according to Case, because agents can take hundreds or thousands of actions a minute. The research also found a counterintuitive pattern: organizations that let agents perform low-risk actions on their own were more likely to invest in logging, monitoring and recovery infrastructure and to have tested agent incident scenarios. Case described this bounded autonomy as a sign of a more mature security program.

Twelve of the 25 respondents had not addressed, or did not plan to address, detecting anomalous agent behavior, and monitoring and reconstructing agent activity ranked as the least mature capabilities. Vellante said these are the capabilities needed if human-in-the-loop controls break down. Case expects the field to change quickly, saying it is very volatile and will likely look far more advanced within a year. The discussion was part of SiliconANGLE and theCUBE's coverage of the summit, and Dell Technologies sponsored that segment, though neither Dell nor other sponsors have editorial control over the content.

Ozelle, a company founded in Silicon Valley in 2014, announced on October 28, 2026 that it will showcase its O-Cyte 1 automated hematology analyzer at MEDICA 2026. The company says that as AI-assisted morphology becomes part of routine hematology, laboratories need more than automatic cell classification, since cell images must remain available for professional review while analyzers also meet daily testing and maintenance needs. The O-Cyte 1 combines complete blood count testing and 7-part white blood cell differentiation with high-resolution cell imaging and AI-assisted classification in one instrument. Its cell images are linked to numerical results so that laboratory staff can examine visual evidence when needed. The announcement was prompted in part by the International Council for Standardization in Haematology, which approved a new digital morphology standardization project at its October 14 to 15 General Assembly.

The analyzer is built for changing workloads and routine service. A standalone unit delivers up to 60 tests per hour, while a six-unit cascade reaches up to 360 tests per hour. Its integrated reagent kit and key fluid-contact components are housed in consumables, which the company says simplifies reagent handling and reduces routine maintenance. Built-in self-checks and replaceable modules are intended to make faults easier to identify and service. Ozelle also says scalable configurations can serve laboratories with different testing volumes and give distributors a path for future capacity expansion.

Ozelle is the company responsible for the product and the announcement, and it describes the O-Cyte 1 as part of its vision for the fourth generation of hematology analysis. The company says this approach aims to make morphology intelligence more consistent, reviewable and scalable across routine workflows. Ozelle will also feature the EHBT-75, which combines 7-diff hematology with cell imaging and morphology analysis, and the EHBT-50, which integrates hematology, immunoassay and dry biochemistry in a compact platform. Visitors can also see Open Dx, its AI Workbench for AI-assisted report review and result sharing. The company will exhibit at MEDICA 2026 from November 16 to 19 in Hall 1, Booth D63, at Messe Düsseldorf in Germany, where it plans to discuss distribution opportunities.

stories.Headline: Instead of peeking at the future ‘outside’, Korea must find its own ‘new AI coordinates’
stories.Summary:
Korea's Kyunghyang Shinmun published an opinion piece on October 28, 2026, arguing that the country should stop looking abroad for models of artificial intelligence policy and build its own framework. The author begins with the sharp split in public debate, where one camp expects AI to boost growth and offset the demographic decline, while the other warns that falling behind will doom the nation. Both camps, the piece argues, treat AI as an unstoppable force and society as something that must simply adapt. The author claims this framing hides the real question of where society should be heading.

The piece makes the case that technology takes its shape from the institutions it meets, using Korea's COVID-19 epidemiological tracking system as an example. The capability to map large datasets existed by 2014, but the system only emerged after the MERS outbreak prompted legal revisions, the removal of barriers between ministries, standardized data formats, and privacy safeguards. The author describes AI as a mirror that reflects existing prejudices and structural problems and a megaphone that amplifies them. The piece then sketches three phases of modern Korean society, a closed hierarchical era, an open liberal era after 1987, and a fractured winner-takes-all society after the 1998 currency crisis. It says this fracture has produced what the author calls a three-no society marked by distrust, discontent, and anxiety, which AI could accelerate.

The author places much of the responsibility on institutions and on the people who design and run them, arguing that opacity has moved from personal networks into algorithms that set platform fees, welfare screening, and credit scores. The piece also cites the Seongsu Bridge collapse, the Sampoong Department Store collapse, and the Sewol ferry disaster as examples of slow-building disasters rooted in past growth-at-all-costs policies. The author warns of three waves of change, one affecting personal cognition as people outsource thinking, one hitting organizations as automated agents replace the routine tasks through which newcomers learn, and one from physical AI reaching care, logistics, construction, and manufacturing. The piece says Korea cannot simply copy the American market model, the Chinese state model, or the European regulatory model, and proposes "dignity" as the goal, built on safety, cohesion, inclusion, and capability. The excerpt ends before the author details the specific measures, so the articles provided do not include the full set of proposed changes or numbers beyond the dates above.
