stories.Headline: Dartmouth Provost Resigns Over AI Use
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth University Provost Santiago Schnell resigned on a Wednesday after a faculty-led review committee concluded that he used artificial intelligence to meaningfully alter his writing and fell short of the university's academic integrity standards. The controversy began in August, when Semafor reported that the AI detector Pangram flagged an editorial Schnell wrote for The Washington Post as at least 80 percent AI generated. The Dartmouth student newspaper later applied the same tool to nine professional articles he published this year and found them to be 96 percent AI written, including the Post essay and two academic papers on mathematics. Schnell acknowledged using AI to help with his writing, but he said it did not substitute for his research, intellectual judgment or authorship.

President Sian Leah Beilock convened an independent advisory committee of faculty and alumni to examine his AI use, whether he met publishers' disclosure requirements, whether he was honest about that use, and whether it violated university policy. The committee's eight-page report, delivered to Beilock on Tuesday, did not rely on AI detectors, which it did not use, and instead examined articles written for publishers that barred or required disclosure of AI use, along with records from Schnell's university Claude account. According to the report, he used the university's enterprise version of Claude to substantially edit a manuscript published in ChemSystemsChem last month, troubleshoot code and generate figures after peer reviewers requested major revisions. The committee also found that the publisher had required disclosure of such use since at least 2023, while Schnell had said the requirement began in 2025. It further concluded that his disclosures and public statements understated how he had used AI, and that he had not provided logs from personal AI accounts when asked.

Beilock wrote in a memo to students, faculty and staff that she expects senior leaders to hold themselves to the highest standards, and she said Schnell resigned out of respect for his colleagues and the institution. The resignation came less than two weeks before faculty leaders were set to hold a no-confidence vote against him. In the same message, Beilock said Dartmouth, which calls itself the birthplace of AI, would continue to keep pace with the technology while modeling transparency and human judgment. Matthew Delmont, a history professor and associate dean of faculty for international and interdisciplinary studies, will serve as interim provost through June 2028.

The launch follows faster shifts in business priorities, skills demand and talent availability across employers.

Cielo cited its own Talent Benchmark research, which found that 87% of organizations increased talent acquisition technology investment over the past 12 months, yet many still struggle to turn that spending into greater hiring agility. Rather than optimizing isolated hiring steps, it treats talent acquisition as a connected business capability.

Cielo says this moves hiring beyond faster task execution toward better decisions and quicker responses to shifting demand. Cielo's chief operating officer, Molly Thiel, said the platform is meant to reduce friction so recruiters can spend more time advising the business and making accountable decisions. stories.Headline: Montana State scientist part of team working to improve weather forecasting with artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Colorado State University scientists are building a forecasting system that uses artificial intelligence to detect destructive hailstorms earlier and more accurately, according to a report dated October 26, 2026. The project is led by atmospheric and radar scientists at the university, including Kristen Rasmussen, an associate professor of atmospheric science. Current forecasts often give hail warnings with less than 30 minutes of notice, while the team hopes to predict hail several hours or even days ahead in Colorado and Wyoming. The effort is funded by the National Science Foundation and combines a short-term nowcasting model developed with NVIDIA and a machine learning model for longer-range storm prediction.

The project is part of the ASCEND Engine, which works with researchers, start-ups, and public and private partners in both states to develop technologies for regional challenges such as severe weather. The engine launched in 2023 and carries a total 10-year federal award of up to $160 million. The system is meant to merge regional radar data with nine years of historic weather observations from across the country. Researchers say the work matters because hail damages crops, roofs and vehicles, and rising homeowners insurance costs in part reflect those risks. The article notes that the window for large hail events is expanding into earlier spring and later fall months.

Chandrasekar, a University Distinguished Professor who manages the regional radar systems, led work with NVIDIA on a model called Hail-StormScope that produces hailstorm forecasts with a two- to three-hour lead time. Russ Schumacher, a professor in the Department of Atmospheric Science, leads the other half of the project, which uses machine learning to assess storm conditions across the country over one- to eight-day windows. His model, called Colorado State University-Machine Learning Probabilities, compares past storm conditions with simulated environments and human forecasts. Schumacher said the team must decide whether to merge the short-term and long-term approaches into one system or keep them separate. Rasmussen said the initial results have been encouraging.

The next step is scheduled for spring 2027, when the team plans to install RM60 sensors from Vaisala near the CSU-CHIVO radar in Greeley to gather ground data for validating the new forecasts. Rasmussen said the models already offer resolution of about 1.3 kilometers and better represent storm interactions around the state's mountains. The article reports that the sensors have not yet been widely used to assess hail. Researchers say the project should improve forecasting and build trust with human forecasters who want to understand how the system reaches its conclusions. The team plans to continue the work with the National Science Foundation and other partners.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open-weight, promptable speech model, on October 28, 2026, through Hugging Face and ModelScope, alongside Granary v2, an expanded open multilingual speech dataset and curation pipeline. The model combines transcription, speaker attribution, translation, and audio question answering in a single checkpoint. It transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13, handling recordings up to an hour long with up to eight speakers. Developers can steer its output with natural language prompts, choose where audio is processed, and adapt it to domain vocabulary and accents. The model is a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts system with about 4 billion parameters active per token, so it can run on hardware ranging from a Jetson AGX Thor or DGX Spark to Blackwell data-center GPUs.

Quantized versions are described as coming soon, and local deployment through NeMo-Speech.cpp is also forthcoming. Granary v2 covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in the first version, and generates three transcript styles per recording. Transcribe is built for recorded audio rather than live streaming. The company also says NeMo Speech fine-tuning tools let developers adapt the model further, and in one medical case study fine-tuning cut word error rate on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt. NVIDIA is the company behind the release, and its materials make the performance claims.

On the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models for English at 5.33% average word error rate. Artificial Analysis places it at 2.8% AA-WER, tied for first among open-weight models. On David AI's multilingual diarization benchmark across 21 languages, it posts the lowest diarization error rate of the 14 systems tested, and on VoiceArena's English full-session benchmark it has the lowest concatenated error rate. Agora has also shown a classroom demo that pairs word-level timestamps with replay recordings. These results come from the company and third-party leaderboards, and the articles note that developers should still spot-check names, speaker changes, and answers against the original recording.

stories.Headline: Maharashtra Govt Sets Up 3-Tier Panels to Oversee AI Policy, Approve Incentives

On Wednesday, October 28, 2026, the Maharashtra government issued a Government Resolution setting up three committees to oversee its Artificial Intelligence Policy 2026. The committees include a state-level executive panel that will approve incentives and subsidies for AI projects. The news was reported by the Press Trust of India and carried by several outlets that day. The first body is a State Level Steering Committee headed by the chief secretary, which will give strategic direction and oversee implementation of the policy. This committee must meet at least once every six months. The second is an Executive Committee led by the secretary of the electronics, information technology and artificial intelligence department, which will approve proposals for incentives and subsidies. It will also coordinate multi-department AI projects, help build partnerships with AI companies and research institutions, and review progress quarterly. The third body, a Technical Committee, will check proposals for technical compliance and eligibility and recommend suitable cases to the Executive Committee. It will also monitor projects once they have been approved.

The government also plans an online portal to help carry out the Maharashtra AI Policy. The policy itself was announced on May 6, and it aims to promote the use of AI technology and encourage AI-based initiatives across government departments. The reports do not name individual officials beyond the posts described, and they do not say what incentive amounts or subsidy rates the committees will offer. They also do not give a timeline for when the online portal will go live. The articles present the committee structure as the government's mechanism for putting the policy into practice, with the Executive Committee holding the authority to approve funding for projects.

stories.Headline: AI and the quiet erosion of human judgment
stories.Summary:
Winnipeg Free Press columnist Rod Lastra, in an opinion piece posted on October 28, 2026, argues that the quiet loss of human judgment is a more pressing concern than the predictions surrounding artificial intelligence. He opens by recalling Paul Simon's 1986 song The Boy in the Bubble, using its image of a world more technologically capable but not necessarily wiser as a frame for the present. Lastra notes that predictions about AI have multiplied since ChatGPT's release in November 2022, and that tech leaders have talked up approaching superintelligence and futures ranging from flourishing to catastrophe. He says these predictions often carry more confidence than evidence.

The column's central concern is whether people can still understand, question and oversee AI outputs as systems grow more capable and take on more complex work. Lastra explains that AI is not a single technology, that fluency does not guarantee accuracy, and that agentic systems can carry out sequences of actions on people's behalf. He describes a paradox in which delegating work to gain efficiency can produce so much output that meaningful human review becomes difficult. He also points to Manitoba's Bill 51, the Public Sector Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity Governance Act, which recognizes human oversight as part of responsible AI governance, while asking whether that capacity could be lost anyway. Signing off on a result, he writes, is not the same as understanding it.

Lastra's thought experiment describes an organization in which one AI analyzes thousands of records, a second summarizes the findings, and a manager approves the recommendation, leaving the question of what was actually reviewed. He warns of oversight fatigue, in which approval becomes routine once recommendations arrive faster than people can examine them, and he cites automated financial trading as an earlier example of transactions outpacing human intervention. The more work is delegated, he argues, the fewer chances people have to practise the judgment needed to supervise it, so dependence can reinforce itself. He says the aim is not to reject AI but to adopt it deliberately, defining its purpose, testing it under real conditions, keeping the ability to intervene and allowing time for review. He adds that AI literacy must mean more than writing prompts.

A separate opinion piece on UPI.com, published October 27, 2026 by Carlos Cantero Ojeda, raises a parallel concern for Latin America. It notes that the fourth Latin American Artificial Intelligence Index, released October 20, 2026 by Chile's National Center for Artificial Intelligence and the U.N. Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, ranks 20 countries, with Chile first, followed by Brazil and Uruguay. Cantero Ojeda argues that technological readiness differs from human agency, which he describes as the capacity to act intentionally, reflect on choices and accept responsibility for them. He draws on the work of Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to argue that AI systems are designed and sustained from outside themselves, so they cannot carry the ethical judgment and moral responsibility that people bear. He describes the weakening of attention and deliberation as "agency starvation," which he attributes partly to platform designs that narrow what people see and make reasoning harder to follow.

stories.Headline: Businesses increasingly adopt AI for cybersecurity while individuals expand privacy protections
stories.Summary:
Businesses across the OECD are turning to artificial intelligence to defend against cyber threats, while individuals are using privacy tools to take more control of their personal data, according to new OECD data released in late October 2026. In 2023, 17.7% of enterprises in the OECD experienced ICT security incidents, a rise of 28.2% from 2018. In 2025, 5.3% of enterprises used AI for ICT security, roughly one quarter of all enterprises using AI. Uses include machine learning systems that detect and prevent attacks and AI-based user authentication. Adoption in 2025 was 23.2% higher than in 2024, 68.6% higher than in 2023, and more than double the 2021 level.

Use of AI for security depends heavily on company size and sector. In 2025, 26.7% of large enterprises used AI for ICT security, compared with 9.6% of medium-sized enterprises and 3.7% of small ones. Among industries, 18.1% of firms in information and communication reported using it, well ahead of professional, scientific and technical activities at 8.9%. Adoption in the ICT sector was about nine times higher than in accommodation and food services, at 2.1%. The OECD suggests these tools spread most in information-intensive sectors, where cyber risks and reliance on digital systems are greatest.

Individuals are also acting more on their own data. Between 2020 and 2025, the share changing browser settings to limit cookies rose by 26.8%, while those refusing personal data use for advertising rose by 17.2% and those restricting access to their location rose by 14.0%. Smaller increases were seen for limiting social media profile access (11.3%) and using anti-tracking software (7.0%). The OECD links these trends to more privacy controls in browsers, operating systems and online platforms, and to greater awareness of data protection. By 2025, more than half of individuals had either restricted location access or refused personal data use for advertising, while the share reading privacy policies before sharing data fell by about 8.4%.

Concern about privacy is rarely the reason people avoid generative AI, with only 4.5% of OECD individuals citing it as their main reason in 2025. Older adults aged 55 to 74 were more likely than those aged 16 to 24 to avoid AI over such concerns, at 5.8% against 1.9%, and less likely to take active privacy steps. Younger people reported fewer worries about AI but frequently used privacy controls and anti-tracking tools. Education also shapes privacy behaviour: individuals with higher attainment were far more likely to refuse personal data use for advertising (68.1% against 39.5%) and to restrict location access (65.8% against 38.9%) than those with low attainment, although concern about generative AI was similar across both groups.

stories.Headline: Meta survey finds most Asia-Pacific small firms use AI
stories.Summary:
Meta has published research showing that most small business owners across Asia-Pacific already use artificial intelligence. The YouGov survey, covering almost 4,000 small business owners in Australia, Singapore, Vietnam, Indonesia, Taiwan, India, Thailand, Japan and Hong Kong, found that 84% use AI. Of those surveyed, 76% said it had a positive effect on productivity, and 71% said it had improved revenue or sales over the past 12 months. The findings, reported on 28 October 2026, point to wide uptake among smaller companies in the region.

The research also shows a gap between using AI and feeling confident about it. Eighty-six percent of owners said small businesses need more guidance to get the full benefits, and 51% named the cost of training as the main barrier. Respondents tied AI to the constraints smaller firms often face, with four in five saying it helps them compete with larger companies and the same share saying it makes starting a business easier. Another 83% said it lets small firms do things that once required much more money or resources. Among owners reporting higher productivity, 58% used the saved time to improve the quality of their existing work, half put it toward growth and planning, and 46% said it helped their current teams get more done.

Meta's survey says that day-to-day use remains centred on routine tasks. Among owners whose businesses used AI in the past year, 51% used it to create or edit content, 43% for local advertising and marketing, 38% for translation, and 37% for customer support and communications. Owners also said they want clearer information on costs, likely returns, and how to handle data privacy and security. Meta cited Husnul Khotimah, founder of the Indonesian modest fashion brand Zayya, as an example. She said she used Meta's Small Business Growth Academy and its advertising tools to expand into Malaysia on a daily budget of about USD $1.68, which Meta said generated 50 enquiries, cut response times from 30 to 60 minutes to under two minutes, and returned more than eight times the ad spend.

Meta is using the findings to promote demand for training. Its Small Business Growth Academy, launched across Asia-Pacific, offers courses on AI-enabled advertising, Reels, WhatsApp for Business and cross-border commerce, delivered through partnerships with governments, chambers of commerce and local programme groups. The report notes that technology companies are keen to present AI as a routine part of how smaller firms operate, not just a tool for large organisations with dedicated digital teams. The article concludes that AI is already part of many owners' everyday work, particularly in marketing and content, and that the harder question is whether businesses can move from basic use to more informed use without costs they cannot easily absorb.

stories.Headline: Qlik Introduces Semantic Models for Shared Business Context Across Analytics and AI
stories.Summary:
Qlik, the data and analytics company, has introduced Semantic Models, a new capability that lets teams define, govern and reuse business definitions within data products. The announcement was made on October 28, 2026, in a press release distributed by GlobeNewswire from Philadelphia. The company says the feature is aimed at reducing duplicated modeling work and giving analytics and AI tools a consistent basis for reading enterprise data. Qlik describes the problem with an example: a question about net revenue depends not only on sales records but also on the company's rules for returns, discounts and reporting periods.

Semantic Models add reusable business logic to Qlik's existing data product features, which already cover curated datasets, ownership, lineage and data quality information. The feature connects governed business terms from a business glossary with the measures and dimensions used across analytics and data products. Qlik also says a new extraction capability, initially in public preview on October 28, will let teams bring definitions from existing Qlik analytics applications into governed, discoverable data products, with general availability planned later in the fourth quarter. The company plans to extend semantic model support to Qlik Answers and MCP tools, targeting general availability or shortly after, and to add AI assistance for creating and maintaining these models. Semantic Models are targeted for general availability on October 28, 2026, in Qlik Cloud Analytics and Qlik Talend Cloud Premium and Enterprise editions, and in Qlik Sense Enterprise SaaS.

Sam Pierson, Chief Technology Officer at Qlik, said that a number can be mathematically correct and still answer the wrong business question, and that teams need to know which definition applies and use it consistently. Henri Rufin, Head of Data & Analytics at Radiall, said in a company statement that the feature gives his team a shared understanding of the business and avoids recreating context for each new use case. Qlik also says it is developing interoperability with Apache Ossie, an open-source initiative at the Apache Software Foundation that is still incubating, with a public preview planned as the work progresses. The company describes its wider aim as helping customers use AI with data they can rely on and control, while working with the systems and partners they already use. Media contact details were listed as Keith Parker at 512-367-2884.

stories.Headline: Teens often turn to AI when feeling distressed; report flags mental health risks
stories.Summary:
A new report from The Jed Foundation, a youth mental health organization, links some uses of artificial intelligence with poorer mental health among teenagers. The group surveyed thousands of middle and high school students and found that more than 80% use AI in some capacity. It did not find a link between overall AI use and worse mental health, but it did find associations among students who used AI for schoolwork, problem-solving advice, companionship, or help when they were emotionally struggling. The report was published this week as a follow-up to a Capitol Hill briefing the researchers held over the summer.

Students who used AI for schoolwork reported higher levels of loneliness and a greater lifetime history of suicidal thoughts. Those who turned to AI for relationship or problem-solving advice showed greater symptoms of anxiety and depression, more loneliness, and higher suicidal risk. Students who used AI for friendship or companionship, or who sought help from it when emotionally struggling, had greater anxiety and depression symptoms, more loneliness, and a history of suicidal thoughts and attempts. They also reported lower resilience and flourishing. Most students, 58%, said they use AI for schoolwork, while 12% said they use it for friendship or companionship.

The report's author, Kayla Anderson, JED's vice president of research and evaluation, said the way adults talk with young people about AI matters a great deal. She noted that 57% of students said they use AI when they feel sad, stressed, lonely or overwhelmed, though only 8% said they specifically sought help with their feelings from it. Anderson said AI should never replace human counsel and connection for young people. She also cautioned that the study found an association rather than a cause, and that it is still unclear how much AI itself drives worse outcomes. She said it is plausible that already struggling kids lean on AI more, and that such use could also worsen their problems.

Anderson said the issue needs to be addressed at the systems level, with tools designed specifically for safety. For parents, she said the first advice is not to let young people use AI as a friend or companion, since AI companions are associated with worse mental health in teens. She added that families should have early and frequent conversations about what young people use AI for, so that they do not hand too much of their thinking and relationship work to the technology. Anderson stressed that such work should stay in human spaces.

stories.Headline: ASMPT sales jump 49% on AI chip packaging as core equipment unit misses
stories.Summary:
ASMPT, the Hong Kong-listed chip equipment maker, reported third-quarter revenue of HK$5.25 billion, about $669 million, up 49% from a year earlier, according to a Bloomberg report published October 28, 2026. Its advanced packaging business drove nearly all of that growth, while its semiconductor solutions segment, which sells front-end manufacturing gear, came in just short of analyst expectations. The company guided fourth-quarter revenue to between $670 million and $730 million. The split result points to packaging, rather than front-end chipmaking tools, as the current bottleneck in AI hardware. Advanced packaging is now growing faster than the equipment that makes the chips themselves.

Thermo-compression bonding equipment, used to stack high-bandwidth memory onto AI accelerators, is the fastest-growing piece. ASMPT's advanced packaging unit posted record first-half revenue of $339 million in 2026, up 17% year over year. Thermo-compression bonding revenue grew 146% in the most recent period covered by the company's disclosures. The company has said the addressable market for its bonding tools alone could top $1.6 billion by 2028. ASMPT's legacy business trails well behind that growth.

The constraint now lies in packaging capacity rather than wafer output. TSMC's CoWoS capacity, the process that binds compute dies to memory stacks, is reportedly booked through 2027. Nvidia alone is expected to need about 1.2 million CoWoS wafers that year, while AMD's needs are projected to rise roughly 308%, from about 130,000 wafers in 2026 to 530,000 in 2027. AMD has reportedly routed about half its packaging orders to ASE, SPIL and Amkor. SK Hynix, which along with Samsung and Micron controls nearly all HBM supply, has committed roughly $12.85 billion to a new packaging facility in Cheongju, South Korea.

ASM International, a separate Dutch equipment maker often confused with ASMPT, reported its own record quarter the same day, with revenue of €1.159 billion, up 44% at constant currencies. It now expects to reach €5.7 billion in 2027 revenue, a target it had originally set for 2030. Similar AI-driven beats have come from SK Hynix and TSMC this year. Companies selling into advanced packaging and HBM are beating guidance, while those in legacy chipmaking equipment are relying on a recovery in the mainstream market.

stories.Headline: Army taps AWS and WWT to boost AI-enabled cybersecurity initiative
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Army has selected Amazon Web Services and World Wide Technology to support Project Griffin, a pilot effort to build an AI-enabled cybersecurity capability, the service announced in late October 2026. The pilot has a combined value of $2.6 million and falls under the Army Rapid Development of Cyber Defense Systems program, which is driven by the project manager for cyber warfare under the portfolio management executive for intelligence and spectrum warfare. Army Cyber Command is also involved in the initiative. The selections followed a solicitation released in August for agentic AI solutions for an Intelligent Response and Orchestration Node capability, and the Army received more than 100 industry submissions before choosing two vendors.

The Army is seeking an agentic, autonomous AI platform that can help cyber defenders neutralize threats faster than human operators can. The goal is to reduce vulnerabilities that arise when network protection depends on manual data review and human action. The system is meant to draw on information from the Army's network sensors and take defensive measures against potential threats. Project Griffin is one of the first efforts under Project ARDS, which uses rapid industry sprints to speed the adoption of AI-enabled cyber defense tools. The pilot is one of three fast-tracked efforts under that initiative.

Brandon Pugh, the secretary of the Army's principal cyber advisor, leads the ARDS work and said the selections let the service move at the speed of business needed to deliver the capability. He said the Army will quickly deploy tools that detect, divert and deceive threat actors, and adopt agentic AI to scale network defense securely. Col. David Bergmann, project manager for cyber warfare, said partnering with commercial industry is a national security imperative because private firms drive rapid innovation in AI, cloud architecture and cyber operations. Officials at AWS and WWT did not immediately respond to requests for comment, though a WWT executive publicly highlighted the selection on LinkedIn.

The pilot comes after other recent Army cybersecurity moves, including the naming of eight companies in May to compete for work under a potential $49 million contract backing the Next-Gen Commercial Operations in Defended Enclaves pilot for small defense suppliers. The Army also enlisted Keysight to test zero trust security on its unified network. Defense officials are increasingly focused on the threat of AI-enabled digital attacks against their systems, and Project Griffin is intended to answer that threat with commercial tools. The articles do not say when the pilot will conclude or when its capabilities will be fielded across the Army's networks.

stories.Headline: OpenAI now lets you text your Dot.
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has begun rolling out a feature that lets users text their Dot, its AI agent, through iMessage or RCS. The company said the feature is arriving in preview for US Pro users, after it had promised the capability for its AI agents. The Verge reported the news on October 28, 2026, noting that the feature is now available. The article itself is short and focused on the launch rather than on details about pricing or wider availability.

Separately, a Vocal Media piece published on October 28, 2026 reported that OpenAI is introducing an invisible watermark for text generated by ChatGPT and Codex. The system, called textGrain, slightly shifts word choices to embed a statistical pattern that is undetectable to readers but can be identified by a detector. It is set to apply by default only to users in the European Union, so a user in Munich would generate watermarked text while a user in Malaysia would not, unless a developer opts in through the API. The watermark does not identify the individual user, and it survives basic copying and pasting.

OpenAI itself acknowledged that the watermark is fragile, according to the article. In internal testing, replacing 10% of words in a 400-token passage with synonyms dropped detection accuracy from 92% to 66%, and swapping 25% of words reduced it to 17%. Detection is also weaker on short passages, math answers, and translated text, and OpenAI is limiting access to the detector to approved researchers and expert organizations for now. The company cautioned that a missing watermark does not prove human authorship, and a present watermark does not show how much human editing shaped the output.

The article places the move within a wider industry effort to establish AI provenance ahead of regulatory deadlines, including the EU AI Act's transparency rules that took effect on August 2. Google uses its SynthID watermark, Meta uses Content Seal, and Microsoft and Adobe back the C2PA standard, while Anthropic announced in August that it would watermark Claude text worldwide and faced user backlash. The article notes that open-source models can generate unwatermarked text and that each company's detector typically recognizes only its own mark. It concludes that text watermarking remains a probabilistic tool rather than definitive proof of authorship.

stories.Headline: Vera Health has secured $28.5M for clinical AI search platform
stories.Summary:
Vera Health, a company that offers an AI search platform for clinicians, announced on October 27, 2026 that it had secured $28.5 million in Series A funding, bringing its total raised to $32 million. Threshold Ventures led the round, with participation from Mantis VC and SV Angel, and existing investors Y Combinator and Gradient also put more money in. Fierce Healthcare reported that Optum Ventures took part as well. The platform is free for licensed clinicians and medical trainees, who can ask questions about diagnoses, medication dosing, guidelines and treatment and receive summaries linked to their sources.

The company plans to use the new capital to improve its platform, scale into more healthcare markets and expand partnerships with medical societies, publishers and health systems. It also intends to keep investing in locally relevant clinical guidance and in tools that let healthcare institutions add their own medical knowledge to the platform through its Vera Spaces offering. Fierce Healthcare reported that the platform scans more than 60 million peer-reviewed publications, clinical guidelines, consensus statements and drug labels, and that it is used by more than 800,000 clinicians in 190 countries, up from a few thousand a year earlier. The company also said it doubled its team from six to 12 people and is now hiring internationally.

Taieb Bennani, a cofounder of Vera Health, has described the company's focus on clinicians and its emphasis on evidence. He said clinicians make decisions in seconds and that the team, which includes clinicians or their relatives, builds the product around that need. Threshold Ventures co-founder and managing partner Emily Melton said in a statement that the platform starts with evidence rather than just an answer, which helps clinicians assess the research behind a decision. Bennani also told Fierce Healthcare that the company's approach rests on honesty, traceability, transparency and context, and that the tool searches for evidence before writing an answer.

The funding comes amid growing competition in clinical AI search. MobiHealthNews noted that OpenEvidence secured $250 million in Series D funding in January, doubling its valuation to $12 billion, and that Doximity recently partnered with Wolters Kluwer Health to bring UpToDate content into its Ask tool. Fierce Healthcare added that established reference companies such as Elsevier's ClinicalKey and Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate are competing with AI-native tools as well as consumer technology firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. The articles do not say what Vera Health will do next beyond the plans already described.

stories.Headline: Nvidia Stock Faces a Test From Its Biggest AI Chip Rival
stories.Summary:
Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, known as TSMC, have both become major players in artificial intelligence, according to a Motley Fool analysis by Adria Cimino published on October 28, 2026. Nvidia designs the graphics processing units that handle major AI tasks, while TSMC manufactures those chips. Both companies have seen revenue climb sharply, and their stock prices have risen more than 400% and 300%, respectively, over three years. The article asks which of the two may be the bigger AI winner. It examines each business before weighing their prospects.

The article describes Nvidia as the market leader in GPUs, a position it attributes to starting work on AI roughly a decade ago and to its annual product updates. Its CUDA parallel computing platform and wide range of products give customers a reason to stay with it, and the author notes that this lock-in helps Nvidia charge premium prices. The company's gross margin consistently tops 70%, and in the most recent quarter its revenue jumped 106% to $96 billion. TSMC, by contrast, holds more than 70% of the pure foundry market according to Counterpoint Research, and it makes chips for most major players, including Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom. Because TSMC benefits no matter which chip designer leads, the author calls it a rather safe AI stock.

The article's assessment is that both companies are likely to keep growing as AI moves into real-world use. TSMC reported its sixth straight quarter of record profit, with revenue of $46 billion for the period, and the author notes that its manufacturing overhead, including facilities and expensive equipment, adds costs that Nvidia does not carry. The author concludes that Nvidia's pricing power and market dominance may keep it a step ahead in growth in the coming years. The piece says both are likely to remain AI success stories, but it names Nvidia and its investors as the probable biggest winners. The article does not describe any specific regulatory action or future event that would change this outlook.

stories.Headline: Bond investors have gotten picky about AI
stories.Summary:
Bond investors have grown more selective about which AI-linked borrowers they will finance, even as AI borrowing keeps rising. The shift follows a sell-off in early October, when yields on bonds issued by CoreWeave, a heavily indebted AI company, climbed sharply, meaning its bond prices fell. Since then the broader corporate bond market has calmed, and enthusiasm around Anthropic and Meta has helped restore confidence in the AI trade that supports stock prices. Axios reporter Matt Phillips, writing on October 28, 2026, says that calm hides lingering caution toward the more leveraged players.

The price moves have spread beyond CoreWeave itself. Bonds that finance data centers leased to CoreWeave, including those issued by Edged Compute, Core Scientific and Applied Digital, saw their yields creep higher after CoreWeave's bonds fell, with CoreWeave's own unsecured bonds reaching yields of around 16 percent. Data center debt tied to Oracle has moved in step with Oracle's own bonds. Roughly $14 billion of bonds maturing in 2045, issued to build a large data center campus in Saline Township, Michigan, wobbled along with Oracle's over the past couple of weeks. Ratings agencies say Oracle's signed 17-year lease for that campus is a major support for those bonds.

Citigroup's high-yield debt analysts said in a note last week that tenant-specific risk was exposed during the October pullback, with CoreWeave and similar neocloud and data center companies bearing most of the selloff. They warned that data center bonds are not immune to tenant default and can reprice quickly as that risk rises. Axios reports that the same pattern is visible among safer investment-grade bonds, where investors now distinguish sharply between borrowers rather than treating AI-related debt as largely interchangeable. The articles do not say how these conditions will evolve.

stories.Headline: When artificial intelligence wears a famous face
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Iowa State University, working with colleagues at Indiana University and the University of Sydney, studied how customers respond when a customer service agent is a digital twin of a celebrity. The study, published in the Journal of Management Information Systems in October 2026, examined a trend called "Celebrity-as-a-Service," in which companies use AI-powered or human-operated replicas of famous people to talk with customers. In the experiments, the team built a prototype that placed actor Hugh Jackman's face onto a digital representative, doing so under U.S. fair use rules for research. Lingyao (Ivy) Yuan, an associate professor of information systems and business analytics, led the work. Her team chose Jackman because he is widely recognized and has a largely positive public image.

The researchers ran two controlled experiments in which participants dealt with either the celebrity version or a non-celebrity version of the same representative, which gave identical help. Participants rated the celebrity agent more favorably on whether it seemed capable, benevolent and honest, even though the service itself never changed. In a second experiment, the team introduced common errors such as mishearing a name or misunderstanding an address. Participants using the celebrity version were more forgiving of these mistakes and less angry about them. The study also found no sign of "algorithm aversion," meaning people were not harsher toward an AI-controlled avatar than toward a human-controlled one.

Yuan explained that people often carry positive feelings about a well-liked person over to whatever that person is associated with, a pattern she described as a halo effect. She said participants seemed to transfer those feelings to the service itself. She argued that the technology is becoming more common and that the key question is how people respond to it and how those responses shape their decisions. The study suggests companies could tailor virtual representatives to a customer's age, language or preferences, which Yuan presented as a possibility rather than a current practice.

Yuan stressed that transparency and ethical guidelines will matter more as the technology develops, so customers always know when they are dealing with AI rather than a real person. She said the technology can offer real value when used in a regulated and ethical way. Her summary was that a familiar face may not change how well a service works, but it can change how people feel about using it. The articles do not describe any specific regulations or further studies that are planned.

stories.Headline: ‘If you’re hungry in the city, this building’s for you,’ Met Council says of new, $25 million, AI-powered Brooklyn warehouse
stories.Summary:
The Met Council, a Jewish anti-poverty organization, opened a new $25 million, AI-powered food distribution warehouse in Canarsie, Brooklyn, on Monday, October 26, 2026. The 22,000-square-foot facility lets people in need order groceries in advance for home delivery or pickup, instead of taking whatever is available at a pantry. Roughly 250 people attended the opening, which the organization called the largest capital project in its history. The warehouse was built to serve up to a million people a year, and the group hopes to eventually triple its current reach beyond the more than 350,000 New Yorkers it serves annually.

The facility uses advanced cold storage, automation and artificial intelligence to manage inventory and distribute food more efficiently. It supports the Met Council's network of more than 200 food pantry partners across the five boroughs, along with year-round kosher and halal distributions. It also helps the group provide medically tailored meals and groceries to eligible Medicaid recipients through New York's Social Care Network program. Officials described the project as a major step in expanding the group's ability to feed hungry New Yorkers. The building was reported to have taken about five years to develop.

David Greenfield, the Met Council's chief executive, said the organization was building infrastructure to fight poverty on a much larger scale, and he called the project a labor of love. He told attendees that anyone who is hungry in the city is welcome at the building, regardless of background or language. Joseph Allerhand, the group's co-president, said the facility shows its commitment to feeding those who need help most, including working-class and middle-class families. Speakers at the event, including New York City Comptroller Mark Levine and state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli, praised the use of technology to reduce waste and serve more people.

The project sits within growing demand for food assistance across the city, and speakers linked the work to public safety and community strength. Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said his own family needed help to get by and that such support can strengthen neighborhoods. Greenfield closed by citing a Torah commandment to care for the widow, the orphan and the stranger, saying an open hand is open to everyone. The articles do not describe any further phases or timelines beyond the reach the organization hopes to reach over time.

stories.Headline: States Don’t Have to Solve the AI Education Equation Alone. Tennessee Shows How
stories.Summary:
States across the country are taking different approaches to AI policy, with governors forming task forces, state education agencies issuing non-binding guidance, and legislatures requiring districts to adopt AI policies. A November 2025 survey found that 93% of 29 state education agency respondents had communicated or planned to communicate a vision for AI in K-12 education, but only 43% had assisted or planned to assist districts with implementation support. Among the 39 states and territories studied for a state early adopter database, just 11% had reached the "integrator" stage of moving past guidance into pilots, evaluation, procurement help, and implementation strategies. The authors, Bree Dusseault and Dana Harrison of the Center on Reinventing Public Education, argue that this gap leaves schools without the practical help they need. The authors say AI is a difficult policy area because both the technology and public opinion change quickly, so guidance and task forces alone fall short.

School and district leaders need state help with vetting products, generating evidence on what works, and building trust in how AI is used. States also need infrastructure that links policy to classroom practice and turns scattered local experiments into shared knowledge. The article notes that many state education agencies lack the funding or internal expertise to lead these efforts. Intermediary organizations, the authors write, can fill that role, and a majority of participants in their study reported pursuing partnerships for strategy development, implementation, or both.

The article uses Tennessee's State Collaborative on Reforming Education, known as SCORE, as its main example. SCORE is a statewide nonprofit without formal authority over district decisions, and its influence comes from long-standing relationships with state leaders, districts, colleges, funders, and technology providers. After Tennessee required districts to adopt AI policies covering safety, academic integrity, and risk mitigation, SCORE convened a working group that met regularly for roughly 18 months, and its recommendations were reflected in the state's Action Plan. SCORE also helps districts evaluate tools without endorsing products, and it helped fund a larger rollout of Coursemojo, an AI-enabled literacy tool, across seven districts, 20 schools, and more than 4,000 students in 2025-26.

The authors say participating leaders and teachers reported positive results, and districts later renewed the work, often with their own funds. The authors stress that the Tennessee model need not be copied exactly, since an intermediary could be a nonprofit, a university, a technical service provider, or a research group, as long as it has trust, staying power, and the ability to connect people who do not normally work together. They warn that without such coordinated support, better-resourced districts may experiment while smaller and higher-need systems struggle to evaluate tools, set safeguards, and provide training, which could widen existing inequities. They conclude that the next phase of state AI leadership will depend less on publishing guidance than on building infrastructure for continuous learning, so that policies set direction and partnerships provide the capacity to follow it.

stories.Headline: Opera launches local browser AI, testing enterprise privacy and AI PC strategies
stories.Summary:
Opera has begun rolling out AI models that run locally in its browser, and it introduced WebAI, a proposed web standard, as an opt-in early preview in its Opera One browser on October 27, 2026. The technology lets websites and browser extensions reach AI models running on the user's own device for tasks such as generating text and classifying content. The preview works on 64-bit Windows PCs with Intel or AMD processors and on Macs with Apple silicon, but not yet on Windows on Arm. Opera says the feature is optional, that models download only after users enable it, and that site-specific permissions control which websites can access them. Opera also says its implementation supports models including Google's Gemma and, on compatible Macs, Apple's on-device foundation model.

The company says the approach lets developers add AI features without running their own AI infrastructure or paying for every request, and it argues that users keep their data on their own device without needing an AI subscription. Opera has said Opera GX and Opera Neon will get the same capability soon, and it plans to add models optimized for different hardware over time. Local processing puts more demand on the computer, so performance depends on the device's hardware, and Opera does not specify a need for a dedicated neural processing unit. Analysts quoted by Computerworld see the change as a possible way to reduce enterprise privacy risk, although the benefit depends on how organizations control access to locally running models.

Pareekh Jain, CEO of Pareekh Consulting, said that processing sensitive information locally could reduce the need to send data to outside AI providers. He warned, however, that it can be harder for IT departments to monitor activity on individual laptops than network traffic. Jain also said malicious websites could try to manipulate local models through hidden prompts, and that rogue browser extensions could reach sensitive information shown on screen. Tulika Sheel, senior vice president at Kadence International, said enterprises would still need controls over which websites and extensions can use local models and how those models and permissions are managed. She also said lower usage costs do not automatically mean lower total costs, since model updates and system integration still carry expenses.

Jain said smaller models could handle tasks such as summarization and rewriting on existing PCs, which could delay some hardware upgrades, while complex workloads will still need dedicated hardware or cloud services. He expects a hybrid future in which browser AI handles simpler tasks and cloud AI supports advanced ones. Opera's move comes as privacy concerns grow about the personal data users hand to AI chatbots, and Opera has made digital privacy a central selling point for years. The articles do not say when WebAI might become a broader standard or how widely enterprises will adopt it.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Rises 7% as Denmark AI Capacity Goes Live, Then Slips After Microsoft Capex Miss
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave closed up 7.32% at $63.93 on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, on heavy volume after new AI capacity in Denmark went live and AI infrastructure shares rebounded. Volume reached 58.3 million shares, about 53% above the stock's three-month average of 38.1 million. Oracle also rose sharply, jumping 10.73% after issuing a strong long-term revenue forecast. The mood reversed after the market closed, when Microsoft reported quarterly capital expenditures and finance leases of $45.2 billion. That figure came in below the $50.7 billion average analyst estimate.

Shares of CoreWeave and Nebius Group each fell almost 5% in extended trading, while IREN gave up about 3%. Alphabet also reported capital spending of $51.36 billion, below the $55.09 billion analysts expected. Microsoft said its Azure revenue rose 48% year over year, and it attributed the gap between its capex and its prior expectations to timing differences in payments and a lower mix of finance leases. Oracle gave back about 3% after Microsoft's report. Microsoft shares rose roughly 3% in after-hours trading following its separate earnings call.

Microsoft's earnings call also brought news of a forecast cut. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood lowered Microsoft's calendar 2026 capital expenditure forecast to $170 billion from $175 billion, a rare reduction in an industry that has mostly kept raising AI spending. Hood said some third-party capacity under GPU-as-a-Service contracts was delayed until the second half of the fiscal year. Business Insider reported that the delays are consistent with recent AI data center projects held up by electricity shortages and local opposition, though that link is an interpretation. Hood said the company expects capital spending to accelerate in the second half as the delayed capacity arrives.

CoreWeave's Denmark milestone matters because demand for its AI-ready cloud infrastructure exceeds supply, so new capacity begins generating revenue once online. The company reported a $104 billion backlog at the end of the second quarter and signed at least $25 billion in new customer commitments during the third quarter. It also had more than $35 billion in total debt by the end of the second quarter, and some of its unsecured debt has traded with yields above 15%. Investors are weighing how CoreWeave will fund the rest of its build-out, and that concern has weighed on the whole group. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk predicted over the weekend that more than 200 neocloud companies will collapse, and Gartner analysts told CNBC they expect 80% of neocloud companies to be absorbed or to cease operations by 2030.

After a steep selloff earlier in the month, CoreWeave had risen 18% over the three sessions before Wednesday's close. Wolfe Research analysts said in a note on Tuesday that they see the stock rebounding into the mid-$70s. CoreWeave went public in 2025 and has gained about 60% since its listing. Investors are now looking to upcoming earnings for more detail on backlog conversion and the company's debt-funding plans.

stories.Headline: Apple adds AI tools to Creator Studio in major update
stories.Summary:
Apple has added new artificial intelligence features and editing tools to its Apple Creator Studio suite, updating Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro, Keynote, Pages and Numbers. The update was announced on October 27, 2026, alongside new iMacs and a 14-inch MacBook Pro powered by the M6 chip. It will be a free App Store update for existing subscribers in November. The package brings MotionVFX content into Final Cut Pro, a new image-editing tool in Pixelmator Pro, video assets in the Content Hub, and beta assistants in Logic Pro and the productivity apps.

In Final Cut Pro for Mac, editors can now reach templates, graphics, titles, transitions and tools such as rotoscoping, tracking and colour grading without leaving the app. Apple has also added its Content Hub, which offers stock video, photos and backgrounds it curates. Pixelmator Pro gains Generate Fill, which changes selected parts of an image based on a text prompt and matches lighting, perspective and texture. Logic Pro receives a redesigned Browser, an expanded Stem Splitter that can separate drums, and a beta assistant built on Apple models and OpenAI technology. Keynote, Pages and Numbers get beta assistants that understand document context, along with Model Context Protocol support that lets external AI tools act inside those apps.

Apple's Brent Chiu-Watson, senior director of worldwide product marketing for apps and iCloud, called it the company's most exciting update since the suite launched and said the MotionVFX content gives subscribers rapid access to professional video effects. He also said the assistants in Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages and Numbers would change how people interact with and learn those apps. Apple has not announced an exact launch date for the new features beyond saying November. The new assistants will arrive in beta, in U.S. English only, on supported Apple Intelligence devices. Freeform will receive reusable text styles and new board background colours, and image editing and the generation of editable shapes from text will reach Freeform in December.

stories.Headline: Opportunities in China's AI undervalued
stories.Summary:
Schroders' Jason Yu told China Daily during a recent Beijing forum, held as part of the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 and hosted by the China Securities Regulatory Commission, that China's AI investment opportunities may be undervalued compared with global peers. The remarks were published on October 29, 2026. Yu argued that China offers long-term structural growth and diversification, since global AI gains have been concentrated in a few technology giants while China runs one of the world's largest AI value chains. Yu also pointed to innovative healthcare and advanced manufacturing as promising themes, and welcomed capital market reforms.

Yu said Chinese companies' ability to deliver cutting-edge technology at competitive costs adds to their appeal. He cited the Shanghai-based STAR Market's sci-tech growth tier as an example of how innovative firms can raise public equity before earning substantial profits. He also welcomed the CSRC's approval of the first batch of 18 actively managed exchange-traded funds. Yu added that these measures could broaden investor choice and improve financing channels for innovative businesses. Schroders, he said, remains committed to the Mainland-Hong Kong Mutual Recognition of Funds scheme and to serving mainland clients.

Yu's comments are a company executive's view, and the articles present them as his assessment rather than established fact. He stressed that capturing these opportunities means finding companies that can turn technology into sustainable earnings and building portfolios suited to client risk tolerance. His view fits with China's push to nurture first-class investment institutions and shift the fund industry toward investor returns. Yu said this requires strong research, risk management and local market knowledge. The articles do not describe any specific next steps beyond Schroders' continued participation in these schemes.

Separately, a Global Times report dated October 27, 2026, examined how Indian software firms may benefit from China's AI development. It described ManageEngine, an Indian-based division of Zoho Corporation, rolling out Zia AI agents for the Chinese market and planning to invest 425 million yuan over five years. Analysts quoted in that report said the two countries' strengths are complementary, with China leading in AI research and deployment and India in IT services. Some Indian firms are reportedly adopting Chinese open-source models such as DeepSeek to lower costs.

stories.Headline: China poised to lead in AI models by 2030, Bloomberg says
stories.Summary:
A Bloomberg Intelligence report, written by Ben Holland and published as an exclusive story, forecasts that China could lead the world in large language models by 2030 and become competitive in other strategic technologies. The study, led by analysts including Francis Chan, projects Chinese leadership in eight of 17 key industries, including the models underpinning artificial intelligence. Chinese companies are also expected to narrow gaps in chips and optical networking components, although full semiconductor self-sufficiency still looks unlikely. The findings suggest shared AI leadership between China and the United States, with neither clearly ahead overall. China is also expected to lead all three new-energy categories assessed, including electric vehicles and energy storage, along with biopharmaceutical manufacturing.

The report notes that the country already leads in humanoid robot production and parts of shipbuilding, and that it has matched US research and development spending. Chinese software optimization could support cheaper deployment of AI systems, even as American models may keep a narrow edge at the technological frontier. Planned changes to benchmarks such as the Hang Seng Tech Index could also broaden investor exposure to advanced hardware, AI and robotics. The analysts caution that these technological gains are unlikely to reverse the broader economic slowdown. Bloomberg Economics forecasts average annual growth of 3.6% over the next decade, compared with 5.2% over the past three years.

AI and automation could ease pressure from a shrinking workforce and weaker property activity, but the analysts said they cannot overcome those challenges alone. Profitability also remains uncertain, since Chinese AI companies face fierce price competition that is unlikely to ease until pricing becomes more disciplined. Trade tensions remain another obstacle, restricting access to foreign markets and advanced components. The analysts nevertheless expect those barriers to redirect the geography of Chinese industrial expansion rather than halt progress in the coming years. The articles do not specify any further timeline or policy steps beyond the 2030 horizon and the decade-long growth forecast.

stories.Headline: Biometric information on tourists necessary
stories.Summary:
Home Affairs Director General Mkhuseli Apleni has said it is necessary to take fingerprints from all tourists and travellers visiting South Africa, a position he set out at a Pretoria meeting attended by key tourism and immigration stakeholders. He argued that fingerprints help identify a person, particularly when a crime has been committed. The meeting, which the article dates to 7 December 2016, was held to discuss developments in the immigration regulations. Apleni stressed that taking fingerprints of everyone entering the country was important.

The Department of Home Affairs had introduced a biometric system the previous April that captures travellers' fingerprints at South Africa's international airports. The department said the system would be rolled out to six of the country's busiest land ports of entry. The system is currently used at OR Tambo International Airport and is expected to reach other major airports. Apleni said the department was working on ways to avoid delays there, particularly at OR Tambo, and that people do not have to wait long to have their fingerprints taken. He also expressed hope that other countries would adopt the same biometric system to reduce delays at ports of entry.

Aneme Malan, Deputy Director-General at the Department of Tourism, said her department was working closely with Home Affairs on visa regulations. She noted that the number of tourists arriving in the country had increased, but said the sector had not yet reached its potential and that some areas needed further engagement. The article also covers rules on children, which Apleni and the stakeholders emphasised. Since June 2015, stricter requirements have applied to anyone under 18 travelling to or from South Africa, whether a citizen or a foreigner. A Parental Consent Affidavit must accompany an unabridged birth certificate or equivalent document when a parent is not travelling with the child.

Parents travelling with their children can apply at any Home Affairs office for a fee of R75, bringing their identity documents and the child's abridged birth certificate, while South Africans abroad can apply at their nearest embassy. The article says the law is aimed at curbing child trafficking. According to Home Affairs, 132 353 children were processed in June 2015 across arrivals and departures, of whom 1 878 did not meet the requirements, leaving compliance at 98%. Foreign children numbered about 57 436 on arrival and 74 917 on departure that month.

stories.Headline: Lumion Highlights AI Agents for After-Hours Inquiries and Lead Follow-Up
stories.Summary:
Lumion, a technology company based in Salt Lake City, Utah, announced on October 27, 2026 that it is promoting AI agents built to handle customer inquiries, automated follow-up, and outreach to prospective customers. The platform combines AI-powered communication, workflow automation, and a unified inbox so organizations can manage calls, text messages, and website inquiries in one place. The company says the agents answer after-hours calls and other messages around the clock, and they can capture conversation details for employees to review later. The announcement targets a familiar problem, namely that inquiries often arrive when staff cannot respond, and delayed replies can cause prospects to move on.

The agents are meant to handle routine questions and record relevant context while leaving employees free to take over conversations that need more attention. A unified inbox gathers interactions from phone, email, and text so staff do not have to check several systems to see a customer's history. The platform also includes lead reactivation, which lets businesses reconnect with older prospects who never enrolled or completed a transaction. Lumion says businesses can start using the agents in as little as two weeks, configured around each organization's information and processes. Afterward, customers can extend the platform into application and onboarding workflows.

Lumion's chief statements come from Bilal Aslim, who is quoted in the announcement. He says a customer inquiry can arrive at any time, while a business team cannot always respond right away. According to Aslim, AI agents can help maintain continuity by responding to initial inquiries, capturing context, and supporting follow-up, so employees can concentrate on work that needs their judgment. The company presents the platform as a way to coordinate these tasks rather than to remove people from customer communication.

The announcement includes one customer example. At a career school, AI outreach to leads inactive for about two years produced two enrollments in the first week and 14 more over the following several weeks, with the first two generating a combined $10,000 in paid deposits. The articles stress that this reflects one customer's experience and that other organizations may see different results depending on lead quality and prospect responses. The company also says it has worked with more than 400 businesses and has managed and generated over $300 million in customer revenue through its platform. It further reports a $10.7 million seed round announced June 16, 2025, led by TTV Capital with participation from Tusk Venture Partners, intended to support market expansion and product innovation.

stories.Headline: SK hynix reports 632% surge in Q3 profit due to AI-driven demand for memory chips - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, the South Korean memory chipmaker, reported on Wednesday that its operating profit for the July to September quarter rose 632 percent from a year earlier. The company said the increase was driven largely by the artificial intelligence industry's strong demand for its advanced memory chips. Operating profit for the period reached 83.33 trillion won, or about $62.8 billion. Net profit climbed 215.7 percent to 39.77 trillion won, and sales reached 104.61 trillion won. The firm said this marked record revenue and operating profit for six straight quarters.

The results fell short of market expectations, as analysts had estimated net profit at 59.67 trillion won, according to South Korea's Yonhap news agency citing its own data. SK hynix also announced an additional plan to return 60 trillion won to shareholders, following completion of a 40 trillion-won shareholder return programme. The company's shares have been under pressure since June, when they retreated from record highs, and have fallen nearly 60 percent from that peak according to one professor cited in the reporting. Investors have pushed for more cash returns through dividends or buybacks.

SK hynix supplies high-bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia and is a pillar of South Korea's tech-led economy. The company's statement attributed its growth to a cycle in which AI-driven productivity gains and new revenue in software development, customer service and search lead to greater AI adoption. Market research analyst MS Hwang of Counterpoint said long-term agreements with major customers signal another phase of price increases across conventional DRAM, NAND and HBM. Hwang added that quarterly earnings have not yet peaked and that the upward trend will likely continue at least through 2027.

Not all observers are as optimistic about the outlook. Hwang warned that weaker AI spending, increased competition and the company's own capacity expansion could drive price volatility heading into 2027, and named a pullback in cloud providers' orders as the most severe threat. Kim Dae-jong, a business professor at Sejong University, said investors appear to be pricing in concern that current earnings levels may not be sustainable one or two years out. The reporting notes that the global race to build AI data centres has transformed the company's fortunes, even as worries grow that the sector may be overvalued.

stories.Headline: Harmonic AI expands Aristotle model for software and chip design verification - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Harmonic, the AI startup co-founded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev, said on Tuesday that it is expanding its Aristotle model beyond mathematical proofs into software and chip design verification. The announcement comes as the growing use of AI to detect software flaws is drawing more scrutiny. Researchers recently used the technology to uncover critical bugs in PHP, which set off a global rush to patch the vulnerabilities. Separately, Amazon is widening software support for its Trainium AI chips through its Neuron platform, a move reported by TechGig on October 20.

Under the expansion, Aristotle can now verify software written in C and chip designs written in Verilog. The tool is available with usage-based pricing. As an example of its capabilities, the US fusion lab DIII-D said Aristotle rebuilt part of its reactor-control software in four hours, working from one research paper and a 254-word prompt. Harmonic is developing what it calls mathematical superintelligence, a reasoning-focused AI system aimed at reducing hallucinations and factual errors.

On Amazon's side, the Neuron platform supports both Trainium AI chips and Inferentia accelerators. A key piece is the Neuron Kernel Interface, known as NKI, which gives programmers tools to create and fine-tune low-level operations for Amazon's custom silicon. AWS describes Neuron as a software development kit for building and running machine-learning workloads on its chips. NKI is aimed at developers who write specialized kernels, the small code segments that perform computations on the chip, and while that control can optimize particular workloads, it also requires them to learn new interfaces and adapt their code.

Harmonic is backed by Nvidia's venture capital arm, NVentures, along with Sequoia and Ribbit Capital. It raised $120 million in a funding round last November that valued the company at $1.45 billion. Amazon is the party behind the Neuron expansion, which it presents as a way for cloud customers to diversify computing supply and manage expenses. The articles do not include direct statements from either company's executives beyond the announcements themselves.

The Amazon effort targets Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem, whose mature tools and large developer community make switching hardware difficult even when alternatives are cheaper or offer more computing capacity. TechGig notes that customer adoption will hinge on software compatibility and the effort of migrating existing code. Companies weighing the platform will consider framework support, performance under their own conditions, reliability, availability and long-term support, and hardware savings could be offset if large application rewrites are needed. The articles do not say what comes next for either company beyond these adoption questions.

stories.Headline: AI-generated models spark job fears and image rights battle in fashion world
stories.Summary:
AI-generated models are raising alarm across the fashion industry after a Reuters investigation found that brands are seeking broad rights over models' images. Reuters interviewed 15 modelling agency directors and reviewed more than a dozen confidential contracts from brands including Diesel, Calvin Klein and L'Oreal. The draft terms asked for permission to swap model faces using AI, to create digital clones without extra pay, and to use body images to train AI tools. Many of the agreements also contained broad legal wording that would give brands wide discretion over how the technology is used.

The shift matters because AI can cut production costs by more than 90 per cent compared with traditional photo shoots. Agencies report falling bookings and some studios have closed, with e-commerce work for fast-fashion platforms, a key source of income for models, under particular pressure. London-based model Adot Gak warned that the industry could soon be dominated by bots if models do not speak up. Fast-fashion brands such as Mango have already adopted computer-generated models at scale, while luxury houses have moved more cautiously. Moncler said it does not currently use AI-generated models on its website or in promotional material.

Several companies responded to the findings, though not all gave the same account. Diesel's parent company, OTB, said the casting sheet was drafted for one campaign and does not reflect its standard contracts. Calvin Klein said it is testing and learning in a fast-moving space and that its use of AI follows regulations and respects the rights of its models. L'Oreal did not comment directly on the clause about altering product appearance but said it uses standard AI tools in post-production that leave model likenesses unaffected. Reale Actives said it hires real talent and blamed the contract language on a third-party production partner.

Legal protections remain uneven, and the New York State Fashion Workers Act is described as a notable exception. From June 2025, that law bars companies from generating or modifying model replicas without explicit consent. Sara Ziff of the Model Alliance is pushing for similar protections in other US states and at the federal level. In Britain, the British Fashion Model Agents Association has issued an AI code of practice requiring explicit consent, but its head, John Horner, warned that without binding rules, models remain exposed. Industry voices say young models may not grasp how long signed AI rights could affect their careers.

stories.Headline: Chinese investment in Vietnam expands into AI, other high-tech sectors, as businesses eye deeper cooperation
stories.Summary:
Chinese investment in Vietnam is expanding beyond traditional manufacturing into artificial intelligence, the digital economy and semiconductors, according to attendees at an investment forum in Beijing on Tuesday. The growing interest was highlighted at the China-Vietnam Economic, Trade and Investment Cooperation Exchange Meeting, jointly hosted by the Vietnamese Embassy in China and the China Overseas Development Association. Businesses there explored investment opportunities and possible partnerships in emerging industries. Vietnamese companies are also seeking closer cooperation with Chinese firms in advanced technologies.

Do Quang Tung, counselor at the Vietnamese Embassy in Beijing, described bilateral economic ties as marked by expanding trade, diversified investment and a clear move toward high-quality, technology-intensive sectors. He said China remains Vietnam's largest trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching about $256.5 billion in 2025 and exceeding $253 billion in the first nine months of 2026. Chinese investors registered $2.27 billion in newly licensed capital in the first nine months of 2026. China also ranked first by number of new projects, with about 850 in the first seven months of the year. Do said this investment is shifting from traditional processing toward railway links, clean energy, the digital economy, AI and semiconductors.

The presence of Chinese investors is already visible in Vietnam's industrial parks, where manufacturers are bringing businesses that sit along their supply chains. Bui The Long, general manager of Green i-Park Corp, said his park hosts 36 Chinese investors, mainly in electronics and electrical appliances, agricultural equipment and lighting products. He said upstream and downstream suppliers have followed these companies into the park. Earlier, Chinese investors were generally smaller in scale, while South Korean and Japanese firms made up a larger share of foreign investment, but Bui said large Chinese companies are now arriving. He also said Vietnam's AI sector is still at an early stage, and he hopes Chinese companies will develop AI projects there.

He Zhenwei, president of the China Overseas Development Association, argued that the next phase of cooperation should improve quality as well as trade volume, particularly in AI and the digital economy. He suggested AI cooperation could focus on localizing large-language models and big data applications in Vietnam. He said the aim should be local application of Chinese technologies rather than simple introduction, helping Vietnam advance industrialization and modernization. Do said the forum helped both sides better understand each other's policies and needs, which he called a crucial foundation for long-term partnerships. He called for more frequent exchanges and welcomed Chinese enterprises investing in high-quality, technology-intensive and environmentally sustainable projects in Vietnam.
