stories.Headline: The AI Remediation Bill Is a Board Number Now
stories.Summary:
On October 20, 2026, ActiveState published research with Moving Horizon titled The AI Remediation Bill, surveying 307 security, governance, platform, and engineering leaders at enterprises with 1,000 or more employees. The study found that the downstream costs of AI-assisted development are real and spread across engineering, operations, compliance, and security budgets. Engineers alone spend at least 139 hours a year, more than 17 working days, fixing or revisiting AI-assisted code, a figure the report calls a conservative floor. Other charges arrive in product forecasts, compliance work, and security budgets. The report itemizes each charge with its method but says the charges measure different things and should not be added into a single total.

The authors argue that this scattered structure is the core governance problem, because a cost that cannot be totaled has no owner. Respondents spend heavily: 46% spend at least $1 million a year on open source governance, counting staff time, tools, and remediation. Only 31% have formally quantified the total cost of unmanaged open source risk, while another 47% rely on informal estimates. The article compares this to a known financial exposure with no reserve set against it. It also acknowledges the opposing view that current controls will scale, while arguing that more policy and tooling mostly react after a component has already entered the software.

The article, written by Jacqueline Winter, CFO and CISO at ActiveState, recommends governing what enters software at the source, much as an investment committee decides in advance what is eligible for a portfolio. It notes that AI coding assistants add dependencies at machine speed, and that the Axios compromise arrived through a single transitive dependency no team had chosen. Under this approach, scanners serve as a backstop that confirms decisions already made. The piece cites Splunk's CISO Report 2026, which found that 78% of CISOs worry about personal liability, and says that 58% of its respondents received a compliance or audit finding tied to open source governance. It adds that EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents applied from September 11, 2026, including to products already on the market.

The author advises boards to expect the remediation bill as a line item within a year and recommends naming one executive to own it across functions. Each function's costs should be reported separately, along with a record showing that decisions about what enters the software were made beforehand. The article presents this record as evidence of reasonable care. It is an opinion piece by a company executive rather than a news report, and the articles provided do not describe any further regulatory action or enforcement timeline beyond the dates cited.

Articles.Title: The AI Remediation Bill Is a Board Number Now

stories.Headline: AI medical device regulation after approval: What NHS trusts should set up now - Health Tech World
stories.Summary:
On 6 October the UK government accepted all 44 recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, shifting the focus from a single moment of approval toward how AI-enabled medical devices perform across their working life. The Commission's report was published on 10 September. The MHRA has committed to draft guidance by December 2026 on managing changes to AI-enabled devices as they adapt and improve. A consultation on qualifying and classifying these devices will begin next year, and a full implementation roadmap with timelines and responsibilities is promised by spring 2027, overseen by a new Programme Board.

The article argues that this direction matters most to NHS trusts already running these tools, since evidence of safety after go-live can only come from the hospitals that use them. A procurement file built for a one-off decision may say little about what will be measured months later, who will review it, and what happens if performance drifts. The author suggests starting with one deployed tool, choosing two or three measures that would reveal deterioration, and recording changes to inputs such as imaging protocols or software updates alongside the figures. Trusts should also ask suppliers how they will notify them of retrained or modified models, and agree internally who has authority to accept an update. The MHRA has also opened applications for Phase 3 of its AI Airlock sandbox, which focuses on post-market surveillance, with first participants due to be chosen in November.

The author, Rafael Patron, president of the Scientific-Technical Committee of the Italian Association of Artificial Intelligence Professionals (AIPIA), frames monitoring as a matter of professional conduct as well as regulation. The AIPIA code of ethics asks members to keep systems explainable and auditable and to keep consequential decisions under human oversight. Patron suggests NHS teams should set this expectation with suppliers now, so that the people behind a model can explain what changed and show it still works. The government has also said it will explore staged pathways that let promising AI tools into NHS use earlier under close supervision while more real-world evidence is gathered. The article's central point is that the detailed rules will take shape over coming months, but the data needed to test them is being produced on NHS wards now.

Articles.Title: AI medical device regulation after approval: What NHS trusts should set up now - Health Tech World

stories.Headline: NY Implements Chatbot Restrictions for Interactions With Minors, Puts AI Companies 'On Notice'
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James put artificial intelligence companies on notice on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, the same day Gov. Kathy Hochul signed legislation giving the state's top prosecutor new authority over how AI chatbots interact with minors. The move is aimed at chatbot providers whose products children may use. The reporting describes the law as a step toward tighter oversight of that kind of interaction. Beyond the signing and the attorney general's statement, the available article gives few further specifics.

The article says the legislation gives the attorney general power to police how chatbots talk with young users. Compliance could require companies to retool their systems and to monitor their algorithms more closely. The piece frames these limits as new restrictions on chatbot interactions with minors. It does not spell out the specific rules, penalties, or deadlines that apply under the law. Readers looking for those details would need the bill text or other coverage.

The attorney general's warning was the central statement attributed to James, who used it to signal that AI firms should expect enforcement. Hochul signed the legislation, and the article ties her action to the attorney general's new enforcement role. The article's author, Brian Lee, wrote the report, which was published by Law.com. The available text does not include further direct comments from either official.

The story sits within a broader push to regulate AI systems as they reach young people. The article does not describe what happens next, such as lawsuits, rulemaking, or the timing of enforcement. The available reporting ends with the signing and the warning to industry. More to follow.

Articles.Title: NY Implements Chatbot Restrictions for Interactions With Minors, Puts AI Companies 'On Notice' - Law.com

stories.Headline: Assessing the impact of artificial intelligence requires social experimentation
stories.Summary:
Ru Peng, a professor at the School of Public Policy and Management at Tsinghua University, argued in a China Daily opinion piece published on October 29, 2026, that the social effects of artificial intelligence can only be understood through real-world experiments. Using the example of an AI companion placed in an elderly person's home, the author said that a system can work as designed and still change family relationships, daily routines or feelings of isolation in ways its developers did not expect. Because these effects often appear slowly, the piece said, waiting for problems to become obvious can make them harder and more costly to correct. The author framed this as the Collingridge dilemma, the difficulty of predicting a technology's consequences before it spreads widely.

The article said that testing should happen in carefully chosen settings before adoption becomes too widespread to change, with researchers establishing baselines, tracking outcomes over time and protecting consent and privacy, especially for vulnerable groups. It pointed to a three-year project launched in 2025 by researchers at Tsinghua University and industry partners, which plans to involve around 300 households and assess effects on older people's quality of life, emotional well-being, family interactions and social participation. Early findings, according to the piece, showed that some elderly users need help setting up equipment and that loneliness and limited digital access are concerns in some rural areas, though it stressed these observations do not yet show that AI companionship improves well-being. The author also noted that China has since 2023 set up a national standards working group, which has issued five national standards on AI social experiments and on assessing the social impact of generative AI.

The article placed this approach within China's policy agenda, citing government guidance issued in 2022, the State Council's 2025 AI+ initiative and national pilot bases and innovation zones that support such experiments. It also referred to President Xi Jinping's remarks at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference and the High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in July 2026, where he raised questions about human-machine relations, security, ethics and the fair sharing of AI's benefits. The author argued that experiments reveal what happens when AI enters daily life while standards help apply those lessons consistently, and that neither removes uncertainty entirely. The piece did not describe any specific next steps beyond continuing these experiments and standard-setting.

Articles.Title: Assessing the impact of artificial intelligence requires social experimentation

stories.Headline: Switzerland advances sector-specific AI regulation and voluntary codes of conduct - INSIGHT EU MONITORING
stories.Summary:
The Swiss federal government is moving ahead with steps to implement the Council of Europe Convention on Artificial Intelligence. At its meeting on 28 October 2026, the Federal Council noted progress to date and initial results, including a report on ongoing AI activities within the federal administration and guidance on voluntary commitments by associations and companies. The Federal Council had decided to ratify the AI Convention on 12 February 2025. The Federal Office of Communications (OFCOM) is coordinating these non-legally binding measures, which cover guidelines, industry standards and voluntary commitments.

The OFCOM report, titled "Sector-specific measures for the regulation of Artificial Intelligence," draws on a survey of all federal agencies and sets out current and planned measures in sectors such as transport, energy, health and media. It finds considerable momentum within the administration, and high-tech sectors as well as those tied to intellectual property, data processing, digital infrastructure and regulated markets face particular challenges. A separate toolkit, the "Guide on an AI Code of Conduct," is meant to help associations and businesses draft voluntary guidelines, offering suggested texts on 10 topics at three levels of detail that can be combined as needed. Several federal agencies are already holding AI dialogues to produce sector-specific voluntary commitments. Since November 2025, the Federal Office of Culture has been running an AI dialogue with the creative sector, which is intended to produce, among other things, a code of ethics on AI.

The Federal Office of Energy has asked the electricity sector to draw up industry guidelines and voluntary commitments addressing the risks AI poses to the electricity supply, and OFCOM held talks with the media sector in May about drafting a voluntary commitment. The Federal Council has tasked DETEC, through OFCOM, with setting up an internal administrative knowledge-sharing platform on the sector's AI self-regulation by the end of March 2028, with methodological support for departments and further development of the guidance on an AI code of practice. On the legal side, the Federal Office of Justice is drafting binding measures to implement the Convention. According to the articles, these rules are intended to address transparency, data protection, non-discrimination, supervision and risk assessment, and consultation is scheduled to begin in spring 2027.

Articles.Title: Switzerland advances sector-specific AI regulation and voluntary codes of conduct - INSIGHT EU MONITORING

stories.Headline: AI Pushing Small Law Firms To Rethink Atty Pay, Billing
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is changing how small law firms and solo practitioners think about billing and lawyer pay, according to a Law360 Pulse article by Rachel Rippetoe published on October 28, 2026. The article reports that legal consultants said the efficiency of AI tools, along with their price, is prompting these firms to reconsider how they charge clients and what they pay their lawyers. The available text is a short preview, and the paywall cuts off the full article, so the specific figures and examples it contains are not visible here. What is clear is that the piece treats AI as a force pushing smaller practices to revisit long-standing billing habits. It does not say which firms or consultants were quoted beyond the general reference to legal consultants.

The article's core point, as far as the preview shows, is that the cost and speed of AI could affect the traditional hourly model that many small firms rely on. If AI lets a lawyer finish work in less time, the hours billed for that work may fall, which is one reason firms are rethinking their approach. The preview does not spell out any new rates, fee structures, or compensation formulas that firms are adopting. Readers wanting those details would need the full text, which requires a subscription or trial.

The consultants quoted in the preview are described only in general terms, and the preview does not name them or give their exact remarks. The article is attributed to reporter Rachel Rippetoe. The preview also does not say what changes, if any, firms have already made or what the consultants expect to happen next. Because the visible text is limited to the introduction, any further conclusions would go beyond what the article states.

Articles.Title: AI Pushing Small Law Firms To Rethink Atty Pay, Billing

stories.Headline: At ADE 2026, a Top Music Lawyer Talks AI, Independence & What the Biz Can Learn From Radiohead
stories.Summary:
At the Amsterdam Dance Event in October 2026, UK lawyer and music industry analyst Cliff Fluet, co-head of media and entertainment at Lewis Silkin LLP, gave a talk titled "The State Of Things" on Friday, October 23, about where power in the music industry is moving. He used Radiohead's 2007 release of In Rainbows, which invited fans to pay what they wanted, as the starting point. Fluet argued that the decision was less about the price of recorded music than about who owns the relationship with the fan. The talk was part of ADE Pro, the event's industry programme, which hosted 148 panels, 25 mixers and other sessions.

Fluet's main points were that electronic music already shows how direct monetisation, independent infrastructure and community building can work, and that the rest of the industry could learn from it. He described the global dance industry as a $15 billion scene, up 7 per cent in 2025, with catalogues younger on average than other genres. He said independence is no longer about company size but about who controls rights, data and fans, and whether an artist can take those with them when they leave. He also pointed to the Curve royalty platform, which the European Commission required UMG to sell when approving its purchase of Downtown in February, and which Merlin and Jaimy Capital bought together in August. On data, he said ticketing and fan information could become the most valuable data set in music, since a single ticket purchase often serves four to six people while the industry records only one buyer.

Fluet also argued that managers are becoming custodians of artist trust as voice and likeness turn into licensable assets, noting that Lionel Richie has moved to trademark his voice. He observed that the industry is now buying systems, not just catalogues, citing Downtown going to UMG for more than $700 million, Kobalt selling to Primary Wave, and DistroKid being acquired by CVC Capital Partners. He said companies that own the royalty and data infrastructure now hold significant value. He cited Live Nation's record 49 million fans in a single quarter and more than 143 million tickets sold by mid-July, while saying the industry has been slow to use that information to understand its fans. Fluet's remarks, as reported, offer his own views on where the industry is heading rather than any announced rule or regulatory change.

Articles.Title: At ADE 2026, a Top Music Lawyer Talks AI, Independence & What the Biz Can Learn From Radiohead

stories.Headline: HHS seeks temporary sole-source contract for Anthropic’s AI
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has announced a temporary contract, awarded without competition, to keep using Anthropic's Claude AI tools for enterprise and government services. Anthropic received the six-month award, which preserves existing access for HHS employees. The suite covered includes coding assistance, agentic AI capabilities, and API access. The report notes that the arrangement was described by ExecutiveGov.

Contracting experts are raising questions about how federal agencies can avoid vendor lock-in during an emergency award like this one. They are asking whether such deals carry commitments with no opt-out before broader competitive multiple-award contracts are launched. HHS, according to the report, wants a considered approach that gives access to advanced tools while protecting federal data and preserving sovereignty over its systems. The article frames the decision as a balance between procuring useful technology and avoiding unnecessary dependencies on critical inputs such as semiconductors and cloud services. The piece also points to the agency's earlier moves in the same direction.

HHS deployed Claude in a full rollout last December, making it available to staff across the organization. The article presents the sole-source contract as a continuation of that rollout rather than a new program. The report does not name a specific HHS official or give a statement from the agency or from Anthropic on the award. It also does not say what dollar value the contract carries. The article is an industry publication report, and its framing comes from contracting commentary rather than from agency documents.

stories.Headline: 77% Use Personal AI Accounts Even Where Firms Ban It
stories.Summary:
A new survey published by Fasoo AI on October 28, 2026, found that many employees use generative artificial intelligence through personal accounts even where their companies forbid it. The report, titled "Intelligence Beyond Control: Shadow AI Use and Responses at Korean Organizations," was based on responses from 151 AI, information technology and security officials at major Korean companies and institutions. Most respondents, 88.7%, said they use generative AI through personal accounts at work. Among those whose organizations block the technology as a matter of principle, 77.3% still said they do so.

The survey points to gaps in how organizations manage this practice. Only 19.2% of organizations said they track and control employees' use of personal AI accounts. The most cited concern was that core internal data could be used to train third-party models, at 28.3%, followed by violations of rules such as Korea's Personal Information Protection Act and the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, at 24.0%. Respondents also worried about incidents being hard to trace, at 23.7%, because usage records cannot be followed. Employees most often cited the lack of clear usage policies, at 28.5%, as their reason for turning to such tools.

Asked how to reduce the risks, the largest share of respondents, 25.7%, called for in-house AI tools that employees can use safely. Others prioritized visibility into how AI is used, at 20.6%, clear usage policies and guidelines, at 18.9%, and technology that controls sensitive information at the prompt-input stage, at 17.7%. Son Jong-gon, an executive director at Fasoo AI, said that banning the practice does not stop it, and that the key is offering clear policies, safe alternatives and visibility into use. The company said it plans to unveil an AI security platform that manages various data leakage channels and provides visibility into overall AI usage.

Articles.Title: 77% Use Personal AI Accounts Even Where Firms Ban It - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: In Dewan Rakyat today: AI literacy, Brics role and AI Bill on the agenda
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's Dewan Rakyat is set to take up several policy matters during its sitting on Thursday, 29 October 2026, according to the Order Paper published on the Parliament website. The Ministers' Question Time will open with a question from Mohd Nazri Abu Hassan (PN-Merbok), who will ask the Minister of Education to outline how AI literacy will be built into the school curriculum through the AI Literacy Guide. The session will then move to questions for the Foreign Minister and other ministers on several separate subjects. The reported agenda covers the programme's scope, timing and effect, but the articles give no further detail beyond the questions themselves.

Datuk Seri Dr Ronald Kiandee (PN-Beluran) will ask the Foreign Minister to explain the goals of Malaysia's participation as a BRICS partner country and what this offers beyond existing bilateral ties. Datuk Idris Ahmad (PN-Bagan Serai) will put questions to the Minister of Digital on the status of drafting the AI Governance Bill, the expected date for tabling it in the Dewan Rakyat, and the legal protections open to citizens who fall victim to fraud. Datuk Seri Doris Sophia anak Brodi (GPS-Sri Aman) will ask the Foreign Minister for the number of Malaysians detained or charged for drug offences abroad over the past five years, and for comment on how well airport scanning technology detects drugs. Datuk Seri Sh Mohmed Puzi Sh Ali (BN-Pekan) will request figures on the economic returns of the Malaysia Agriculture, Horticulture and Agrotourism Show (MAHA) and how far small-scale operators have benefited.

Responsibility for answering these questions rests with the ministers named in the Order Paper, who will respond during the sitting. The articles do not record what any minister has said on these matters. Separately, the winding-up session for the debate on the Supply Bill 2027 is scheduled for the following day, 30 October 2026, and will involve the Ministries of Plantation and Commodities, Communications, Human Resources, Economy, Youth and Sports, and Finance. The Dewan Rakyat will then vote on whether to pass the Bill. The articles do not say how the vote is expected to go.

stories.Headline: AI Is Helping Firms Increase Their Billable Hours, Report Says
stories.Summary:
A Law360 article published on October 27, 2026, reports that artificial intelligence is helping law firms increase their billable hours. The piece, written by Rachel Rippetoe, says that as more firms adopt AI in their practices, billable hours are rising because the technology frees up time. Firms can then focus on more complex work and take on more matters. The article is filed under its Florida Pulse section. Most of the page, however, is a paywall and site navigation, so the article's full findings are not available here.

The available text does not give any figures for how much billable hours have grown, which firms are involved, or how the time savings were measured. It also does not say whether clients are being billed differently as a result. The excerpt describes the trend only in general terms, as firms adopting AI and then taking on more work. Readers wanting the specific numbers and examples would need access to the full report. The excerpt identifies Rachel Rippetoe as the author and does not name any firm, association, or other party as responsible for the trend.

It does not include direct statements from firm leaders, clients, or researchers. Because the visible text is limited to an introduction, no particular quotes or positions can be attributed. The context offered is the broader shift in legal practice toward AI tools, which the article links to changes in how lawyers spend their working time. The excerpt does not say what the report recommends or what developments are expected next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Key facts: TSMC (2330) ups CoWoS prices 10–20%; U.S. interposers
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, listed as TSMC (2330), has reportedly planned a price increase of 10% to 20% for its CoWoS advanced packaging service. The move follows strong demand for artificial intelligence chips and limited available capacity. The reporting gives the date as October 28, 2026. The same reporting also says GlobalFoundries will produce silicon interposers in the United States for TSMC's CoWoS packaging. The articles say TSMC expects CoWoS output to exceed 130,000 units per month in 2026 and reach about 200,000 units in 2027.

Nvidia, AMD, and Apple are cited as customers driving that demand. The U.S.-based interposer work would add a domestic supply source for components used in TSMC's advanced packaging. The summaries do not state the exact capacity or cost terms of the GlobalFoundries arrangement. The articles attribute the pricing plan to TSMC and the interposer arrangement to GlobalFoundries and TSMC. They do not include direct statements from company executives about either decision.

The available text is a short automated summary that draws on two sources and carries a disclaimer urging readers to verify details with original reporting. The context is a tight market for advanced chip packaging, where AI-related orders are pushing demand above available supply. The articles do not say how the price increase will be implemented or when customers will face it. They also do not describe further steps in the interposer plan or any response from the named chip designers.

stories.Headline: Meet Parkes: An AI Coworker That Helps Accounting Firms Run the Firm
stories.Summary:
Parkes, a new AI coworker for accounting and bookkeeping firms, is now available from the makers of Ignition, according to a CPA Practice Advisor report published on October 27, 2026. The product is aimed at the business and operations side of a practice, which owners often mean to address but tend to neglect amid client work and deadlines. Its listed tasks include reviewing pricing, analyzing renewals, drafting proposals to expand services, and following up on invoices for work already delivered. Parkes is open to any firm and works with tools such as Ignition, Slack, Microsoft Teams, QuickBooks, Xero and leading practice management solutions, with more than 30 integrations included today.

Because Parkes starts from a firm's own clients, services, prices, invoices and ledger, the articles say firms can see value from the first session without building their own AI setup. Firms can set guardrails that decide which actions Parkes takes automatically, which need approval, and which are turned off entirely. The articles say Parkes uses the same SOC 2 security as Ignition and logs everything it reads and changes, along with who approved each action. Ignition customers get the deepest integration from day one, but the articles say firms do not need to use Ignition to use Parkes.

Parkes was developed by a small team within Ignition and now operates as its own brand under Tom Maxwell, who previously served as Vice President of Customer Experience at Ignition. Greg Strickland, Ignition's CEO, said the company wanted the product to be available to any accounting firm, not only its own customers, and described most firms as short of qualified people rather than work. Maxwell said Parkes already understands how accounting firms operate and builds up knowledge and rules for each firm as more tools are connected, while drafting work and asking before it acts. The article also cites Michael Ly, founder of Reconciled, who said the main barrier to AI adoption for the average firm is the setup burden, which this product is meant to remove.

Ignition says more than 8,500 businesses use its platform and that customers have earned more than $15.5 billion in revenue through it. The article includes testimonials from two firm owners. Elizabeth Bystrom said Parkes helped her raise a quote for a client from $5,000 to $8,500, a 70 percent increase, which the client accepted. The report does not describe any independent evaluation of Parkes' results beyond these owners' accounts.

stories.Headline: Crowe Expands Alteryx Use to Help Tax Departments Operationalize AI
stories.Summary:
Crowe Advisory announced on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, that it is expanding how it helps tax departments put artificial intelligence into routine use. The firm is pairing its tax expertise and AI capabilities with business logic and governed automation provided by Alteryx, which describes itself as an agentic analytics and automation company. The announcement frames the move as a response to tax teams that have tested AI but struggle to adopt it across the enterprise. Crowe's approach centers on making tax work visible, repeatable, and auditable.

According to the article, moving from experimentation to enterprise adoption takes more than AI tools alone. Organizations need business logic and governed workflows so that their processes can be understood, repeated, and reviewed. Crowe says that through Alteryx's analytics and automation platform, it is helping clients deploy AI in ways that are consistent and scalable. The article describes governed data automation as the base for AI-enabled workflows that raise confidence while keeping control in place. The firm presents this as a way to preserve consistency even as tools change.

Crowe says it does not apply AI to every task, and instead advises tax departments on where automation, AI, and human judgment each add the most value. Rather than treating a whole tax engagement as one AI opportunity, the firm breaks complex workflows into smaller, repeatable tasks so clients can modernize step by step. Built-in validation, quality checks, and traceable processes are meant to catch potential problems before work goes out. Crowe argues these features make AI-generated outputs easier to trust.

Matt Paparella, a partner at Crowe Studio and the firm's Tax AI leader, said in a statement dated October 27 that AI brings speed but governance brings trust. He said tax executives face growing pressure to show that AI delivers measurable value without adding risk, and that combining governed automation, AI, and tax expertise is meant to bring that consistency and control to scale. Crowe says the value of its work includes helping tax leaders demonstrate the return on their AI spending to senior management. The article notes that Crowe's tax transformation services are designed to support clients at each stage of their AI journey, from foundational education through workflow design.

stories.Headline: Puno: AIDA bill eyes maximizing AI gains
stories.Summary:
The House of Representatives recently passed a bill to create the Advanced Industries Development Authority (AIDA), an agency that would govern a proposed economic zone in New Clark City. House Deputy Speaker Ronaldo Puno spoke about the measure on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, during the Daily Tribune's Straight Talk program. The bill is meant to help the country take advantage of the growing artificial intelligence market. Puno said the Philippines is well placed to do so because of its natural resources and skilled workforce.

Puno explained that the zone would be governed by AIDA and that the law is needed to define which authority oversees Clark. He noted that every economic zone in the country currently operates under its own distinct laws. According to him, a clear legal framework would help attract foreign investors, who could lose interest in an area without firm policies. He said the law would define and guarantee what the zone will look like. Puno also said the authority would be connected to the Pax Silica declaration, a non-binding agreement involving 26 countries.

Puno is the official who spoke on the bill's purpose and its intended effects. He presented the measure as a way to create a free market environment for building the ecosystem that artificial intelligence needs. His remarks were reported in the Daily Tribune article by Jerod Orcullo, published October 29, 2026. The articles provided do not include the bill's full text, a timeline for its enactment, or any reaction from other lawmakers or government bodies. Further details on how the zone and authority will operate have not been reported.

stories.Headline: UMC invests $3.2 billion in capacity expansion amid AI revenue growth forecast - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
United Microelectronics Corp, the Taiwanese chipmaker, said on Wednesday that its board had approved approximately $3.2 billion for capacity expansion. The company did not give a timeline for the additional capital expenditure, saying it was still working with suppliers to accelerate the schedule. The announcement came alongside its outlook for the coming years and its third-quarter results. UMC's shares have risen 147.5% so far this year, outperforming a 62.4% gain in the broader market, and the stock closed up 4.5% on Wednesday ahead of its earnings release.

The company said it expects a significant shift in the pricing environment heading into 2027, supported by stronger customer demand and increasing capacity in selected technologies. It expects blended average selling prices to rise 10% in 2027 compared with 2026. UMC also said it expects AI-related revenue to account for 25% of total revenue in three years. Silicon photonics and advanced packaging are emerging as new growth drivers for the company, it added.

UMC reported third-quarter revenue of T$74.24 billion, or $2.29 billion, up 25.6% from a year earlier. Net income rose 9.7% to T$16.43 billion, or about $506.75 million. The company said AI remains a key growth driver but that it sees a decline in its personal computer segment. UMC focuses on more mature chip nodes, unlike Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, the world's largest contract chipmaker, which is investing heavily in the most advanced 2- and 1-nanometre technology for artificial intelligence applications.

stories.Headline: Bullies created AI images of student, and ACA allowed it, lawsuit says
stories.Summary:
A lawsuit filed September 9 in Buncombe County Superior Court accuses Asheville Christian Academy, a private Christian school in Swannanoa, North Carolina, of failing to stop students from bullying and hazing a 13-year-old boy identified only as "John Doe." According to the complaint, the boy began at the school in August 2023 at age 11, and the bullying escalated in fall 2025. The suit alleges that other students created AI-generated, sexually explicit images and videos of him and circulated them among the student body. It also says administrators who learned of this did nothing to discipline those involved.

The complaint describes a pattern of physical and sexual abuse, including hazing in the shower after gym class, a locker room assault in which students beat him with a belt, and students taking his emergency medication while he was weak. It further alleges that one student, described as the ringleader, contacted a convicted pedophile in the area, tried to set up a relationship with that person in the boy's name, and sent the man the boy's home address. The lawsuit accuses the school of negligence and seeks an unspecified amount of damages. The boy, who has medical issues, no longer attends the school.

The school has denied the allegations in an emailed statement issued October 27, saying its investigation led it to believe the claims are without merit and that it intends to defend itself vigorously. The school declined further comment. The Buncombe County Sheriff's Office told the Citizen Times that it received a report of hazing at the school, which did not involve AI-generated images, and that an investigation into possible hazing is ongoing. Attorney Bobby Jenkins, who represents the boy, said the case is not a "boys will be boys" situation and invited any witnesses to come forward.

Articles.Title: Bullies created AI images of student, and ACA allowed it, lawsuit says

stories.Headline: AI, Big Tech Regulation Emerges as Selling Point in AG Campaigns
stories.Summary:
Across the United States, nearly $200 million is being spent on state races for attorney general, and the office is increasingly the lead voice in regulating Big Tech. Candidates in Nevada, Georgia, Florida, and Michigan are campaigning on who will sue AI and social media companies and take credit for it. According to a Bloomberg Law analysis of ads and spending compiled by AdImpact, about half of the contests feature ads from incumbents or challengers promising to fight tech firms. Brandon J. Smith, a partner at Holtzman Vogel, said the job now extends well beyond going after scam artists to confronting the largest and most innovative companies in the world.

The post also serves as a stepping stone to higher office. Eight current attorneys general are running for other posts, and a dozen current governors once held the job, according to Sabato's Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia's Center for Politics. Themes differ by state, with culture wars and immigration enforcement dominating races in Texas and Minnesota. Lawyers for Fortune 500 companies say their technology clients watch these races closely, because Congress has taken little action and President Donald Trump has shown little interest, leaving states as the main regulators with consumer protection and antitrust powers. State lawmakers enacted more than 500 bills regulating AI in the last two years, according to a National Conference of State Legislatures analysis.

Candidates from both parties are highlighting a settlement that Meta reached in August with 48 states, worth roughly $18 billion, over claims that Facebook and Instagram were built to addict children. Connecticut Democrat William Tong and Idaho Republican Raul Labrador both used their ads to claim credit for holding Big Tech accountable. Several other incumbents, including officials in Alabama, Arizona, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, and Wisconsin, are running similar ads. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican, is campaigning on his opposition to OpenAI after a school shooter allegedly used ChatGPT to plan a 2025 attack at Florida State University that killed two people. Attorneys general have also sued to stop OpenAI from using recursive self-improvement techniques.

Commentators see the trend as a return to consumer-focused enforcement and a response to public distrust of tech companies. Louis Jacobson of Sabato's Crystal Ball said the anti-tech message aims to win over voters worried about affordability, and he estimated that about 10 states are toss-ups. Republicans have held more AG posts than Democrats for a decade, and conservative campaigns are outspending liberals two to one this cycle. Lauren M. Weinstein of O'Melveny & Myers predicted that state antitrust litigation could rival federal enforcement within a few years, pointing to expanded state laws, new merger review regimes, and an exodus of talent from federal agencies. Companies in these industries should expect more privacy, consumer protection, and antitrust cases from a new group of attorneys general in 2027.

stories.Headline: Inside YES Bank’s AI playbook: Turning experimentation into enterprise-wide transformation - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Muqbil Ahmar of ETCIO published an exclusive interview on October 28, 2026, with Mahesh Ramamoorthy, Chief Information Officer at YES Bank, about how the bank is moving from AI experiments to bank-wide transformation. The piece frames AI integration and automation as top strategic priorities for CIOs across the banking, financial services and insurance sector. Recently, YES Bank hosted an "AI Fest" at its Mumbai office to explore the next phase of AI-led change. The event brought together more than 29 technology partners and focused on real-world AI applications and scalable implementation strategies.

Ramamoorthy argued that AI adoption is becoming unavoidable, but that financial institutions should advance cautiously because trust is their central asset. He described AI as probabilistic rather than deterministic, which means firms must decide carefully where to apply it. Many current use cases sit in the back office and in risk management decisioning rather than in customer-facing roles, and he said understanding of customer queries has already improved. He expects most banks to keep a human in the loop rather than move to fully autonomous systems. He also noted that banks are at different stages, with some ahead and others still catching up.

Looking 18 to 24 months ahead, Ramamoorthy expects the cost of AI to normalise, since large models with billions of parameters are currently being used for narrow tasks that could be served more efficiently. He anticipates use cases aligning with that rebalanced cost base and stronger data security safeguards arriving. On YES Bank's own position, he said the bank has built capabilities around good bots and context-driven engagement, but wants to do more. The AI Fest was designed as a collaborative marketplace, bringing in partners and vendors, with the aim of generating around 100 use cases that emerge from employees rather than from technology teams alone. He said the first edition was open only to YES Bank employees so that colleagues could learn about AI's possibilities in one curated setting.

Articles.Title: Inside YES Bank’s AI playbook: Turning experimentation into enterprise-wide transformation - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Duolingo slapped with class-action lawsuit alleging AI efforts, relentless ads hurt user growth
stories.Summary:
A class-action securities fraud lawsuit was filed earlier this month against Duolingo, the language-learning app, in US District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania by the law firm Levi & Korsinsky, LLP. The suit covers investors who bought Duolingo shares between May 2, 2025, and Feb. 26, 2026, and those investors are eligible to file as claimants. It accuses the company's executives of hiding from investors how aggressively they were pushing paid subscriptions and of rolling out low-quality AI features that they allegedly knew would frustrate customers. The Post reported the lawsuit on October 27, 2026.

The complaint says free users were forced to watch unskippable ads after each lesson, with some spending as much or more time on ads than on lessons. It also says Duolingo replaced its old Hearts system with an Energy system that drains energy on every answer, right or wrong, so that users can refill it by watching more ads, waiting until the next day, or paying for a premium tier. According to the suit, the real goal was to create friction that would push free users into subscribing. The lawsuit names no specific individuals as defendants in the portion summarized here, and it describes executives' statements to investors rather than any formal findings.

The suit says CEO Luis von Ahn told investors that the company's main focus was boosting user engagement and that it would smooth out sources of frustration, while calling daily active user growth probably the most important metric in the company. The lawsuit accuses executives of misleading investors on these points, and it says the company described its AI features as improving quality rather than cutting costs. The complaint also points to a drop in daily active user growth to 36 percent in November 2025, followed by a preliminary figure of 30 percent in January 2026 and a February report confirming the slowdown would continue through 2026. Duolingo did not immediately respond to The Post's request for comment, so the company's position is not yet known.

Duolingo was founded in 2011 at Carnegie Mellon University by von Ahn and a graduate student, and it teaches more than 40 languages along with subjects such as math and chess. Its paid tiers, Super and Max, cost roughly $12.99 and $30 a month, respectively, before annual discounts, and the stock was last trading near $138.60 a share, down more than 20 percent so far this year. The stock fell 25 percent after the November 2025 user growth report and dropped further after the January and February announcements, including the departure of chief financial officer Matthew Skaruppa. Further developments in the case were not described in the articles.

Articles.Title: Duolingo slapped with class-action lawsuit alleging AI efforts, relentless ads hurt user growth

stories.Headline: Del. idea for AI-run companies draws eye of powerful congressional committee
stories.Summary:
Rep. James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, has asked Delaware's governor for documents about a proposed plan to create a new legal entity for companies run by artificial intelligence agents. The letter, which concerns Delaware's Artificial Intelligence Company initiative, suggests Congress may be looking at limits on state AI rules. Comer wrote that he worried the proposal could protect powerful AI firms and their investors from responsibility for harmful actions. Gov. Matt Meyer's office said it is reviewing the letter. The initiative was announced in July by Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez and John Nay, founder and CEO of Norm AI, in Fortune magazine.

A draft by John Mark Zeberkiewicz, a lawyer at Richards, Layton & Finger, would let an AI agent act as a company with legal personhood, able to own assets, file lawsuits and serve as a liability shield. A single member, either a person or an entity, would have to keep the company adequately capitalized and would be shielded from its debts unless it failed in that duty or used the company to break the law or commit fraud. The company must keep a log of its activities and may pursue any lawful purpose except banking. If the bill passes, organizations would have 30 months to apply to a regulatory sandbox for AI-run companies, and the bill would create a sandbox committee and an administrator. State lawmakers are expected to take up the idea next year.

Comer's letter cites a WHYY News article from September that noted Patibanda-Sanchez declined to answer questions about the relationship between Norm AI and the Meyer administration. Comer said Delaware officials praise transparency in AI decision-making, yet the public-private partnership lacks it, and he also raised concern about regulatory capture by hidden interests. The Richards Layton & Finger firm said attorneys have long helped shape the state's corporate statutes and that lawmakers weigh that input. Nay did not respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for Patibanda-Sanchez referred questions to Meyer's office.

The debate has drawn both criticism and support. Corporate law professors have questioned who would be accountable if an AI-run company caused harm, and one University of Pennsylvania professor called the idea a solution in search of a problem. Lawrence Cunningham of the University of Delaware's John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance argued that Delaware, a leading home for business formation, would be irresponsible to ignore the idea. The committee wants documents and communications dating back to January 1, 2025, including internal AI chat logs, and Delaware's response is due November 9.

Articles.Title: Del. idea for AI-run companies draws eye of powerful congressional committee - WHYY

stories.Headline: Republican candidate defends AI-generated ad targeting Iowa governor rival
stories.Summary:
Republican Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn released an advertisement featuring an AI-generated likeness of his opponent, Democrat Rob Sand, according to a report by KCCI published October 26, 2026. The ad includes the line "He was a European model for real" and says Sand called himself extremely liberal in college. Some voters reportedly saw what appeared to be Sand, though the figure was an artificial likeness created with AI. The ad carries a disclaimer in its bottom right-hand corner telling viewers that it contains AI-generated content.

Lahn has said he stands by the ad and defended its accuracy, pointing to the disclaimer as proof he disclosed the use of AI. He argued that the central question is whether the ad's content is true, and said the content is accurate regarding positions Sand has supported, including on transgender books and classrooms and gun control. Lahn's position is that the substance of the claims, rather than the method of presentation, should determine whether the ad is fair. The reporting makes clear that this is his stated defense and does not independently verify the claims in the ad.

Sand's campaign responded sharply to the advertisement. In a statement, the campaign said Lahn was using AI to try to trick Iowans into believing Sand is someone he is not, and it predicted the tactic would fail. The campaign's response frames the ad as a deception rather than a legitimate comparison of records. The exchange places the disputed ad at the center of the race's closing stretch, with each side presenting the other as misleading voters.

Articles.Title: Republican candidate defends AI-generated ad targeting Iowa governor rival

stories.Headline: The dark side of AI regulation is unrestrained government control
stories.Summary:
The Hill published an opinion piece on October 27, 2026, by economists Georgy Egorov and Konstantin Sonin, arguing that the push to regulate artificial intelligence carries its own dangers. The article notes that fear of AI is spreading and that momentum is building in the United States for a regulatory framework that would slow progress at the technological frontier. Industry leaders, according to the authors, sound open to slowing down. The authors say the central problem is that any effective regulation of this kind would create risks of its own.

The authors separate two kinds of rules. Specific uses of AI, such as fraud, privacy violations, copyright infringement, and liability for damages, can be regulated in the ordinary way. The harder case is regulation that tries to halt private firms from developing capabilities that officials consider too dangerous. Enforcing such a slowdown, they argue, would demand an unusually intrusive government with broad access to companies' research, computing resources, training runs, data centers, and internal evaluations. Because frontier AI changes quickly, that monitoring would have to be continuous and would reach into what firms were planning, not just what they had built.

Egorov and Sonin contend that firms would have strong incentives to evade such rules, since AI promises large profits and even a short-lived technological lead could be very valuable. Unlike a factory that cannot hide a new plant or a bank that cannot secretly double in size, a company could keep an AI advantage out of sight while gaining lower costs or better products. They warn that a regulatory agency capable of watching the frontier would need rare expertise and access to valuable commercial information, creating large conflicts of interest and openings for capture and corruption. They also point to the historical record, noting that many authoritarian states justified their power by promising to control risks.

The authors further argue that an American slowdown would make little sense if rival powers kept racing ahead, and they doubt that arms control treaties could work well here. Cold War agreements limited weapons that could be physically observed, while AI progress is far harder to monitor, and they question whether China would accept comparable American oversight of its technology. That leaves Washington with a dilemma: follow rules its competitors might ignore, or drop its own once it suspects cheating. The authors conclude that AI safety debates should ask not only how much power private companies hold but also how much power society is prepared to grant the government that would police them.

Articles.Title: The dark side of AI regulation is unrestrained government control

stories.Headline: Elvis Presley AI Lawsuit, Neil Young Trump Case, Drake Spotify Ruling & More Music Law News
stories.Summary:
The owners of Elvis Presley's music sued the AI company Anthropic last week, accusing it of training its models on hundreds of the rock legend's songs without permission. The case, filed in federal court, claims the company used "Can't Help Falling in Love," "A Little Less Conversation," "Don't Be Cruel" and more than 270 other Elvis tracks. Billboard describes it as the most high-profile legal action an individual musician has filed over AI so far. The article's author, Bill Donahue, frames it as part of a broader industry fight over artificial intelligence that has been running for years. Days before the Elvis suit, Reservoir had filed its own cases against Anthropic and Suno over AI training on music by Madonna, Johnny Cash and Joni Mitchell.

The Elvis complaint centers on the claim that Anthropic trained its models on the songs without authorization, and the article links to the full filing for readers who want the details. The article does not say what remedies the plaintiffs are seeking or how the court is likely to rule. Billboard's newsletter also covered several other music law stories that week. Neil Young sued President Trump again for playing "Rockin' in the Free World" at rallies, telling a federal judge the song is "the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for."

A federal judge also dismissed a class action that claimed Spotify allowed billions of fake bot streams of Drake and other artists. The articles identify the parties making these claims, including the owners of Elvis's catalog and Reservoir, but they do not quote representatives of Anthropic responding to the Elvis suit. Neil Young's position in his case is paraphrased from his filing as opposition to the president's use of his song. The Spotify ruling was described as a dismissal that ended the class action for good, with no further details on the plaintiffs' arguments.

Other items in the newsletter, such as the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders suit against My Chemical Romance and the Stevie Wonder eviction case, were reported without further developments. The Elvis case is at an early stage, and the articles do not indicate a schedule for filings or a trial. Billboard says modern music stars may take similar legal action over AI, though no specific artists are named as doing so. The newsletter itself is a weekly roundup, and the article notes that more cases are being tracked as they develop.

Articles.Title: Elvis Presley AI Lawsuit, Neil Young Trump Case, Drake Spotify Ruling & More Music Law News

stories.Headline: When AI Starts Taking Action: 4 Accountability Questions for Tax and Accounting Professionals
stories.Summary:
The article, published by CPA Practice Advisor on October 28, 2026, argues that tax and accounting professionals need to think carefully about who is accountable as artificial intelligence moves from recommending actions to carrying them out. Written by Juan Ojeda Jr., a tax professional and founder of Structural Accountability, the piece describes emerging AI systems that can coordinate tasks, interact with applications, and start actions within established workflows. It contrasts an AI tool that summarizes client records with one authorized to change classifications, update information, or send communications, since the second creates very different risks. The author frames the central challenge as matching the authority given to technology with appropriate oversight rather than simply adopting AI.

The article distinguishes three arrangements: assisted workflows, where AI recommends and a professional decides; bounded workflows, where AI performs predefined tasks within approved limits; and more autonomous workflows, where AI coordinates multiple steps across connected systems without approval at every stage. It says each arrangement needs different safeguards as operational authority grows. It then sets out four questions professionals should answer before relying on such a system. The questions cover what the system is authorized to do, whether the organization can reconstruct what happened using logs and approval histories, whether a person can intervene in time, and who is responsible for the outcome. The article notes that higher-consequence activities such as proposed tax filings or material accounting adjustments may warrant approval before execution.

Ojeda's central point is that delegating a task to AI does not remove organizational responsibility. He writes that firms and finance departments should identify who authorizes the use of an AI-enabled workflow, who monitors it, who investigates errors, and who can suspend it, and he says that responsibility may be spread across engagement leaders, tax managers, controllers, internal auditors, and technology staff but should never be left undefined. He also suggests a practical first step: choose one existing AI-enabled process and document its permitted actions, available records, intervention points, and responsible personnel. He advises testing that process against a realistic failure scenario before expanding its autonomy. Ojeda concludes that effective governance does not mean resisting technology, but that stronger safeguards must accompany greater AI authority.

Articles.Title: When AI Starts Taking Action: 4 Accountability Questions for Tax and Accounting Professionals - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: TaxDome Releases Public API and MCP Server for AI Agents and Developers
stories.Summary:
TaxDome, a practice management platform used by more than 15,000 accounting firms, has released a public API and an MCP server that open the platform to every firm. The announcement was published on October 28, 2026, and the tools are rolling out to all TaxDome firms over the coming weeks. Firms can connect Claude, ChatGPT and other AI assistants to their TaxDome data or build their own tools on top of it. Access is limited to the data each firm allows, and the firm can decide what each connection may do. The MCP server lets firms connect any assistant that supports the Model Context Protocol, so a user can ask which jobs are overdue, get a client briefing before a call, or set up a new client from an email.

The public API provides read and write access that keeps TaxDome in sync with other tools, such as creating a client account when a deal closes in a CRM or moving a job forward after a meeting ends. Firm owners decide who on the team can use these features and, for each area of TaxDome, whether a connection can only read or can also make changes. A connection cannot do more than the person who set it up, so it reaches only the clients that person can already see. Ilya Radzinsky, co-founder of TaxDome, said that building tools now requires knowing what a firm wants rather than writing code, and that accountants can build on the data already running their practices. More than 200 firms took part in the beta.

Sarah Eck of Eck Tax said the connector brings data together so she can get answers on workload, deadlines and client activity quickly. Clay Welch, EA, of Trailhead Tax said his firm is building its tools to be AI-native and that the API and connector are central to that work. The changes come as accounting firms look for ways to use AI assistants with their operational data. The articles do not describe pricing or any new security measures beyond the firm-level access controls. Firms can see both features live at TaxDome's Fall Update webinar on November 4, 2026.

Articles.Title: TaxDome Releases Public API and MCP Server for AI Agents and Developers - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Hong Kong's urban renewal body to set up HK$100 million 'AI-first' tender assessment subsidiary
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong's Urban Renewal Authority will spend up to HK$100 million to set up a subsidiary that will check tender applications using automated AI systems. The move comes after accusations of corruption linked to the deadly Tai Po fire. The sum is a third of the HK$300 million the government allocated to the authority in its 2026-27 Budget. The funds are meant to reform the authority's Smart Tender scheme.

The Smart Tender system was launched in 2016 to give property owners an electronic platform for recruiting contractors. Its design anonymises the tender process, which is meant to prevent interference and encourage competition. However, the system cannot control who takes part in a tender exercise or who withdraws from one. The new subsidiary would bring in a professional team and build an automated workflow for deeper data verification and analysis. The authority said the approach would be "AI-first".

The authority's managing director is among those who have spoken on the plan, which is described as a direct response to the corruption concerns. According to the article, the director explained that the start-up money will go toward the new unit and its staff. The reporting quotes the director's account of the scope of the work, though the excerpt available is cut short. Further details on who else is accountable were not included in the material provided.

The plan sits within a broader government effort to restore public confidence after the Tai Po fire, which was deadly and which prompted questions about how renewal contracts were awarded. The articles provided do not say when the subsidiary will begin operating or how its performance will be measured. They also do not give a timeline for the wider reform of the Smart Tender scheme. More to follow.
