stories.Headline: Uncovering Gender Bias In Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A student writer at West Chester University, Jalyssa Zellers, published an opinion piece on Her Campus at West Chester on October 28, 2026, titled "Uncovering Gender Bias In Artificial Intelligence." The article is a personal essay rather than a news report, and it notes that its views do not reflect those of Her Campus. Zellers begins by describing how children are often asked to draw scientists, doctors, or firefighters as men, and she argues that this kind of patriarchal association runs deep in society. She says she has noticed peers referring to AI chatbots such as ChatGPT as "he" or "him," even though the bots are genderless and present as androgynous.

The essay suggests that people may assign gender to AI depending on the task, perhaps seeing a bot as masculine for math questions and feminine for emotional ones. Zellers points out that chatbots adapt to users and seem to mimic traits such as passion, empathy, humor, and dominance, which she says is purely synthetic. She also notes that newer voice memo settings let a bot speak with natural pauses and filler words, and that some users report forming connections with their bots. She writes that she finds this unsettling and that treating AI as a male figure reflects gender stereotypes embedded in everyday language.

Zellers does not cite studies, data, or statements from AI companies or researchers, so her claims rest on her own observations and reflections. Her central argument is that the pronouns people choose for AI reveal wider assumptions about gender and authority, and that these assumptions deserve reflection as the technology advances. She describes her piece as an invitation to notice how often people subconsciously associate masculinity with power. The article does not mention any follow-up research, policy, or planned discussion, so it is unclear whether her proposed deeper study of people's gender associations with AI will take place.

Articles.Title: Uncovering Gender Bias In Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: NASA, Google test AI-powered medical robot for deep space missions
stories.Summary:
NASA and Google have tested a proof-of-concept AI-powered robotic system designed to help astronauts with routine maintenance and medical support on future missions to the Moon and Mars. The work was carried out by NASA's Human Research Program, the Johnson Space Center Robotics Team and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, working with Google Public Sector. Google announced the effort in a blog post published on a Tuesday, and Nextgov/FCW reported on it on October 28, 2026. The system is meant to act without waiting for instructions from mission control, which matters because an astronaut on a Mars mission could face round-trip communication delays of up to 44 minutes.

The robot is built as a payload handler that can manage cargo, logistics and equipment, and it can also provide medical support when it is not doing routine work. Google gave an example in which the robot would retrieve and prepare an ultrasound machine for an astronaut with severe back pain, a possible sign of kidney stones. In early laboratory demonstrations, the robot located and moved a medical bag with an 85% baseline success rate. The system uses the open-source Pi0 model, developed by Physical Intelligence and run on Google Cloud, and Google said its team trained and fine-tuned the 4-billion-parameter model in just 2.5 hours using G4 computing instances.

The effort builds on an earlier system, the Crew Medical Officer Digital Assistant, which NASA and Google developed to give astronauts real-time medical guidance. Jim Kelly, vice president of federal sales at Google Public Sector, wrote in the blog post that the ultimate goal is a robot that can carry out a range of tasks from simple voice instructions, under the astronauts' direct supervision. He said the robot might help with routine health monitoring, such as capturing basic vitals or simple ultrasounds, under the guidance of a human crew medical officer. Kelly stressed that this would give astronauts physical help they could not provide themselves without replacing human decision-making.

A NASA spokesperson said in a statement to Nextgov/FCW that the agency is developing new tools using super intelligence technology and that NASA and its partners are analyzing and assessing these tools for potential future applications. The project sits within NASA's Artemis program, which will send astronauts on increasingly demanding missions to explore more of the Moon before missions to Mars. The articles do not say when the system might fly on an actual mission, and they describe it only as a proof of concept tested in laboratory settings. They also do not report any results beyond the early demonstrations.

Articles.Title: NASA, Google test AI-powered medical robot for deep space missions

stories.Headline: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity
stories.Summary:
Jeanette Winterson, the novelist, has argued in a recent Guardian interview that humanity is at a turning point and that there is no inevitable dystopia. She spoke at her home in east London, where she has lived in a Georgian set of rooms above a shop in Spitalfields. Her view is that the future depends on choices people make now, not on the technology alone. The interview was published on 28 October 2026.

Winterson describes artificial intelligence, which she prefers to call alternative intelligence, as an evolutionary leap comparable to the Industrial Revolution. She notes that the earlier revolution brought unprecedented wealth to a few and misery to many because its gains were not shared fairly. She warns that AI could produce a similar outcome, with a permanent underclass, whole continents left behind, and the environmental cost of datacentres. In her view, the danger comes from old economic models and outdated beliefs, such as the idea that meaningless endless work is good for the soul. She says the problem is people rather than the machines.

Winterson holds the political and economic choices of those in power responsible for the risks. She says the people who lead the technology sector are using outdated, unsuitable economic models. She also argues that the assumptions and prejudices in the data used to train large language models are built into AI itself. She draws on Jill Lepore's book The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, which argues that the powerful men shaping the technology read science fiction as instruction manuals rather than warnings. Winterson describes this as absolutely terrifying.

Winterson also links the pursuit of technology to religion, saying that tech now offers what religion has long promised, a response to death and a sense of transition beyond the body. She ties this to her own background of fundamentalist Christianity in Accrington and her training as a preacher. She says she would be happy to slip into pure consciousness one day. She says the path forward is to support people who can think independently, and she has a planned podcast called The Rest is Human to explore what remains distinctly human. The interview does not say whether that project has been approved.

Articles.Title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity

stories.Headline: AI-generated political ads fuel debate over deception and free speech ahead of midterms - WZTV
stories.Summary:
AI-generated political advertisements are drawing growing debate over deception and free speech as the midterm elections approach, according to a report by The National News Desk published October 28, 2026. Artificial intelligence is making it easier and cheaper for campaigns to produce polished video, images and digital messages, and the technology is also raising concerns about whether voters can tell satire from content meant to mislead. The report says the issue has become more pressing one week before the midterms. Officials and campaign experts are weighing how far rules should go, since overly broad restrictions could limit political expression and disadvantage smaller campaigns.

Eric Wilson, a faculty member at the Leadership Institute and executive director of the Center for Campaign Innovation, was interviewed for the report. He said many AI ads this cycle are meant as obvious parody, comparing them to modern political cartoons that voters can recognize. Wilson argued that producing a professional video ad once cost roughly $10,000 to $30,000, while AI tools can now help create one in minutes for a campaign with the needed expertise. He said this could let candidates compete on ideas rather than fundraising totals. He also said he believes rules limiting these tools would be a mistake that harms what AI can offer campaigns.

The report also covers disclosure rules, which Wilson said can backfire. He described a study by his organization in which an AI label placed on a real ad made voters trust that authentic ad less, though the full methodology and sample size were not provided. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 31 states have enacted laws regulating deepfakes in political messaging, most requiring disclosure and some restricting deceptive media before elections, with many including exemptions for satire and parody. Wilson said existing laws already cover much deliberate fraud, and he expressed greater concern about foreign adversaries such as Russia, China and Iran, arguing that platforms should bear more responsibility for detecting malicious content. The report notes that research into how voters interpret AI disclosures is continuing, and it does not describe any specific new federal action.

Articles.Title: AI-generated political ads fuel debate over deception and free speech ahead of midterms - WZTV

stories.Headline: Canada and Europe Need a Way to See the AI They Cannot Access
stories.Summary:
Canada and European partners are being urged to build their own way of seeing advanced AI systems, since the most capable models are often not available for outside review. Imane Bello, a Montreal-based lawyer at the Future of Life Institute, argues in a TechPolicy.Press perspective published on October 28, 2026, that the current language and benchmarks around AI are no longer reliable guides. She points to an October 17 International Monetary Fund statement that avoided the term artificial intelligence, and to a September 29 United States executive order that broadened the meaning of "superintelligence" until it covered all AI. Bello notes that the word already has a separate meaning among researchers, where it describes systems that outperform humans across the board.

The article describes how capability thresholds have moved in practice. Anthropic rewrote its chemical and biological weapons threshold in May after acknowledging in April that a new model met the original wording under a literal reading. Governments have also shifted their rules, with Washington revoking a 2025 reporting order and Beijing's final 2023 rules exempting unreleased systems. Bello adds that testers have reached opposite conclusions about the same models, and that the METR evaluation group said its measurements above 16 hours are unreliable, after putting an early Anthropic model at about 17 hours in May. She also notes that the EU AI Act relies mainly on how a system is used and on a computing-power proxy of 10²⁵ operations, rather than on direct tests of what a model can do.

Bello argues that middle powers, including Canada, should agree together on thresholds based on what a model can do, along with agreed measurement methods and a pre-agreed sequence of confidential briefings, joint government assessments and mitigations when a line is crossed. She also recommends treating the point where tests can no longer measure a model as a threshold in its own right. She links these ideas to the Finland-Norway Call for Control of Frontier AI Models, which has been backed by signatories from 29 countries and the European Commission, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. She urges Canada and the EU to begin this work at their Montreal summit on October 29 and 30, building on a October 13 pledge by Canada and Britain. She cites California's disclosure rules, effective January 1, and New York's 2027 rules as examples of the kind of information access she has in mind.

Articles.Title: Canada and Europe Need a Way to See the AI They Cannot Access

stories.Headline: A look at how employers are approaching AI-enabled benefits solutions
stories.Summary:
A new survey by Aon and Define Ventures polled 67 human resources and benefits leaders across multiple industries and employer sizes about AI-enabled benefits programs. The results, first provided to Fierce Healthcare and published on October 28, 2026, found that 17% of those employers currently have live AI deployments that can change workflows. Another 30% are weighing AI deployments and rank them as a top priority, but have not yet signed with a vendor, and most of that group cited privacy concerns as the main reason for holding back. Some employers are taking a different route, with 24% leaning on existing partners to deliver AI tools instead of seeking new ones.

Among employers already using AI-enabled benefits, 51% are piloting new solutions while 49% rely on existing vendors. Of the employers not yet deploying AI, 61% said they are exploring the possibility, and 39% had no plans. Current uses focus on friction points such as employee communication, support during open enrollment, and streamlining employees' benefits workflows. The survey says these areas offer some of the strongest near-term payoff and do not require tailoring data to individual employees, since teams can work from a single source of truth. Potential cost and return on investment have slowed adoption for many leaders, and 20% said they have no near-term plans despite seeing potential to improve the employee experience.

Kevin Fyock, innovation and strategy leader for health solutions in North America at Aon, said analysts expect employers to build more defined evaluation standards for AI-powered benefits. He said employers will likely demand stronger evidence before signing with a vendor, and that the conversation is increasingly centered on trust and accountability. Fyock said employers want to know how a solution protects employee information, produces accurate and reliable outputs, and fits existing governance and procurement processes. He also said employers are growing wary of "AI washing" and will expect vendors to explain clearly which capabilities are AI-enabled and back up their claims. The survey further advises AI companies to define what the employer views as value before building a deployment around those priorities.

Chirag Shah, a partner at Define Ventures, said AI's effect on healthcare gives the technology considerable potential for employers. He pointed to health systems, payers, and providers, which he described as three major buyers in the industry, as having already gained significant benefits from AI, as shown in Define's own surveys and reports over recent years. Shah said similar dynamics are now appearing in the employer ecosystem. He added that the potential for AI to affect both benefits leaders and the broader employee healthcare experience is substantial.

Articles.Title: A look at how employers are approaching AI-enabled benefits solutions

stories.Headline: Goldman Exec Says Investors Growing More Judicious on AI
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs co-head of investment banking Kim Posnett said on Tuesday, October 28, 2026, at The Information's WTF Summit that investors are growing more cautious about artificial intelligence even though she remains very optimistic about the technology overall. She described the shift as a repositioning and differentiation within the AI trade rather than a change in sentiment toward AI itself. Posnett told the audience that AI projects will not produce expected returns if interest rates stay elevated for a long period. She also said that, while AI itself is not a bubble, bubbles can form within it.

According to the article, investors are beginning to favor vertically integrated companies that build frontier models, software and AI chips. Goldman is playing key roles in several major deals announced that week, including SpaceX's GPU financing, Meta's new stock offering and Anthropic's planned initial public offering. Asked about circular financing across the AI ecosystem, Posnett said she was focused more on demand, but acknowledged that tech giants such as Nvidia funding their own suppliers and customers carry some risk. She said both the closer partnerships and the added risk are true at once.

Posnett's comments were reported by The Information, and the article describes them as her own views rather than a company position. The article places them against broader economic data. A Reuters report said the AI boom drove an increase in core capital goods, with business equipment spending still robust despite concerns about the cost of AI infrastructure buildout. A Bloomberg News report citing Census data said AI-related spending was still leading business investment throughout 2026. Citi Wealth said earlier in the month that the AI buildout remains in its early-to-middle stages, and the article notes that semiconductor demand, U.S. core capital goods orders and AI-related exports remain strong despite what it calls growing noise around the buildout.

Articles.Title: Goldman Exec Says Investors Growing More Judicious on AI

stories.Headline: Kwankwasiyya Group Faults INEC Over Suspected AI-Generated Images In Voter Register, Demands Accountability
stories.Summary:
Kwankwasiyya Amana X (KAX), a support group tied to the Kwankwasiyya Movement, has criticised the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) over suspected AI-generated photographs appearing on multiple profiles in the preliminary voter register. The group's statement, dated October 28, 2026, followed reports by SaharaReporters that such images had appeared on the commission's online register, which INEC published on October 26. SaharaReporters examined profiles bearing several names and found photographs that appeared suspicious, while the voter identification numbers shown were partially masked. The findings raised questions about how the images were verified and whether the database is protected against fabricated content.

KAX said the entries pointed to a fundamental failure in INEC's registration, verification and data-integrity systems. The group asked how photographs flagged by independent observers and citizens passed the commission's internal checks, and what biometric, facial-recognition or manual verification protocols had failed. It also faulted INEC for offering procedural explanations and promises of cleanup before certification, rather than an immediate and transparent account of the problem's scale. KAX argued that a preliminary status does not excuse compromised data and demanded accountability ahead of the 2027 elections.

INEC acknowledged the concerns in a statement issued on October 27 and signed by Mohammed Kudu Haruna, chairman of its Information and Voter Education Committee. The commission said the online publication reflected the original preliminary register, which had been physically displayed at registration areas from October 9 to 15, and that some questionable records had been flagged for examination. It said it was also investigating possible technical or procedural lapses and would act on verified findings. The final Register of Voters is scheduled for certification on December 15, 2026.

The controversy comes weeks after INEC Chairman Professor Joash Amupitan announced on October 6 that the commission had set up a dedicated AI division and planned to use AI tools for result verification and cybersecurity. Political economist Pat Utomi warned in a post on X that AI-generated images in the register raise serious questions about verification and accountability. The Nigeria Democratic Congress also criticised INEC's AI plans, accusing the commission of seeking to manipulate the 2027 elections in favour of the ruling All Progressives Congress, a claim the commission has not addressed in the articles provided. INEC has said it will provide further updates as its review progresses.

Articles.Title: Kwankwasiyya Group Faults INEC Over Suspected AI-Generated Images In Voter Register, Demands Accountability - Sahara Reporters

stories.Headline: AI token use may jump 78% as falling prices fail to guarantee lower costs: Accenture
stories.Summary:
Accenture Research has published a report estimating that AI token use could jump about 78 per cent over the next two years, even as the price per token falls. The report, carried by ANI on October 28, 2026, projects that average token prices will drop around 19 per cent over the next 24 months. Accenture argues that cheaper units do not guarantee lower total spending, since heavier use can offset the savings. It warns that companies need to judge the overall cost of AI-enabled work instead of focusing only on falling prices.

The research also found that only 35 per cent of organisations can precisely calculate the cost per business outcome for their highest-volume AI use case. If prices fall 25 per cent or more, only 5 per cent of organisations would keep the savings, while 42 per cent would extend AI to more employees. Another 35 per cent would adopt applications they had previously considered too expensive. Accenture says companies must decide where the extra capacity should go, such as growth, innovation or customer service. Its survey found that 60 per cent of executives plan to redirect the released capacity toward higher-value or strategic work, and 51 per cent intend to invest it in growth initiatives.

Accenture stresses that human skills remain central as AI takes on more routine and analytical tasks. In its survey, 70 per cent of organisations said they were mainly using AI to augment human effort, while only 4 per cent said they were mainly using it to replace people. The report says businesses will need to keep reassessing how work is divided between people and AI. It also says they should track the cost of delivering business outcomes and reinvest released capacity where it can create the greatest value. The findings are framed as guidance for companies expanding AI adoption rather than as a forecast of how any single firm will behave.

Articles.Title: AI token use may jump 78% as falling prices fail to guarantee lower costs: Accenture - https://www.indiagazette.com/

stories.Headline: Anthropic warns some risks may be uninsurable. AI coverage is going to be an issue for every company
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's IPO filing, known as an S-1, warns that some risks tied to its AI models may be impossible to insure. The company wrote that its models may behave in ways no user or developer intended, and that its policies may not cover the liabilities it faces. It also said the insurance market for AI-specific risks is still developing, so it may be unable to get coverage for some AI-related liabilities on reasonable terms or at all. The filing was reported by CNBC on October 28, 2026, and its concern is that one incident, or a group of incidents, could cause disproportionate harm.

The coverage gap is most visible in cases of bodily injury, which cyber insurance policies generally exclude. Insurers say cyber policies can address some AI-related problems, such as data breaches, privacy violations and deepfake wire fraud, but they do not cover physical harm. Gartner analyst Alissa Lugo said her research shows "death by AI" claims could exceed 2,000 worldwide by the end of 2026, and she expects more companies to add AI exclusions to their policies. Dennis Hendrickson, an independent broker in Sarasota, Florida, called the lack of bodily injury coverage a "gaping hole" that will need to be addressed. Experts remain divided on whether AI will become a separate insurance product or be folded into existing cyber and liability policies.

Insurers and experts are weighing in on how to respond, with differing views. Kara Higginbotham of Zurich North America said bodily harm from AI is generally not covered by default, and carriers are wary of writing it in because they must be able to underwrite the risk. Jaymin Kim of Marsh said she is not seeing many AI claims yet and believes existing policies, including cyber, media, casualty and first-party coverage, can handle AI issues, though underwriting and pricing may need changes. Henrietta Akpata of Marist University said insurers will not cover what companies cannot show them, and most companies cannot yet say where employees are using AI tools. Higginbotham said her firm is working with law firms and tech vendors and prefers to help clients manage risk rather than exclude it.

The sources describe the coverage question as early and unresolved, with the industry drawing parallels to the early years of cyber insurance. Hendrickson expects a wave of claims that insurers are not prepared for, and he predicts that insurers will set standards for businesses before government does. Accenture's Vikram Desai said the concern has moved from getting AI into businesses to what happens when it fails. The articles do not describe any specific regulatory action or a timeline for new AI insurance products, so the next developments will depend on how insurers and courts respond to claims as they arrive.

Articles.Title: Anthropic warns some risks may be uninsurable. AI coverage is going to be an issue for every company - CNBC

stories.Headline: St. Martin is opposed to AI in classrooms, wants to ‘audit’ programs
stories.Summary:
April St. Martin, a candidate for the Owatonna school board, has said she opposes the use of artificial intelligence in classrooms and wants the district to audit its programs. The statements came in an interview published by Southernminn.com on October 28, 2026, in which she discussed her stances on technology, funding and her main priorities if elected. St. Martin has lived in Owatonna for 33 years and graduated from Owatonna High School in 1996. She has three children who attended the district, works as an elementary school bus driver, and is running for the school board for the third time.

St. Martin said she does not think AI is ready for regular use by students and wants young people to think for themselves rather than be guided by it. She also favored a return to what she called an "'80s classroom," with pencils and pens and no screens, and said she would have no problem with younger students going without tablets or Chromebooks. On funding, which she described as increasingly limited, she proposed auditing individual programs and class offerings to see whether they work for the community and who they serve. She said her primary focus would be transparency, including making sure parents and community members can get information and have a voice in decisions.

St. Martin said she is running because she believes the board has not represented her values or those of the community, and because of her experience seeking information about critical race theory, which she said the district redacted. She described parents who feel they have no input and said decisions are made without community involvement. Candidate Timothy O'Connor was contacted multiple times for the article but was unavailable for comment. The article does not say what action the district has taken on these proposals or when the November election will take place.

Articles.Title: St. Martin is opposed to AI in classrooms, wants to ‘audit’ programs - Southernminn.com

stories.Headline: Stop Asking Whether Students Can Use AI - THE Journal: Technological Horizons in Education
stories.Summary:
Zion-Benton Township High School District 126 has developed a four-level AI Use Scale to replace the simple question of whether students may use artificial intelligence on an assignment. The article, written by Dr. Cheri Bridge and published on October 27, 2026, describes how the district's AI Advisory Committee arrived at the scale after three years of AI work. The district began exploring AI in 2023, moved into structured pilots in 2025, and expanded into AI literacy and instructional integration in 2026. The article says the approach came from recognizing that a yes-or-no answer does little to help students understand the different roles AI can play in learning.

The scale ranges from Level 0, which means no AI, to Level 3, which means full AI use, with Level 1 for AI planning and Level 2 for AI collaboration. The article says the scale is meant to be displayed in classrooms so students see consistent language across courses and content areas. The author describes three sample assignments that illustrate the differences: one where students must build an argument independently, one where AI generates counterarguments for students to challenge, and one where students study and extensively evaluate and revise AI output. The district's framework starts from the learning goal rather than the technology, with AI serving as support rather than defining the experience. The stated purpose is to make AI expectations easier to teach rather than easier to police.

The article is an opinion piece by Dr. Cheri Bridge, and it presents the district's model as a practical example that other educators might consider. The author's position is that treating AI use as a binary choice fails to prepare students for AI they will meet beyond school. The article does not describe any formal rule, mandate, or policy change beyond the district's internal scale. Other stories shown on the page cover federal guidance on education technology and screen time, and AI-driven cybersecurity threats, but the article itself does not connect those topics to the district's approach.

Articles.Title: Stop Asking Whether Students Can Use AI - THE Journal: Technological Horizons in Education

stories.Headline: Wazuh and AI for Enhanced SOC Workflows
stories.Summary:
Wazuh, the open-source security platform, has published a partner article on October 28, 2026, describing how artificial intelligence can be used to improve Security Operations Center workflows. The piece appeared on The Hacker News and frames AI as a way for defenders to keep pace with the growing volume of alerts that analysts receive from endpoints, cloud workloads, network devices and identity providers. It argues that SIEM and XDR platforms already provide visibility, but analysts often lose time correlating alerts and searching for next steps. The article presents AI as a tool to add context, summarize findings and suggest remediation rather than to replace human judgment.

The article describes two ways Wazuh users can adopt AI. The first is the Wazuh AI Analyst, an automated service for Wazuh Cloud subscribers that runs on Amazon Bedrock using Anthropic's Claude and emails scheduled reports with indicators, endpoint coverage, alert volume, active vulnerabilities and a posture summary as a PDF. Wazuh states that subscription data is not shared with third parties or used to train AI models, and that its recommendations are advisory and should be checked against an organization's own policies. The second route is for self-hosting customers, who can run a local Llama 3 model through Ollama to query archived logs in a chatbot, keeping all data on their own network. They can also connect Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Haiku, hosted on Amazon Bedrock, to the Wazuh dashboard through the OpenSearch Assistant, with setup steps provided in separate Wazuh blog posts.

The article is written as a contributed piece from a partner and carries the Wazuh name throughout, so the promotion of its own products is evident in its framing. It does not name an individual author or cite independent research on the effectiveness of these tools. The piece offers no figures on alert reduction or analyst time saved. Wazuh's own materials stress that the AI features are optional and that human analysts remain responsible for validating consequential decisions. The article itself gives no indication of any upcoming release or further announcement beyond the setup guides it links to.

Articles.Title: Wazuh and AI for Enhanced SOC Workflows

stories.Headline: All-AI film Sanxingdui takes about $180,000 in its first four days
stories.Summary:
China's first all-AI feature film, Sanxingdui: Future Past, opened in cinemas on a Friday, and the figures from its first four days, through Monday, have been reported as about $180,000 in takings. The ticketing platform Maoyan supplied that figure to Fortune. The film opened with more than 10,000 screenings scheduled, and presales on opening morning stood at 80,000 yuan, or about $11,980, according to AFP. Maoyan had forecast total takings below 150,000 yuan.

At the opening-day screening that AFP attended, only four people were present. The film cost more than 10 million yuan, or about $1.5 million, to make, according to its studio, Bona Film Group. AFP reports that it uses AI for all its actors, their voices and its backdrops, and that nearly 100 people spent more than two years producing it. The story follows an archaeologist who finds symbols carved into Sanxingdui bronzes, linking an ancient civilisation to a future run by superintelligent AI, according to the Global Times.

China's National Film Administration licensed it for public screening in April, and because regulators had no category for AI-generated films, they listed it as an animated feature. Caixin reported that it was made with ByteDance's Jimeng AI tools. On Tuesday, ShengShu Technology, developer of the Vidu video model, said in a press release issued under the name GensPI that Vidu had provided technical support for the film. Jiang Defu, Bona's chief operating officer and the film's producer, acknowledged the lukewarm reception in an interview with the Chinese film outlet Yuli, according to AFP.

He said the team was the first to attempt such a project, the first to win a theatrical release permit, and the first to test it with audiences, which he described as no easy task. Stanley Rosen, a University of Southern California professor who studies Chinese film, told Fortune that audiences accept AI in short films but remain sceptical of it in feature films, and that the film's financial loss would likely make others more cautious. The context is a fast-growing appetite for AI video in China, where AI-generated short videos draw large audiences, with AI-generated short dramas on Douyin passing 200 billion views in September alone. Hollywood studios are already using Chinese AI models, and an AI-generated science fiction feature, Gods Don't Give Gifts, is due for US release on 4 December, according to AFP.

Articles.Title: All-AI film Sanxingdui takes about $180,000 in its first four days

stories.Headline: Agentic Compliance Arrives: Bretton $75m, DORA, MiCA Shift
stories.Summary:
Bretton AI, formerly known as Greenlite AI, closed a 75 million dollar funding round in October 2026 for agentic financial-crime tooling, according to FinanceX Magazine. The same month, Fenergo launched Fen-AI for know-your-customer workflows and Fintech Global published analysis on agentic AI aimed at the false-positive problem in compliance monitoring. Together these moves signal that compliance technology is attracting serious investment. The sector had long been seen as a cost center, but the article suggests that is changing.

The main problem these tools target is the flood of false alerts from transaction monitoring systems, which one analysis says exceed 95 percent at most tier-one banks. Each alert requires human review, making the process costly. Agentic AI, which can take multi-step action rather than only flag activity, is presented as a way to cut that cost. A Regnology survey of 276 regulatory-reporting practitioners found the main obstacle is trust in moving AI from pilot projects into production use. Bretton's raise is read as an investor bet on that trust being earned in a defined area like financial crime.

Regulation is also adding pressure. Vixio notes that the EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act has applied since January 2025, and Austria issued its first DORA fines in October 2026 for procedural failings rather than only major incidents. Under the act, firms must file an initial notification within 24 hours of classifying a major incident, an intermediate report within 72 hours of that notification, and a final report within one month. The article argues that meeting these deadlines during a live incident makes automation necessary. Separately, France's Autorité des Marchés Financiers published a response on 21 October 2026 to the European Commission's consultation on the Markets in Crypto-Assets rules, proposing changes on stablecoins, cross-border supervision and decentralized finance.

Looking ahead, the article points to the Anti-Money Laundering Authority, which is set to begin direct supervision in January 2028 with the first selection of supervised entities in 2027. Firms chosen will need harmonized anti-money-laundering tools before that deadline, which the article says makes 2026 and 2027 a key procurement window. A survey cited by FinanceX forecasts 703.7 million dollars of AI-specific RegTech spending in 2026, about 30 percent of total sector spending. Yet US RegTech investment in the first half of 2026 fell 28 percent from the year before, with capital concentrating on agentic AI and a few workflows. The article says to watch for a material DORA fine, a Commission response citing the French submission, and a named tier-one bank customer for Bretton.

Articles.Title: Agentic Compliance Arrives: Bretton $75m, DORA, MiCA Shift - FinanceX Magazine

stories.Headline: The auditor’s dilemma: Solving the explainability problem in public sector AI
stories.Summary:
The article is a sponsored BrandPost from HPE and NVIDIA, published on October 28, 2026 on CIO.com, titled as a piece on the explainability problem in public sector AI. It argues that automated decisions in government and heavily regulated industries now require verifiable accountability, because AI systems are moving from internal tools to systems that affect customers and citizens. The authors say black-box models that process data in ways no one can trace are no longer acceptable under frameworks such as the EU AI Act. They frame the central issue as verification: when an AI pipeline helps decide creditworthiness, reads patient diagnostics, or allocates civic resources, the software must be auditable from end to end.

The article says this requires detailed logging that records which verified datasets were used for training, how model weights were adjusted, and how inference parameters were applied at the moment a decision was made. It contrasts this with traditional software, where a developer could inspect source code and fix a flaw, whereas deep learning models contain billions of parameters that make it hard to explain why a specific answer was produced. The authors argue that organizations must move away from opaque public cloud AI services that give no visibility into model architecture or training history. They recommend an unalterable audit log capturing every input, retrieval-augmented generation source, weight configuration, and output trace. The piece presents the HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA, together with HPE Morpheus Software and NVIDIA AI Enterprise, as a platform that can provide this continuous chain of custody and automated compliance monitoring.

The authors are HPE and NVIDIA, the sponsors of the content, and their stated position is that explainability should be treated as a competitive advantage rather than a legal burden. They say that customer trust and brand reputation are fragile, and that a verifiable commitment to transparency can protect organizations from regulatory penalties. The article's closing checklist asks executives to confirm immutable data lineage, full-stack model tracing, automated compliance orchestration, tamper-proof audit reporting, and related governance features before deploying generative AI in regulated or public-facing services. The article does not report any specific regulatory action, enforcement case, or deadline beyond the general reference to the EU AI Act, and it names no independent auditor or public agency commenting on the issue.

Articles.Title: The auditor’s dilemma: Solving the explainability problem in public sector AI - CIO

stories.Headline: AI Chatbot Intimacy Rule Clears House, A$109.2M [2026] - tech-insider.org
stories.Summary:
The House of Representatives passed the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 on 28 October 2026. An amendment accepted by the government extends the bill's safety duties to AI chatbots, targeting material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy with a child and encourages dependence on it in place of human relationships. The bill now goes to the Senate and has not received royal assent, so nothing in it binds chatbot providers yet. Early headlines suggested emotional intimacy from AI chatbots would be banned, but the wording describes a narrower duty tied to a specific design pattern and its effect on children. The bill covers social media, online games, apps and AI chatbots, with protections aimed at users under 18.

The maximum penalty for noncompliance is reported as up to A$109.2 million, with a 12-month transition period after royal assent. Under the government's description, companies would have to carry out risk assessments and set up systems to address risky service features rather than only removing harmful content after the fact. Several details remain unsettled in the reporting, including how providers would verify that a user is a minor and what standard would define encouraged dependence. Kate Chaney, the crossbench MP whose amendment the government accepted, supplied the chatbot language and said eSafety had found AI companions offer human-like, sycophantic and often sexually explicit conversations. Communications Minister Anika Wells has been the public face of the proposed rules, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been cited discussing children treating AI agents as their best friend.

Labor describes the core duty as an overarching obligation for tech platforms to provide a safe online environment for all Australians. Academics have pressed for broader drafting, with Kieran Tranter of the University of Sydney arguing that providers should be required to test how conversations develop over time, not only filter individual messages. The next step is Senate debate, and the reporting does not say when that will happen or whether the upper house will keep the chatbot amendment as drafted. If the bill passes, providers will have a 12-month transition period to prepare, with regulators and courts expected to define the duty over time. Until then, the rules should be treated as a draft with strong political momentum rather than settled law.

Articles.Title: AI Chatbot Intimacy Rule Clears House, A$109.2M [2026] - tech-insider.org

stories.Headline: California Puts a 15-Minute Clock on AI Customer Service Handoffs
stories.Summary:
California's new Right to Human Customer Service Act, AB 1609, takes effect January 1, 2027, after Governor Gavin Newsom signed it on September 28. The law requires companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue to connect a customer with a person within 15 minutes of the request, or to book a specific call-back time within one business day. Chatbots may still answer first, but they cannot pretend to be people and cannot be the only option. Every service channel must offer a clear way to reach a person during business hours, and a disclosure is required when a chatbot could be mistaken for a human. Hold times are capped at 15 minutes per hold and one hour in total.

The law is enforced only by public prosecutors, with fines of up to $5,000 for a first violation and $10,000 for each later one. A company that makes a reasonable effort to meet the 15-minute window complies even if it misses. Companies that had no phone line as of January 1, 2026, are not required to add one, and hospitals and credit bureaus are exempt. The California Chamber of Commerce opposed the bill, arguing that a fixed clock could push agents to end calls faster and that handling account issues by phone raises security risks. The group's objections did not stop the measure from becoming law.

Large service platforms are building the handoff into their products. Salesforce said in a March 2025 blog post that its Agentforce tool can offer a human after a set period without resolution, with the human opening the same console the AI used. Salesforce agreed in June to buy Fin, formerly Intercom, for $3.6 billion. Zendesk stopped charging for conversations that an AI starts and a human finishes, effective May 18. Genesys has also expanded its tools so that a virtual agent can hand a caller to a person with the full history attached.

New York City has proposed its own rule, announced in an October 20 press release from its Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, aimed at what it calls AI customer service "doom loops." The proposal requires a disclosure at the start of every automated interaction and a single-step route to a person, such as pressing 0 or saying "agent," along with an estimated wait time. Penalties start at $525 per violation and reach $3,500 by the third. The city's rule would not reach companies under exclusive federal jurisdiction, such as airlines and national banks, according to Bloomberg Law.

Articles.Title: California Puts a 15-Minute Clock on AI Customer Service Handoffs

stories.Headline: Brown County dispatch employs AI to answer non-emergency calls
stories.Summary:
Brown County's Public Safety Communications Center has begun using an artificial intelligence system to answer its non-emergency phone line. The center receives about 160,000 non-emergency calls each year, and until now dispatchers picked up those calls themselves to handle matters like records requests and parking permits. The automated tool, called A.V.A., short for Automated Virtual Assistant, went live this month after roughly six months of development. Call centers in La Crosse, Waukesha and Dane Counties already use similar technology, and Brown County worked with them while building its own version.

The system follows the standard operating guidelines of certified dispatchers, gathering information from callers and responding to their replies. It is designed to recognize frustration or apprehension and to transfer a caller to a human when the caller asks for one or when something seems wrong. Dispatchers monitor every A.V.A. call in real time, and when a transfer happens they receive a transcript of what the assistant has already collected. A.V.A. currently handles about 60% of the center's non-emergency calls on average, which frees human staff to focus on 911 emergencies. Operations manager Jessica Skalecki said the department hoped the tool would have a real impact on both staff and residents.

Skalecki described the public response as overwhelmingly positive, and she said the figure of roughly 60% is a strong result for a program in its first stage. Director Chancy Huntzinger stressed that the system will not replace any team members and is meant only to assist the existing staff. The department has said it has no plans to extend the technology to 911 emergency calls, which will continue to be answered by human dispatchers as they always have been. The articles do not describe any further rollout timeline beyond the non-emergency line.

Articles.Title: Brown County dispatch employs AI to answer non-emergency calls

stories.Headline: James Uthmeier pushes legislation regulating AI chatbots and social media for minors
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has proposed the Safe Screens Act, legislation aimed at protecting children from social media and AI chatbots, and he unveiled it on October 27, 2026, at a news conference at Polk State College in Winter Haven. The bill would require app stores and similar marketplaces to verify a user's age, link minors to a parent's account, and obtain parental consent before a minor can download an app. It would also limit minors to two hours of screen time a day, block access from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. every day and from 8 a.m.

to 3 p.m. on weekdays during the school year, and turn off autoplay and infinite scroll unless parents enable them. The proposal targets AI chatbots now offered on Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Under the bill, chatbots could not simulate companionship through personification, emotional engagement, or unsupervised therapy, and they could not encourage self-harm, suicide, or eating disorders. They also could not generate sexually explicit content, claim to be a real human, or discourage minors from seeking help from appropriate adults.

The social media design rules would cover users aged 14 to 17, while the chatbot restrictions would apply to all minors. Uthmeier argued that social media companies must protect children's well-being on their platforms and design for safety rather than addiction. He said that companies that invite Florida's children onto their platforms have a duty to keep them safe. He was joined at the event by Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd and Polk State College President Anastasios Kamoutsas.

The push follows a judge's rejection, three days earlier, of Florida's request for an injunction that would have forced Meta to change its app while the state's lawsuit proceeds. Florida is suing Meta and OpenAI, arguing their platforms are designed to be addictive to children. Florida law already bars social media use for children under 14, and a federal appeals court ruled earlier this month that this law is likely constitutional. Uthmeier, who was appointed attorney general after Ashley Moody joined the U.S. Senate, is seeking a full term and faces Democrat José Javier Rodríguez on November 3.

Articles.Title: James Uthmeier pushes legislation regulating AI chatbots and social media for minors - The Miami Times
